title: Transcendental Bliss.
thesis: Zhuangzi's claim here is not zoological wonder but epistemic surgery: the standards by which small creatures judge possibility are structurally inadequate to the scale at which Tao operates.

translation_literal:
In the darkness of the northern sea there is a fish called Kun. This Kun is so vast that no one knows how many thousands of miles across it stretches. It transforms into a bird called Peng. The back of this Peng spans no one knows how many thousands of miles; when it rouses itself and flies, its wings are like clouds draped across the sky. When the sea shifts and heaves, this bird sets out to journey toward the southern sea — that southern sea is the Pool of Heaven (tiān chí 天池).

The Universal Harmony is a record of marvels. It says: "When Peng journeys to the southern sea, it beats the water for three thousand miles, then spirals up on a whirlwind ninety thousand miles high, and leaves riding the winds of the sixth month." Heat-shimmer over the fields, motes of dust — living things blow one another about with their breath. The blue of the sky — is that its true color? Or is it that the sky is so far off it has no limit we can reach? When Peng looks down from above, it too must see only this same blue.

When water is not piled deep enough, it has no strength to carry a large boat. Pour a cup of water into a hollow in the floor and a mustard seed will float there like a boat; set the cup itself in it and it sticks fast — the water is shallow and the boat too big. So too, if the wind is not piled deep enough, it lacks the strength to bear great wings. That is why Peng must rise ninety thousand miles, so the wind is beneath it; only then can it ride the wind, with the blue sky on its back and nothing to obstruct it — only then does it set its course south.

The cicada and the little dove laugh at it: "When we make an effort and fly up, we can reach the elm or the sandalwood — and sometimes we don't even make it and just drop back to the ground. What is all this about climbing ninety thousand miles to go south?" One who goes to the green outskirts takes three meals and comes back with a belly still full; one going a hundred miles pounds grain the night before; one going a thousand miles gathers provisions for three months. What do these two little creatures know?

Small understanding cannot reach great understanding; short life cannot reach long life. How do we know this is so? The morning mushroom knows nothing of dusk and dawn; the summer cicada knows nothing of spring and autumn — these are the short-lived. South of Chu there is a tree called Mingling, for which five hundred years is a single spring and five hundred years a single autumn. In high antiquity there was a great Chun tree for which eight thousand years was a spring and eight thousand a autumn — these are the long-lived. Yet Pengzu is nowadays famous for his longevity, and everyone tries to match him. Is that not pitiful?

This is just what Tang asked Ji about. In the barren north there is a dark sea, the Pool of Heaven. There is a fish there, thousands of miles wide, and no one knows its length; it is called Kun. And there is a bird called Peng, its back like Mount Tai, its wings like clouds hung across the sky. It spirals up on a whirlwind, curling like a ram's horn, ninety thousand miles, breaking through the clouds and mist, bearing the blue sky, and only then heads south, making for the southern sea. A quail in a marsh laughs at it: "Where does it think it is going? I leap up and fly, and before I've gone more than a few yards I come down, fluttering among the brush and weeds — this too is the very best of flying. So where is it going?" This is the difference between small and great.

Thus a man whose knowledge fits him for one office, whose conduct suits one district, whose virtue pleases one ruler and wins the trust of one state — he sees himself just as those small creatures do. Song Rongzi would smile at such a man. Though the whole world praised him, he would not be spurred on; though the whole world condemned him, he would not be discouraged. He had settled the boundary between inner and outer, and drawn the line between honor and disgrace — that was all. Toward the world he was not anxious to rush about. Yet even so, there was still something he had not planted firmly.

Liezi could ride the wind and travel, cool and skillful, returning only after fifteen days. Toward the bringing of good fortune he was not anxious. Still, though he was spared the trouble of walking, he depended on something. But suppose one mounts the truth of heaven and earth, rides the shifts of the six energies (liù qì 六氣), and so roams the boundless — what would such a one need to depend on? Therefore it is said: the Utmost Person (zhì rén 至人) has no self; the spirit-person has no merit; the sage has no name.

Yao offered to hand over the world to Xu You, saying: "When the sun and moon have risen, and yet a torch still burns — as a source of light, is it not hard to justify? When the seasonal rains have fallen, and yet someone still waters the ground — as irrigation, is that not wasted labor? If you would take your place, Master, the world would be well governed, and yet I go on presiding over it. I see my own inadequacy. Please, let me hand over the world to you." Xu You replied: "You govern the world, and it is already well governed. Were I now to take your place, would I be doing it for the name? A name is only the guest of the reality — would I make myself into a mere guest? The wren nesting in the deep forest needs no more than a single branch; the mole drinking from the river needs no more than a bellyful. Go home and rest, my lord — I have no use for the world. Even if the cook fails to run the kitchen, the impersonator of the dead and the priest do not leap over the wine cups and platters to take his place."

Jian Wu said to Lian Shu: "I heard some words from Jie Yu — grand but groundless, going off and never coming back. I was startled and frightened by his talk; it was like the Milky Way with no end, wildly extravagant, nothing to do with ordinary human feeling." Lian Shu asked, "What did he say?" Jian Wu answered: "On the far-off mountain of Guye there lives a spirit-person, with skin like ice and snow, gentle and delicate as a young girl. He eats none of the five grains but breathes the wind and drinks the dew. He rides the clouds and vapors, drives a flying dragon, and wanders beyond the four seas. When his spirit is concentrated, he keeps creatures from sickness and blight and ripens the harvest each year. I took this to be madness and did not believe it." Lian Shu said: "Indeed — the blind cannot share in the sight of patterns and ornament, the deaf cannot share in the sound of bells and drums. But is it only the body that can be blind and deaf? The understanding can be so as well. These words of his describe you as you are now. Such a person, with such power, would gather all things into one — while the age begs him to save it from chaos. Why should he wear himself out over the affairs of the world?"
commentary:
This opening flight of the Zhuangzi works by staging scale against scale until every fixed measure of "big" and "small" comes apart in the reader's hands. Peng, whose wings blanket the sky, and the cicada who barely clears the treetops, both laugh — but the passage is careful not to simply crown Peng and mock the cicada. Peng too must wait for the sea to heave and the sixth-month wind to pile up beneath it; its greatness is a greatness of *dependence*. The cicada's error is not that it is small but that it takes its own horizon for the whole of what flying can be. The text then extends the same logic to time: the morning mushroom cannot conceive of a month, the summer cicada cannot conceive of a year, and even the eight-thousand-year Chun tree is only 'long-lived' relative to something. Pengzu, famous for lasting centuries, is pitiable precisely because people measure themselves against him — as if length of life settled anything.

What the story dissolves is the assumption that there is a single ladder of value that we can climb. Each creature sees from where it stands and calls that the summit. The provisioning image drives it home with dry practicality: a day-trip needs three meals, a long journey needs three months of grain — the preparation fits the distance, and neither is 'right' in the abstract. So the passage moves through a hierarchy of freedom — the competent official, then Song Rongzi who has stopped caring about praise and blame, then Liezi who rides the very wind — and refuses to stop at any of them, because each still *depends* on something. Even riding the wind is bondage if you need the wind. The vanishing point is the one who "mounts the truth of heaven and earth" and needs nothing external at all: this is the person with no self, no merit-seeking, no name to defend. Xu You refusing the empire and the spirit-person of Guye are two faces of this: real freedom is not achieved by getting a bigger stage but by no longer requiring one. The name is only the 'guest' of the reality; the sage declines to live as a guest in his own life.

Key Terms

**逍遙 xiāo yáo** — Free, aimless wandering or roaming; the untethered ease that is the chapter's ideal of freedom.
**六氣 liù qì** — The 'six energies' or atmospheric forces (yin, yang, wind, rain, dark, light); the sage 'rides' their shifts rather than depending on any one.
**至人無己 zhì rén wú jǐ** — 'The Utmost Person has no self' — the highest freedom is the dropping of a fixed, defended ego, along with the craving for merit and name.
practice: The next time you catch yourself measuring your progress against another person or timeline, pause and ask: what wind am I waiting for that I cannot see? Name one condition — a season, a relationship, a skill not yet ripe — that your current transformation actually depends on, then whisper it aloud as if the Peng itself were listening for your answer.

鯤之大，不知其幾千里也。
化而為鳥，其名為鵬。
鵬之背，不知其幾千里也；
怒而飛，其翼若垂天之雲。
是鳥也，海運則將徙於南冥。
南冥者，天池也。
齊諧者，志怪者也。
諧之言曰：「鵬之徙於南冥也，水擊三千里，摶扶搖而上者九萬里，去以六月息者也。
」野馬也，塵埃也，生物之以息相吹也。
天之蒼蒼，其正色邪？
其遠而無所至極邪？
其視下也，亦若是則已矣。
且夫水之積也不厚，則其負大舟也無力。
覆杯水於坳堂之上，則芥為之舟；
置杯焉則膠，水淺而舟大也。
風之積也不厚，則其負大翼也無力。
故九萬里，則風斯在下矣，而後乃今掊風；
背負青天而莫之夭閼者，而後乃今將圖南。
蜩與學鳩笑之曰：「我決起而飛，槍榆枋而止，時則不至而控於地而已矣，奚以這九萬里而南為？
」適莽蒼者，三餐而反，腹猶果然；
適百里者，宿舂糧；
適千里者，三月聚糧。
之二蟲又何知！
小知不及大知，小年不及大年。
奚以知其然也？
朝菌不知晦朔，蟪蛄不知春秋，此小年也。
楚之南有冥靈者，以五百歲為春，五百歲為秋；
上古有大椿者，以八千歲為春，八千歲為秋。
此大年也。
而彭祖乃今以久特聞，眾人匹之，不亦悲乎！
湯之問棘也是已。
窮髮之北有冥海者，天池也。
有魚焉，其廣數千里，未有知其脩者，其名為鯤。

我騰躍而上，不過數仞而下，翱翔蓬蒿之間，此亦飛之至也，而彼且奚適也？
」此小大之辯也。

而宋榮子猶然笑之。

雖然，猶有未樹也。

彼於致福者，未數數然也。
此雖免乎行，猶有所待者也。

時雨降矣而猶浸灌，其於澤也，不亦勞乎！
夫子立而天下治，而我猶尸之，吾自視缺然。
請致天下。
」許由曰：「子治天下，天下既已治也。
而我猶代子，吾將為名乎？
名者，實之賓也，吾將為賓乎？

偃鼠飲河，不過滿腹。

吾驚怖其言，猶河漢而無極也，大有徑庭，不近人情焉。
」連叔曰：「其言謂何哉？
」曰︰「藐姑射之山，有神人居焉，肌膚若冰雪，淖約若處子。
不食五穀，吸風飲露。
乘雲氣，御飛龍，而遊乎四海之外。
其神凝，使物不疵癘而年穀熟。
吾以是狂而不信也。

豈唯形骸有聾盲哉？
夫知亦有之。
是其言也，猶時女也。
之人也，之德也，將旁礡萬物以為一世蘄乎亂，孰弊弊焉以天

anchor_chapter: Zhuangzi's opening is scale-work, not natural history. Small creatures measure the world by their basin; what looks impossible from one depth is proportionate from another. Peng is not moral superiority over the cicada—it is the disclosure of a wider medium. The question is whether your standard of "realistic" names reality or only the size of your vessel.

若夫乘天地之正，而御六氣之辯，以遊無窮者，彼且惡乎待哉！
故曰：至人無己，神人無功，聖人無名。
堯讓天下於許由，曰：「日月出矣而爝火不息，其於光也，不亦難乎！
時雨降矣而猶浸灌，其於澤也，不亦勞乎！
夫子立而天下治，而我猶尸之，吾自視缺然。
請致天下。
」許由曰：「子治天下，天下既已治也。
而我猶代子，吾將為名乎？
名者，實之賓也，吾將為賓乎？
鷦鷯巢於深林，不過一枝；
偃鼠飲河，不過滿腹。
歸休乎君，予無所用天下為！
庖人雖不治庖，尸祝不越樽俎而代之矣。
」肩吾問於連叔曰：「吾聞言於接輿，大而無當，往而不返。
吾驚怖其言，猶河漢而無極也，大有徑庭，不近人情焉。
」連叔曰：「其言謂何哉？
」曰︰「藐姑射之山，有神人居焉，肌膚若冰雪，淖約若處子。
不食五穀，吸風飲露。
乘雲氣，御飛龍，而遊乎四海之外。
其神凝，使物不疵癘而年穀熟。
吾以是狂而不信也。
」連叔曰：「然，瞽者無以與乎文章之觀，聾者無以與乎鐘鼓之聲。
豈唯形骸有聾盲哉？
夫知亦有之。
是其言也，猶時女也。
之人也，之德也，將旁礡萬物以為一世蘄乎亂，孰弊弊焉以天

pratibha_layers.label: Pratibha Translation
pratibha_layers.body:
In the northern darkness there is a fish called Kun [*kūn* 鯤], immeasurably vast. It transforms into a bird called Peng [*péng* 鵬], whose back is likewise immeasurable. When it rises in full force, its wings hang like sky-wide clouds.

When the sea-winds turn, this bird prepares to move to the southern darkness, the Heavenly Pool. The old records say: when Peng makes this migration, it beats the waters for three thousand *li*, rides the whirlwind upward ninety thousand *li*, and then travels with the wind-breath of six months.

If water does not gather deeply, it cannot bear a great boat. Pour a cup of water into a shallow hollow and a mustard seed can serve as a boat; place an actual cup there and it grounds at once. The water is too shallow and the vessel too large.

So too with wind. If wind does not gather deeply, it cannot bear great wings. Only when the air is deep enough can Peng carry blue sky on its back, pass beyond all obstruction, and set its course southward.

pratibha_layers.label: Pratibha Commentary
pratibha_layers.body:
Zhuangzi's claim here is not zoological wonder but epistemic surgery: the standards by which small creatures judge possibility are structurally inadequate to the scale at which Tao operates. The contested move is this: what appears "exaggerated" from one horizon may be simple proportion from another. The cicada's ridicule of Peng is not ignorance in a moral sense; it is scale-lock, the inability to imagine conditions larger than one's own atmosphere. Zhuangzi uses the boat-in-shallow-water analogy to show that capacity is never intrinsic alone - it is relational to depth, medium, and context.

This matters philosophically because it destabilizes ordinary judgments about what is realistic, practical, or excessive. The text refuses a single universal metric for action. A life can be "too much" only relative to the basin in which one measures it. In Daoist terms, the sage does not force all beings into one register; he recognizes patterned differences in scope and timing. Peng is not morally superior to the cicada, but it discloses a domain inaccessible to cicada-consciousness. The existential application is immediate: whenever you dismiss a possibility as impossible, ask whether you are describing reality or merely the depth of your current vessel. Zhuangzi's opening move is to loosen identity from local scale so one can inhabit a wider sky without resentment toward smaller forms.

pratibha_layers.label: Practice (Abhyasa)
pratibha_layers.body: When you label a current aim "unrealistic," pause and write two columns: in the first, list the assumptions of your present scale (time, energy, identity, fear); in the second, rewrite the same aim as if your "air-depth" were ten times larger, then take exactly one concrete step from the second column today.

items.definition: from the graph of "road/path" and "speaking/guiding" -> in this passage, the tacit ordering principle that allows each being to move according to its own scale -> default translation "Way" can sound like a fixed doctrine, but here it means a dynamic relational field, which is why Peng's motion and the cicada's motion can both be lawful yet incommensurable.

"to wander at ease, to roam unbound" -> names the mode of freedom implied by Peng's ascent: movement unconstrained by cramped utility -> "free wandering" often sounds like leisure; Zhuangzi means ontological non-constriction, a shift in what counts as binding.

literally "without forced doing" (*wú* = without, *wéi* = contrived action) -> contextual meaning here: action that fits the depth of conditions rather than imposing narrow intention -> default translation "non-action" is misleading because Peng is not inactive; the teaching is unforced congruence, not passivity.

mythic fish and bird pair linked by transformation -> in this passage they model metamorphic scale: identity is not fixed substance but capacity across conditions -> translating them as "Leviathan/Rukh" imports Abrahamic and Persian mythic baggage that can blur Zhuangzi's point about transformation and proportion.

items.resonance: "What is night for all beings is wakefulness for the disciplined one." Both texts introduce scale-differentiated cognition: ordinary and awakened perspectives do not rank data the same way, so they disagree about what is possible.
items.divergence: The Gita frames this in terms of disciplined inward steadiness under dharma, whereas Zhuangzi frames it through perspectival plurality and spontaneous fit; the former stabilizes a normative axis, the latter pluralizes axes.

items.citation: Vijnana Bhairava Tantra, dharana on sky-like expansion of awareness
items.resonance: Both passages use vastness as a practical epistemology: enlarge the containing field and previously rigid limits dissolve.
items.divergence: The VBT interiorizes vastness into direct contemplative recognition of consciousness, while Zhuangzi narrativizes vastness through image and parable; one is explicit method, the other is perspectival reeducation.

items.citation: Nicholas of Cusa, *De Docta Ignorantia* I.1
items.resonance: Cusanus argues finite intellect cannot measure the infinite by finite ratios; Zhuangzi's cicada/Peng contrast makes the same structural point through allegory.
items.divergence: Cusanus resolves disproportion theologically through learned ignorance before the absolute, while Zhuangzi resolves it existentially through relaxed attunement to differing scales of life.

title: The Identity of Contraries.
thesis: The philosophical claim is sharper than "reality is uncertain." Zhuangzi is targeting identity-certainty itself: the self that claims to be the fixed subject of experience is retrospectively constructed from whichever standpoint is currently dominant.

translation_literal:
Ziqi of the Southern Wall sat leaning on his armrest, gazing up at the sky and breathing out slowly, vacant as though he had lost his partner-self. Yan Cheng Ziyou, standing in attendance before him, said, "What is happening here? Can the body truly be made like withered wood, and the mind truly be made like cold, dead ashes? The one leaning on the armrest now is not the one who leaned there before." Ziqi said, "Yan, isn't your question a good one! Just now I lost my 'me' — do you understand? You have heard the piping of humans but not the piping of earth; you have heard the piping of earth but not the piping of tiān 天, of heaven." Ziyou said, "May I ask what you mean?" Ziqi said, "The Great Clod belches out its breath, and its name is wind. So long as it doesn't stir, nothing happens; but once it stirs, then ten thousand hollows begin to roar. Have you alone never heard that long-drawn howling? In the mountain forests, the sheer heights, the hollows and cavities in great trees a hundred spans around — like noses, like mouths, like ears, like beam-sockets, like cups, like mortars, like pools, like puddles — they whistle, whir, shout, snuff, cry out, wail, moan, chatter; the wind ahead sings 'yu' and the wind behind answers 'yong.' A gentle breeze makes a small harmony, a whirlwind a great one, and when the fierce gust passes, all the hollows fall empty. Have you alone never seen the branches swaying and quivering after?" Ziyou said, "So earth's piping is just these hollows, and human piping is just pipes of bamboo. May I ask about heaven's piping?" Ziqi said, "It blows through the ten thousand things, each differently, and lets each be itself. Each takes for itself what it takes — so who is it that does the rousing?"

Great understanding is broad and easy; small understanding is picky and cramped. Great words are clear and calm; small words are chatter and quarrel. In sleep our spirits mingle; awake, our bodies open up to the world. Every contact becomes entanglement, and day by day the mind wars. Some are drifting, some deep, some tight-shut. Small fears leave us anxious; great fears leave us stunned. Minds shoot forth like a crossbow-trigger — this is how they preside over 'right' and 'wrong.' They hold back as though bound by oath — this is how they cling to winning. They wane like autumn and winter — this describes their daily wasting. They sink into what they do until nothing can bring them back. They shut down as though sealed — this describes them drying up in old age. Minds near death cannot be made to return to the light.

Joy and anger, grief and delight, worry and regret, changing and holding still, ease and abandon, openness and posturing — music from empty hollows, mushrooms from rising damp. Day and night these alternate before us, and no one knows where they sprout from. Enough! Enough! Morning and evening we come upon these — is this the source from which they arise? Without that 'other' there is no 'me'; without 'me' there is nothing to take hold of it. This much is near the truth, yet we do not know what makes it so. There seems to be a true ruler, but we cannot find any sign of it. That it can act is credible enough, yet we never see its form — it has reality but no visible shape.

The hundred bones, the nine openings, the six organs — all present and accounted for. Which shall I feel closest to? Do you delight in them all equally, or have you a favorite among them? If so, are they all mere servants and maids? Are servants and maids unable to govern one another? Or do they take turns being lord and subject? Or is there some true lord present among them? Whether we manage to grasp its reality or not, this neither adds to nor subtracts from its truth.

Once we receive this finished form, we do not lose it until it is used up. Grinding and clashing against things, racing along its course with nothing able to stop it — is this not sad? To toil one's whole life and never see the work completed, worn out and exhausted with no idea where one is headed — can this not be called grief? People call this 'not dying,' but what use is that? As the body decays the mind decays with it — can this not be called the great grief? Is human life really this blind? Or am I the only one who is blind, and are there others who are not?

If a person follows the mind already formed in them and takes it as teacher, who could ever be without a teacher? Why should it only be those who understand the succession of things and choose with their own minds? Even fools have such a teacher! To have 'right' and 'wrong' before the mind is even formed — that is like setting off for Yue today and arriving yesterday. That is making the nonexistent exist. Making the nonexistent exist — even the godlike Yu could not fathom it, so what am I to do?

Now, speech is not just blowing air; the speaker says something. But what he says is never fixed. Is there really something being said? Or has nothing ever been said? People suppose it differs from the chirping of hatchlings — but is there really a distinction, or is there none? How can the dào 道 be so hidden that there is 'true' and 'false'? How can speech be so hidden that there is 'right' and 'wrong'? Where can the dào go and not remain? Where can speech exist and not be allowed? The dào is hidden by small completions; speech is hidden by flowery display. So we get the 'right' and 'wrong' of the Confucians and the Mohists, each affirming what the other denies and denying what the other affirms. If you want to affirm what they deny and deny what they affirm, nothing beats using clarity (míng 明).

Every thing is a 'that'; every thing is a 'this.' From the standpoint of 'that,' one cannot see it; from one's own knowing, one knows it. So it is said: 'that' comes out of 'this,' and 'this' depends on 'that' — this is the doctrine of 'this' and 'that' being born together. Yet just as they are born they die, and just as they die they are born; just as something is allowable it is not, and just as it is not it is; depending on 'right' there is 'wrong,' depending on 'wrong' there is 'right.' Therefore the sage does not go that route but illuminates things by the light of heaven — and this too is just 'going by what is.' 'This' is also 'that,' and 'that' is also 'this.' 'That' has its own 'right' and 'wrong,' and 'this' has its own 'right' and 'wrong.' So is there really a 'this' and a 'that'? Or is there really no 'this' and 'that'? When 'this' and 'that' no longer find their opposite, this is called the pivot of the dào (dào shū 道樞). Once the pivot finds the center of its ring, it can respond endlessly. 'Right' is one endlessness, and 'wrong' is another. So it is said: nothing beats using clarity. To use a finger to show that a finger is not a finger is worse than using a non-finger to show that a finger is not a finger; to use a horse to show that a horse is not a horse is worse than using a non-horse...
commentary:
This chapter opens with a demonstration before it makes an argument. Ziqi sits in a state his student cannot name — body like dead wood, mind like cold ash. The student notices the change without understanding it: 'the one sitting here now is not the one who sat here before.' Ziqi's answer names the whole enterprise: 'I lost my me' (wú sàng wǒ). Not that the self was destroyed, but that the fixed, defended, always-comparing ego dropped away, leaving something that still breathes and gazes but no longer clenches. Everything that follows unfolds from this loss.

The three pipings are the structural heart. Human piping is bamboo flutes — deliberate, made, expressive of intention. Earth's piping is the wind moving through countless hollows, each shaped differently, each producing its own sound. Then comes the question that cannot be answered from inside the system: heaven's piping. Ziqi refuses to name it as a third thing above the other two. Instead he says the wind 'blows through the ten thousand things, each differently, and lets each be itself — so who does the rousing?' Heaven's piping is not a separate music; it is the whole event of sounds arising with no player behind them. The dissolved distinction here is agent versus action, self versus world. We assume that for sound there must be a piper, for the mind's turmoil there must be a ruler. Zhuangzi lets the assumption hang unanswered: 'there seems to be a true ruler, but we cannot find any sign of it.'

The long middle passage turns this on the human interior. Our emotions — joy, anger, grief, delight — arise 'like music from empty hollows, like mushrooms from rising damp.' They appear before us day and night, and we cannot locate their root. The mind that presides over right and wrong 'shoots forth like a crossbow-trigger,' clings to winning, wastes away like autumn into winter. The tragedy Zhuangzi diagnoses is not that we die but that we spend a whole life grinding against things, defending a 'me' that was never the true ruler in the first place. And then the crucial line: 'to have right and wrong before the mind is even formed is like setting off for Yue today and arriving yesterday' — an impossibility. Fixed judgments feel like they precede us; in fact they are our own manufacture projected backward as if given.

The closing section on 'this' and 'that' (shì/bǐ) delivers the philosophical mechanism. Every 'this' is someone else's 'that.' Right and wrong are not properties of things but positions relative to a standpoint, and each standpoint generates its own complete set of judgments — hence the endless quarrel of Confucians and Mohists, each affirming exactly what the other denies. Zhuangzi's move is not to pick a winner but to step off the wheel: the sage 'illuminates by the light of heaven.' The image of the pivot (dào shū) is precise: a door-hinge does not itself swing; it sits at the empty center of the ring and so can meet every position that comes around. To find that center is not to have no view but to no longer be trapped inside the reciprocal manufacture of opposites. The whole passage thus dissolves the deepest distinction of all — that between self and other, and between the affirming subject and the world it judges.

Key Terms

**喪我 (sàng wǒ)** — 'Losing the me' — the dropping away of the fixed, self-defending ego, not the annihilation of the person.
**天籟 (tiān lài)** — 'Heaven's piping' — not a third music above earthly and human sound, but the whole self-arising of things with no separate agent behind it.
**道樞 (dào shū)** — 'The pivot of the dào' — the empty hinge-center from which one can respond to every position without being caught inside the endless quarrel of right and wrong.
practice: Try this once today. When you next feel a strong emotional reaction — irritation at an email, anxiety before a meeting, a flash of being right in an argument — pause and ask, in Ziqi's terms, 'Where did this sprout from?' Watch for the hollow it blew through. You will notice the feeling arose on its own, unbidden, 'like a mushroom from damp,' before any 'you' chose it. Then do the 'this and that' reversal: state the exact opposite position and honestly say what someone standing there would see. You are not trying to agree with them or dissolve your view into mush. You are locating the hinge — the point where you can hold your own position while seeing it as one position among others, generated by where you happen to stand. Even thirty seconds of this loosens the crossbow-trigger of the judging mind. Done repeatedly, it is a small daily rehearsal of 'losing the me' — not erasing yourself, but unclenching the defended self just enough to breathe out and look up.

"The breath of the universe," continued Tzŭ Ch'i, "is called wind. At times, it is inactive. But when active, every aperture resounds to the blast. Have you never listened to its growing roar?

"Caves and dells of hill and forest, hollows in huge trees of many a span in girth;—these are like nostrils, like mouths, like ears, like beam-sockets, like goblets, like mortars, like ditches, like bogs. And the wind goes rushing through them, sniffing, snoring, singing, soughing, puffing, purling, whistling, whirring, now shrilly treble, now deeply bass, now soft, now loud; until, with a lull, silence reigns supreme. Have you never witnessed among the trees such a disturbance as this?"

"Well, then," enquired Tzŭ Yu, "since the music of earth consists of nothing more than holes, and the music of man of pipes and flutes,—of what consists the music of Heaven?"

"The effect of the wind upon these various apertures," replied Tzŭ Ch'i, "is not uniform. But what is it that gives to each the individuality, to all the potentiality, of sound?

"Great knowledge embraces the whole:

small knowledge, a part only. Great speech is universal:

Speech, according to Chuang Tzŭ's ideal, always covers the whole ground in question, leaving no room for positive and negative to appear in antagonism.

"For whether when the mind is locked in sleep or whether when in waking hours the body is released, we are subject to daily mental perturbations,—indecision, want of penetration, concealment, fretting fear, and trembling terror. Now like a javelin the mind flies forth, the arbiter of right and wrong.

Then, as under autumn and winter's blight, comes gradual decay, a passing away, like the flow of water, never to return. Finally, the block when all is choked up like an old drain,—the failing mind which shall not see light again.

"Joy and anger, sorrow and happiness, caution and remorse, come upon us by turns, with ever-changing mood. They come like music from hollowness, like mushrooms from damp. Daily and nightly they alternate within us, but we cannot tell whence they spring. Can we then hope in a moment to lay our finger upon their very Cause?

"But for these emotions I should not be. But for me, they would have no scope. So far we can go; but we do not know what it is that brings them into play. 'Twould seem to be a soul; but the clue to its existence is wanting. That such a Power operates, is credible enough, though we cannot see its form. It has functions without form.

As will be gathered later on, Chuang Tzŭ conceives of the soul as an emanation from God, passing to and from this earth through the portals of Life and Death.

"Take the human body with all its manifold divisions. Which part of it does a man love best? Does he not cherish all equally, or has he a preference? Do not all equally serve him? And do these servitors then govern themselves, or are they subdivided into rulers and subjects? Surely there is some soul which sways them all.

"But whether or not we ascertain what are the functions of this soul, it matters but little to the soul itself. For coming into existence with this mortal coil of mine, with the exhaustion of this mortal coil its mandate will also be exhausted. To be harassed by the wear and tear of life, and to pass rapidly through it without possibility of arresting one's course,—is not this pitiful indeed? To labour without ceasing, and then, without living to enjoy the fruit, worn out, to depart, suddenly, one knows not whither,—is not that a just cause for grief?

"What advantage is there in what men call not dying? The body decomposes, and the mind goes with it. This is our real cause for sorrow. Can the world be so dull as not to see this? Or is it I alone who am dull, and others not so?

"If we are to be guided by the criteria of our own minds, who shall be without a guide?

The mind should be a tabula rasa, free from all judgments or opinions of its own as to the external world, and ready only to accept things as they are, not as they appear to be.

What need to know of the alternations of passion,

when the mind thus affords scope to itself?—verily even the minds of fools! Whereas, for a mind without criteria

Or, like placing nowhere somewhere,—topography which even the Great Yü

The famous engineer of antiquity (B.C. 2205), who drained the empire of a vast body of water and arranged its subdivision into nine provinces.

would fail to understand; how much more I?

"Speech is not mere breath. It is differentiated by meaning. Take away that, and you cannot say whether it is speech or not. Can you even distinguish it from the chirping of young birds?

"But how can Tao be so obscured that we speak of it as true and false? And how can speech be so obscured that it admits the idea of contraries? How can Tao go away and yet not remain?

How can speech exist and yet be impossible?

Hence the affirmatives and negatives of the Confucian and Mihist schools,

Mih Tzŭ was a philosopher of the fourth century B.C., who propounded various theories which were vigorously attacked by the Confucianists under Mencius. We shall hear more of him by-and-by.

each denying what the other affirmed and affirming what the other denied. But he who would reconcile affirmative with negative and negative with affirmative,

"There is nothing which is not objective: there is nothing which is not subjective. But it is impossible to start from the objective. Only from subjective knowledge is it possible to proceed to objective knowledge. Hence it has been said,

'The objective emanates from the subjective; the subjective is consequent upon the objective. This is the Alternation Theory.' Nevertheless, when one is born, the other dies. When one is possible, the other is impossible. When one is affirmative the other is negative. Which being the case, the true sage rejects all distinctions of this and that. He takes his refuge in God, and places himself in subjective relation with all things.

It was to this end that Tzŭ Ch'i "buried himself."

"And inasmuch as the subjective is also objective, and the objective also subjective, and as the contraries under each are indistinguishably blended, does it not become impossible for us to say whether subjective and objective really exist at all?

What is positive under the one will be negative under the other. Yet as subjective and objective are really one and the same, their positives and negatives must also be one and the same.

It is as though we were to view them through a kind of mental Pseudoscope, by which means each would appear to be the other.

"When subjective and objective are both without their correlates, that is the very axis of Tao. And when that axis passes through the centre at which all Infinities converge, positive and negative alike blend into an infinite One. Hence it has been said that there is nothing like the light of nature.

Probably an allusion to Lao Tzŭ's "Use the light that is within you to revert to your natural clearness of sight." We should then be able to view things in their true light. See Tao-Tê-Ching, ch. lii., and The Remains of Lao Tzŭ, p. 34.

"To take a finger in illustration of a finger not being a finger is not so good as to take something which is not a finger. To take a horse in illustration of a horse not being a horse is not so good as to take something which is not a horse.

"So with the universe and all that in it is. These things are but fingers and horses in this sense. The possible is possible: the impossible is impossible. Tao operates, and given results follow. Things receive names and are what they are. They achieve this by their natural affinity for what they are and their natural antagonism to what they are not. For all things have their own particular constitutions and potentialities. Nothing can exist without these.

"We can never know anything but phenomena. Things are what they are, and their consequences will be what they will be."—J. S. Mill.

So are ugliness and beauty, greatness, wickedness, perverseness, and strangeness. Separation is the same as construction: construction is the same as destruction. Nothing is subject either to construction or to destruction, for these conditions are brought together into One.

"Only the truly intelligent understand this principle of the identity of all things. They do not view things as apprehended by themselves, subjectively; but transfer themselves into the position of the things viewed.

And viewing them thus they are able to comprehend them, nay, to master them;—and he who can master them is near. So it is that to place oneself in subjective relation with externals, without consciousness of their objectivity,—this is Tao. But to wear out one's intellect in an obstinate adherence to the individuality of things, not recognising the fact that all things are One,—this is called Three in the Morning."

"A keeper of monkeys," replied Tzŭ Ch'i, "said with regard to their rations of chestnuts that each monkey was to have three in the morning and four at night. But at this the monkeys were very angry, so the keeper said they might have four in the morning and three at night, with which arrangement they were all well pleased. The actual number of the chestnuts remained the same, but there was an adaptation to the likes and dislikes of those concerned. Such is the principle of putting oneself into subjective relation with externals.

"Wherefore the true Sage, while regarding contraries as identical, adapts himself to the laws of Heaven. This is called following two courses at once.

He is thus prevented from trying to walk through walls, etc., as later Taoists have professed themselves able to do, of course with a view to gull the public and enrich themselves. "God," says Locke, "when he makes the prophet, does not unmake the man."

So Carlyle in his essay on Novalis:—"To a Transcendentalist, matter has an existence but only as a Phenomenon.... It is a mere relation, or rather the result of a relation between our living souls and the great First Cause."

"The knowledge of the men of old had a limit. It extended back to a period when matter did not exist. That was the extreme point to which their knowledge reached.

By time or space. "Being, in itself," says Herbert Spencer, "out of relation, is itself unthinkable." Principles of Psychology, iii. p. 258.

"The third epoch saw matter conditioned, but contraries were still unknown. When these appeared, Tao began to decline. And with the decline of Tao, individual bias arose.

"Have then these states of falling and rising real existences? Surely they are but as the falling and rising of Chao Wên's music,—the consequences of his playing.

Hui Tzŭ argued. Herein these three men excelled, and in the practice of such arts they passed their lives.

"Hui Tzŭ's particular views being very different from those of the world in general, he was correspondingly anxious to enlighten people. But he did not enlighten them as he should have done,

and consequently ended in the obscurity of the 'hard and white.'

Hui Tzŭ regarded such abstractions as hardness and whiteness as separate existences, of which the mind could only be conscious separately, one at a time.

Subsequently, his son searched his works for some clue, but never succeeded in establishing the principle. And indeed if such were possible to be established, then even I am established; but if not, then neither I nor anything in the universe is established!

"Therefore what the true Sage aims at is the light which comes out of darkness. He does not view things as apprehended by himself, subjectively, but transfers himself into the position of the things viewed. This is called using the light.

"There remains, however, Speech. Is that to be enrolled under either category of contraries, or not? Whether it is so enrolled or not, it will in any case belong to one or the other, and thus be as though it had an objective existence. At any rate, I should like to hear some speech which belongs to neither category.

Contraries being disposed of, there remains the vehicle Speech, i.e. the actual terms in which it is stated that contraries have ceased to be.

"If there was a beginning, then there was a time before that beginning. And a time before the time which was before the time of that beginning.

"If there is existence, there must have been non-existence. And if there was a time when nothing existed, then there must have been a time before that—when even nothing did not exist. Suddenly, when nothing came into existence, could one really say whether it belonged to the category of existence or of non-existence? Even the very words I have just now uttered,—I cannot say whether they have really been uttered or not.

"There is nothing under the canopy of heaven greater than the tip of an autumn spikelet. A vast mountain is a small thing. Neither is there any age greater than that of a child cut off in infancy. P'êng Tsu himself died young. The universe and I came into being together; and I, and everything therein, are One.

"If then all things are One, what room is there for Speech? On the other hand, since I can utter these words, how can Speech not exist?

"If it does exist, we have One and Speech = two; and two and one = three. From which point onwards even the best mathematicians will fail to reach:

how much more then will ordinary people fail?

"Hence, if from nothing you can proceed to something, and subsequently reach three, it follows that it would be still more easy if you were to start from something. To avoid such progression, you must put yourself into subjective relation with the external.

"Before conditions existed, Tao was. Before definitions existed, Speech was. Subjectively, we are conscious of certain delimitations which are,—

Right and Left
Relationship and Obligation
Division and Discrimination
Emulation and Contention

For the true Sage, beyond the limits of an external world, they exist, but are not recognised. By the true Sage, within the limits of an external world, they are recognised, but are not assigned. And so, with regard to the wisdom of the ancients, as embodied in the canon of Spring and Autumn,

the true Sage assigns, but does not justify by argument. And thus, classifying he does not classify; arguing, he does not argue."

"The true Sage," answered Tzŭ Ch'i, "keeps his knowledge within him, while men in general set forth theirs in argument, in order to convince each other. And therefore it is said that in argument he does not manifest himself.

Others try to establish their own subjective view. The true Sage remains passive, aiming only at the annihilation of contraries.

"Perfect Tao does not declare itself. Nor does perfect argument express itself in words. Nor does perfect charity show itself in act. Nor is perfect honesty absolutely incorruptible. Nor is perfect courage absolutely unyielding.

"For the Tao which shines forth is not Tao. Speech which argues falls short of its aim. Charity which has fixed points loses its scope. Honesty which is absolute is wanting in credit. Courage which is absolute misses its object. These five are, as it were, round, with a strong bias towards squareness. Therefore that knowledge which stops at what it does not know, is the highest knowledge.

"Who knows the argument which can be argued without words?—the Tao which does not declare itself as Tao? He who knows this may be said to be of God. To be able to pour in without making full, and pour out without making empty, in ignorance of the power by which such results are accomplished,—this is accounted Light."

Of old, the Emperor Yao said to Shun, "I would smite the Tsungs, and the Kueis, and the Hsü-aos. Ever since I have been on the throne I have had this desire. What do you think?"

"These three States," replied Shun, "are paltry out-of-the-way places. Why can you not shake off this desire? Once upon a time, ten suns came out together, and all things were illuminated thereby. How much more then should virtue excel suns?"

Illustrating the use of "light." Instead of active force, substitute the passive but irresistible influence of virtue complete. The sun caused the traveller to lay aside his cloak when the north wind succeeded only in making him draw it tighter around him.

Yeh Ch'üeh asked Wang I,

A disciple and tutor of remote antiquity. Said to have been two of the four Sages on the Miao-ku-shê mountain mentioned in ch. i.

saying, "Do you know for certain that all things are subjectively the same?"

"How can I know?" answered Wang I. "Do you know what you do not know?"

"How can I know?" replied Yeh Ch'üeh. "But can then nothing be known?"

"How can I know?" said Wang I. "Nevertheless, I will try to tell you. How can it be known that what I call knowing is not really not knowing, and that what I call not knowing is not really knowing? Now I would ask you this. If a man sleeps in a damp place, he gets lumbago and dies. But how about an eel? And living up in a tree is precarious and trying to the nerves;—but how about monkeys? Of the man, the eel, and the monkey, whose habitat is the right one, absolutely? Human beings feed on flesh, deer on grass, centipedes on snakes, owls and crows on mice. Of these four, whose is the right taste, absolutely? Monkey mates with monkey, the buck with the doe; eels consort with fishes, while men admire Mao Ch'iang and Li Chi,

Beauties of the fifth and seventh centuries B.C., respectively. The commentators do not seem to have noted the very obvious anachronism here involved.

at the sight of whom fishes plunge deep down in the water, birds soar high in the air, and deer hurry away.

Yet who shall say which is the correct standard of beauty? In my opinion, the standard of human virtue, and of positive and negative, is so obscured that it is impossible to actually know it as such."

"If you then," asked Yeh Ch'üeh, "do not know what is bad for you, is the Perfect Man equally without this knowledge?"

"The Perfect Man," answered Wang I, "is a spiritual being. Were the ocean itself scorched up, he would not feel hot. Were the Milky Way frozen hard, he would not feel cold. Were the mountains to be riven with thunder, and the great deep to be thrown up by storm, he would not tremble. In such case, he would mount upon the clouds of heaven, and driving the sun and the moon before him, would pass beyond the limits of this external world, where death and life have no more victory over man;—how much less what is bad for him?"

Chü Ch'iao addressed Chang Wu Tzŭ

as follows:—"I heard Confucius say, 'The true sage pays no heed to mundane affairs. He neither seeks gain nor avoids injury. He asks nothing at the hands of man. He adheres, without questioning, to Tao. Without speaking, he can speak; and he can speak and yet say nothing. And so he roams beyond the limits of this dusty world. These,' added Confucius, 'are wild words.'

Han Fei Tzŭ tells us that Lao Tzŭ, whose doctrines Confucius seems to be here deriding, said exactly the opposite of this; viz: "The true Sage is beforehand in his attention to mundane affairs," i.e. "takes time by the forelock." Neither utterance, however, appears in the Tao-Tê-Ching. See The Remains of Lao Tzŭ, p. 44.

Now to me they are the skilful embodiment of Tao. What, Sir, is your opinion?"

"Points upon which the Yellow Emperor doubted," replied Chang Wu Tzŭ, "how should Confucius know?

Lao Tzŭ and the Yellow Emperor have always been mixed up in the heads of Taoist writers, albeit separated by a chasm of some two thousand years. Confucius is here evidently dealing with the actual doctrines of Lao Tzŭ.

You are going too fast. You see your egg, and expect to hear it crow. You look at your cross-bow, and expect to have broiled duck before you. I will say a few words to you at random, and do you listen at random.

"How does the Sage seat himself by the sun and moon, and hold the universe in his grasp? He blends everything into one harmonious whole, rejecting the confusion of this and that. Rank and precedence, which the vulgar prize, the Sage stolidly ignores. The revolutions of ten thousand years leave his Unity unscathed. The universe itself may pass away, but he will flourish still.

"How do I know that love of life is not a delusion after all? How do I know but that he who dreads to die is not as a child who has lost the way and cannot find his home?

When the Duke of Chin first got her, she wept until the bosom of her dress was drenched with tears. But when she came to the royal residence, and lived with the Duke, and ate rich food, she repented of having wept. How then do I know but that the dead repent of having previously clung to life?

"Those who dream of the banquet, wake to lamentation and sorrow. Those who dream of lamentation and sorrow wake to join the hunt. While they dream, they do not know that they dream. Some will even interpret the very dream they are dreaming; and only when they awake do they know it was a dream. By and by comes the Great Awakening, and then we find out that this life is really a great dream. Fools think they are awake now, and flatter themselves they know if they are really princes or peasants. Confucius and you are both dreams; and I who say you are dreams,—I am but a dream myself. This is a paradox. Tomorrow a sage may arise to explain it; but that tomorrow will not be until ten thousand generations have gone by.

"Granting that you and I argue. If you beat me, and not I you, are you necessarily right and I wrong? Or if I beat you and not you me, am I necessarily right and you wrong? Or are we both partly right and partly wrong? Or are we both wholly right and wholly wrong? You and I cannot know this, and consequently the world will be in ignorance of the truth.

"Who shall I employ as arbiter between us? If I employ some one who takes your view, he will side with you. How can such a one arbitrate between us? If I employ some one who takes my view, he will side with me. How can such a one arbitrate between us? And if I employ some one who either differs from, or agrees with, both of us, he will be equally unable to decide between us. Since then you, and I, and man, cannot decide, must we not depend upon Another?

Such dependence is as though it were not dependence. We are embraced in the obliterating unity of God. There is perfect adaptation to whatever may eventuate; and so we complete our allotted span.

"But what is it to be embraced in the obliterating unity of God? It is this. With reference to positive and negative, to that which is so and that which is not so,—if the positive is really positive, it must necessarily be different from its negative: there is no room for argument. And if that which is so really is so, it must necessarily be different from that which is not so: there is no room for argument.

"Take no heed of time, nor of right and wrong. But passing into the realm of the Infinite, take your final rest therein."

Our refuge is in God alone, the Infinite Absolute. Contraries cannot but exist, but they should exist independently of each other without antagonism. Such a condition is found only in the all-embracing unity of God, wherein all distinctions of positive and negative, of right and wrong, of this and of that, are obliterated and merged in One.

Herbert Spencer says, "The antithesis of subject and object, never to be transcended while consciousness lasts, renders impossible all knowledge of the Ultimate Reality in which subject and object are united." Principles of Psychology, i. p. 272.

The Penumbra said to the Umbra, "At one moment you move: at another you are at rest. At one moment you sit down: at another you get up. Why this instability of purpose?" "I depend," replied the Umbra, "upon something which causes me to do as I do; and that something depends in turn upon something else which causes it to do as it does. My dependence is like that of a snake's scales or of a cicada's wings.

How can I tell why I do one thing, or why I do not do another?"

Once upon a time, I, Chuang Tzŭ, dreamt I was a butterfly, fluttering hither and thither, to all intents and purposes a butterfly. I was conscious only of following my fancies as a butterfly, and was unconscious of my individuality as a man. Suddenly, I awaked, and there I lay, myself again. Now I do not know whether I was then a man dreaming I was a butterfly, or whether I am now a butterfly dreaming I am a man. Between a man and a butterfly there is necessarily a barrier. The transition is called Metempsychosis.
translation:
Ziqi of the Southern Wall sat leaning on his armrest, gazing up at the sky and breathing out slowly, vacant as though he had lost his partner-self. Yan Cheng Ziyou, standing in attendance before him, said, "What is happening here? Can the body truly be made like withered wood, and the mind truly be made like cold, dead ashes? The one leaning on the armrest now is not the one who leaned there before." Ziqi said, "Yan, isn't your question a good one! Just now I lost my 'me' — do you understand? You have heard the piping of humans but not the piping of earth; you have heard the piping of earth but not the piping of tiān 天, of heaven." Ziyou said, "May I ask what you mean?" Ziqi said, "The Great Clod belches out its breath, and its name is wind. So long as it doesn't stir, nothing happens; but once it stirs, then ten thousand hollows begin to roar. Have you alone never heard that long-drawn howling? In the mountain forests, the sheer heights, the hollows and cavities in great trees a hundred spans around — like noses, like mouths, like ears, like beam-sockets, like cups, like mortars, like pools, like puddles — they whistle, whir, shout, snuff, cry out, wail, moan, chatter; the wind ahead sings 'yu' and the wind behind answers 'yong.' A gentle breeze makes a small harmony, a whirlwind a great one, and when the fierce gust passes, all the hollows fall empty. Have you alone never seen the branches swaying and quivering after?" Ziyou said, "So earth's piping is just these hollows, and human piping is just pipes of bamboo. May I ask about heaven's piping?" Ziqi said, "It blows through the ten thousand things, each differently, and lets each be itself. Each takes for itself what it takes — so who is it that does the rousing?"

Great understanding is broad and easy; small understanding is picky and cramped. Great words are clear and calm; small words are chatter and quarrel. In sleep our spirits mingle; awake, our bodies open up to the world. Every contact becomes entanglement, and day by day the mind wars. Some are drifting, some deep, some tight-shut. Small fears leave us anxious; great fears leave us stunned. Minds shoot forth like a crossbow-trigger — this is how they preside over 'right' and 'wrong.' They hold back as though bound by oath — this is how they cling to winning. They wane like autumn and winter — this describes their daily wasting. They sink into what they do until nothing can bring them back. They shut down as though sealed — this describes them drying up in old age. Minds near death cannot be made to return to the light.

Joy and anger, grief and delight, worry and regret, changing and holding still, ease and abandon, openness and posturing — music from empty hollows, mushrooms from rising damp. Day and night these alternate before us, and no one knows where they sprout from. Enough! Enough! Morning and evening we come upon these — is this the source from which they arise? Without that 'other' there is no 'me'; without 'me' there is nothing to take hold of it. This much is near the truth, yet we do not know what makes it so. There seems to be a true ruler, but we cannot find any sign of it. That it can act is credible enough, yet we never see its form — it has reality but no visible shape.

The hundred bones, the nine openings, the six organs — all present and accounted for. Which shall I feel closest to? Do you delight in them all equally, or have you a favorite among them? If so, are they all mere servants and maids? Are servants and maids unable to govern one another? Or do they take turns being lord and subject? Or is there some true lord present among them? Whether we manage to grasp its reality or not, this neither adds to nor subtracts from its truth.

Once we receive this finished form, we do not lose it until it is used up. Grinding and clashing against things, racing along its course with nothing able to stop it — is this not sad? To toil one's whole life and never see the work completed, worn out and exhausted with no idea where one is headed — can this not be called grief? People call this 'not dying,' but what use is that? As the body decays the mind decays with it — can this not be called the great grief? Is human life really this blind? Or am I the only one who is blind, and are there others who are not?

If a person follows the mind already formed in them and takes it as teacher, who could ever be without a teacher? Why should it only be those who understand the succession of things and choose with their own minds? Even fools have such a teacher! To have 'right' and 'wrong' before the mind is even formed — that is like setting off for Yue today and arriving yesterday. That is making the nonexistent exist. Making the nonexistent exist — even the godlike Yu could not fathom it, so what am I to do?

Now, speech is not just blowing air; the speaker says something. But what he says is never fixed. Is there really something being said? Or has nothing ever been said? People suppose it differs from the chirping of hatchlings — but is there really a distinction, or is there none? How can the dào 道 be so hidden that there is 'true' and 'false'? How can speech be so hidden that there is 'right' and 'wrong'? Where can the dào go and not remain? Where can speech exist and not be allowed? The dào is hidden by small completions; speech is hidden by flowery display. So we get the 'right' and 'wrong' of the Confucians and the Mohists, each affirming what the other denies and denying what the other affirms. If you want to affirm what they deny and deny what they affirm, nothing beats using clarity (míng 明).

Every thing is a 'that'; every thing is a 'this.' From the standpoint of 'that,' one cannot see it; from one's own knowing, one knows it. So it is said: 'that' comes out of 'this,' and 'this' depends on 'that' — this is the doctrine of 'this' and 'that' being born together. Yet just as they are born they die, and just as they die they are born; just as something is allowable it is not, and just as it is not it is; depending on 'right' there is 'wrong,' depending on 'wrong' there is 'right.' Therefore the sage does not go that route but illuminates things by the light of heaven — and this too is just 'going by what is.' 'This' is also 'that,' and 'that' is also 'this.' 'That' has its own 'right' and 'wrong,' and 'this' has its own 'right' and 'wrong.' So is there really a 'this' and a 'that'? Or is there really no 'this' and 'that'? When 'this' and 'that' no longer find their opposite, this is called the pivot of the dào (dào shū 道樞). Once the pivot finds the center of its ring, it can respond endlessly. 'Right' is one endlessness, and 'wrong' is another. So it is said: nothing beats using clarity. To use a finger to show that a finger is not a finger is worse than using a non-finger to show that a finger is not a finger; to use a horse to show that a horse is not a horse is worse than using a non-horse...
abhyasa: Try this once today. When you next feel a strong emotional reaction — irritation at an email, anxiety before a meeting, a flash of being right in an argument — pause and ask, in Ziqi's terms, 'Where did this sprout from?' Watch for the hollow it blew through. You will notice the feeling arose on its own, unbidden, 'like a mushroom from damp,' before any 'you' chose it. Then do the 'this and that' reversal: state the exact opposite position and honestly say what someone standing there would see. You are not trying to agree with them or dissolve your view into mush. You are locating the hinge — the point where you can hold your own position while seeing it as one position among others, generated by where you happen to stand. Even thirty seconds of this loosens the crossbow-trigger of the judging mind. Done repeatedly, it is a small daily rehearsal of 'losing the me' — not erasing yourself, but unclenching the defended self just enough to breathe out and look up.

pratibha_layers.body:
南郭子綦隱机而坐，仰天而噓，荅焉似喪其耦。
顏成子游立侍乎前，曰：「何居乎？
形固可使如槁木，而心固可使如死灰乎？
今之隱机者，非昔之隱机者也？
」子綦曰：「偃，不亦善乎，而問之也！
今者吾喪我，汝知之乎？
女聞人籟而未聞地籟，女聞地籟而未聞天籟夫！
」子游曰：「敢問其方。
」子綦曰：「夫大塊噫氣，其名為風。
是唯無作，作則萬竅怒呺。
而獨不聞之翏翏乎？
山林之畏佳，大木百圍之竅穴，似鼻，似口，似耳，似枅，似圈，似臼，似洼者，似污者；
激者、謞者、叱者、吸者、叫者、譹者、宎者、咬者，前者唱于而隨者唱喁。
泠風則小和，飄風則大和，厲風濟則眾竅為虛。
而獨不見之調調，之刀刀乎？
」子游曰：「地籟則眾竅是已，人籟則比竹是已，敢問天籟。
」子綦曰：「夫吹萬不同，而使其自已也。
咸其自取，怒者其誰邪？
」大知閑閑，小知間間；
大言炎炎，小言詹詹。
其寐也魂交，其覺也形開。
與接為構，日以心鬥。
縵者、窖者、密者。
小恐惴惴，大恐縵縵。
其發若機栝，其司是非之謂也；
其留如詛盟，其守勝之謂也；
其殺若秋冬，以言其日消也；
其溺之所為之，不可使復之也；
其厭也如緘，以言其都洫也；
近死之心，莫使復陽也。
喜怒哀樂，慮歎變慹，姚佚啟態；
樂出虛，蒸成菌。
日夜相代乎前，而莫知其所萌。
已乎，已乎！
旦暮得此，其所由以生乎！
非彼無我，非我無所取。
是亦近矣，而不知其所為使。
若有真宰，而特不得其眹。
可行己信，而不見其形，有情而無形。
百骸、九竅、六藏，賅而存焉，吾誰與為親？
汝皆說之乎？
其有私焉？

其遞相為君臣乎？
其有真君存焉？
如求得其情與不得，無益損乎其真。
一受其成形，不亡以待盡。
與物相刃相靡，其行盡如馳，而莫之能止，不亦悲乎！
終身役役而不見其成功，苶然疲役而不知其所歸，可不哀邪！
人謂之不死，奚益！
其形化，其心與之然，可不謂大哀乎？

其我獨芒，而人亦有不芒者乎？
夫隨其成心而師之，誰獨且無師乎？

愚者與有焉！

是以無有為有。

夫言非吹也，言者有言。
其所言者特未定也。

其未嘗有言邪？

言惡乎隱而有是非？

言惡乎存而不可？

彼是方生之說也。

是以聖人不由，而照之於天，亦因是也。

彼亦一是非，此亦一是非，果且有彼是乎哉？

pratibha_layers.label: Pratibha Translation
pratibha_layers.body:
Once, Zhuang Zhou dreamt he was a butterfly - vividly, joyfully butterfly, moving exactly as butterfly-nature moves. In that state he did not know himself as Zhou.

Then suddenly he woke, and there he was: Zhou, unmistakably Zhou.

Yet now he does not know: was it Zhou dreaming butterfly, or butterfly dreaming Zhou? Between Zhou and butterfly there is surely a distinction. This is what is called the transformation of things [*wù huà* 物化].

pratibha_layers.label: Pratibha Commentary
pratibha_layers.body:
The philosophical claim is sharper than "reality is uncertain." Zhuangzi is targeting identity-certainty itself: the self that claims to be the fixed subject of experience is retrospectively constructed from whichever standpoint is currently dominant. The counterintuitive move is that waking does not automatically secure ontological privilege over dreaming. Waking may provide continuity for practical life, but it does not grant absolute authority over all modes of appearing. In this way, the butterfly anecdote is a precision critique of metaphysical egocentrism.

The final phrase, *wù huà* (transformation of things), prevents a skeptical reading. Zhuangzi is not saying no distinction exists; he explicitly says there is a distinction (*fen*). What he denies is a final standpoint outside transformation from which one could freeze distinction into essence. Identity is real as function, unstable as absolute. Daoist thought here diverges from crude relativism: appearances are not arbitrary, but they are phase-bound. Existentially, this shifts how one holds roles and narratives. "I am this kind of person" becomes a useful temporary pattern, not a metaphysical prison. The passage invites supple responsibility: act fully from the current form, while remembering form itself is migratory. That memory softens fear of change and loosens hostility toward other forms of life, because each standpoint is partial participation in a larger process of transformation.

pratibha_layers.label: Practice (Abhyasa)
pratibha_layers.body: Tonight before sleep, write one identity statement you are gripping ("I am the one who..."), then in the morning rewrite it in two alternate forms that are equally true from different standpoints, and carry all three versions without collapsing to only one.

items.definition: "leveling/equalizing things" (*qí* = level or make even, *wù* = things/beings) -> in this passage, the decentering of privileged standpoint claims -> default translation "identity of contraries" can imply abstract logic; Zhuangzi is enacting experiential equalization of perspectives.

"transformation of things/beings" -> contextual meaning: shifts of identity-form across conditions without positing a fixed core self as owner -> "metempsychosis" over-psychologizes and suggests a doctrine of transmigrating soul; Zhuangzi's term is broader processual transformation.

"self-satisfied, at ease in itself" -> describes butterfly-mode as fully immanent ease, not reflective self-awareness -> translated loosely as "conscious of following fancies," which misses the phenomenological point that one can be complete in a mode without meta-certainty.

items.resonance: waking and dream are both appearances within consciousness, differentiated functionally but not absolutely. Structurally, both texts deny final reality-status to ordinary waking certainty.
items.divergence: Gaudapada resolves the issue through nondual Atman as the unchanging witness; Zhuangzi does not posit an equivalent permanent witness and keeps transformation foregrounded.

items.citation: Dhammapada / early Buddhist dream analogies for conditioned experience
items.resonance: both traditions use dream imagery to expose grasping at fixed identity and fixed world-claims.
items.divergence: Buddhism links the analysis to dependent origination and no-self as a soteriological path with explicit ethical architecture; Zhuangzi emphasizes perspectival play and ontological fluidity without the same doctrinal scaffold.

items.resonance: Eckhart's detachment from created forms parallels Zhuangzi's release of rigid identification with any single form.
items.divergence: Eckhart's movement is toward union with the divine ground, while Zhuangzi's movement is toward unforced participation in ceaseless transformation; one culminates in theological language, the other in process-language.

title: Nourishment of the Soul.
thesis: The claim is that true mastery is not increased force but refined non-forcing: action aligned with intrinsic pattern minimizes friction and preserves life-energy.

In striving for others, avoid fame. In striving for self, avoid disgrace. Pursue a middle course. Thus you will keep a sound body, and a sound mind, fulfil your duties, and work out your allotted span. Prince Hui's cook was cutting up a bullock. Every blow of his hand, every heave of his shoulders, every tread of his foot, every thrust of his knee, every whshh of rent flesh, every chhk of the chopper, was in perfect harmony,—rhythmical like the dance of the Mulberry Grove, simultaneous like the chords of the Ching Shou. translation_literal:
My life has a boundary, but knowing has none. To chase what has no limit with what does—that is exhausting; and to keep on knowing after realizing this is exhausting indeed! In doing good, stay clear of reputation; in doing bad, stay clear of punishment. Follow the central meridian as your guiding thread—this lets you protect your body, keep life whole, care for your parents, and live out your natural years.

Cook Ding was cutting up an ox for Lord Wenhui. Wherever his hand touched, his shoulder leaned, his foot stepped, his knee pressed—the flesh fell away with a tearing hiss; the blade sang as it plunged, never off the beat, in time with the Mulberry Grove dance, matching the rhythm of the Jingshou music. "Ah, marvelous!" said Lord Wenhui. "That skill could reach such heights!" Cook Ding set down his knife and replied: "What your servant loves is the dào 道—it goes beyond mere skill. When I first began cutting oxen, all I saw was the whole ox. After three years, I no longer saw the ox as a whole. And now—I meet it with my spirit (shén 神) and do not look with my eyes. Sense and perception stop, and the spirit moves as it wishes. I rely on the natural structure (tiān lǐ 天理), striking into the great gaps, guiding through the large hollows, following what is inherently so. My blade never even brushes the tangled ligaments and joints—much less the big bones! A good cook changes his knife yearly, because he cuts. An ordinary cook changes his monthly, because he hacks. Now my knife has lasted nineteen years and has carved thousands of oxen, yet the edge is as if fresh from the whetstone. Those joints have spaces, and the blade's edge has no thickness. Enter what has no thickness into what has space, and there is room to spare—that is why after nineteen years my blade is like new. Still, whenever I come to a knotted place, I see the difficulty, grow wary and alert, my gaze settles, my movement slows, I ease the blade in delicately, and with a soft thud the whole thing falls apart like earth crumbling to the ground. Then I stand holding my knife, looking all around, savoring the moment, satisfied—then I wipe the blade and put it away." Lord Wenhui said: "Excellent! From Cook Ding's words I have learned how to nourish life."

Gongwen Xuan saw the Commander of the Right and was startled: "What kind of man is this? How did he lose a foot? Was it Heaven (tiān 天), or was it men?" The answer: "Heaven, not men. When Heaven gave me life it made me one-footed. A man's appearance is given by Heaven. So I know it was Heaven, not men."

The marsh pheasant takes a peck every ten steps, a drink every hundred, but it does not wish to be kept in a cage. There its spirit would be strong, but it would not be well.

When Lao Dan died, Qin Shi came to mourn, wailed three times, and left. A disciple asked: "Was he not your master's friend?" "He was." "Then is it right to mourn him like this?" "Yes. At first I took him to be that man, but now I do not. When I went in to mourn, there were old ones weeping for him as for their own child, young ones weeping as for their own mother. For them to have gathered so, there must have been those who spoke though not asked to speak, who wept though not asked to weep. This is to flee from Heaven and pile on excess feeling, forgetting what one has received—the ancients called it the punishment for fleeing Heaven. That he came was your master's timing; that he went was his following along. Rest in the timing and dwell in the following, and grief and joy cannot enter—the ancients called this being loosed from the bonds of the Lord." The fingers finish their work of adding kindling, but the fire passes on, and no one knows it will ever end.
commentary:
This chapter's title, "Nourishing Life" (yǎng shēng), frames a series of vignettes that dissolve the anxious opposition between striving and yielding. The opening move is a warning against the endless pursuit of knowledge: life is bounded, knowing is boundless, so treating unlimited accumulation as a life goal only wears you down. The proposed alternative is to "follow the central meridian"—dū 督 is both the body's central channel and, metaphorically, the middle way that avoids the extremes of chasing praise or courting punishment.

Cook Ding is the heart of the passage, and his story dissolves the distinction between effort and effortlessness, between skilled 'doing' and spontaneous 'not-doing.' The novice sees a solid, opaque ox—an obstacle to be forced through. The master sees only the structure's natural gaps, and moves his no-thickness blade through the spaces that were always there. Note that this is not passivity: at the knotted places Ding slows, watches, grows alert. Mastery here is not the abolition of care but its precise placement—attention flows to the difficulty rather than muscling through it. The dulled knife of the ordinary cook is the mind that grinds itself against reality; the ever-fresh edge is the person who moves with the grain of things.

The surrounding fragments extend the theme by loosening other fixed distinctions. The one-footed commander refuses to read his condition as injustice or human fault—he places it within tiān, the natural given, and so is freed from resentment. The caged pheasant collapses the equation of security with well-being: comfort inside the cage is not the same as flourishing. And Qin Shi's cool mourning dissolves the boundary between life and death: excessive grief, he says, is 'fleeing from Heaven,' clinging to what was only ever a temporary arrangement. The closing image seals it—fingers and firewood are consumed, but the flame is handed on. What matters is not the perishable body but the ongoing transmission of the living process, which has no known end.

Key Terms

**督 dū** — The central meridian/channel; figuratively, following the middle course that avoids destructive extremes.
**天理 tiān lǐ** — The natural structure or inherent grain of things, which the skilled person works along rather than against.
**神 shén** — Spirit or intuitive awareness; the mode by which the master 'meets' his work once ordinary sense-perception has stopped.
practice: When your blade (knife, pen, voice, attention) next meets resistance—in cutting, writing, speaking, or thinking—pause and let your hand go slack for three breaths. Feel where the thing you're working on already wants to separate, already has its own grain and spaces. Move only through those gaps, not against them. The resistance will tell you where not to press.

神雖王，不善也。

弟子曰：「非夫子之友邪？
」曰：「然。
」「然則弔焉若此，可乎？
」曰：「然。
始也吾以為其人也，而今非也。
向吾入而弔焉，有老者哭之，如哭其子﹔少者哭之，如哭其母。
彼其所以會之，必有不蘄言而言，不蘄哭而哭者。

」指窮於為薪，火傳也，不知其盡也。

anchor_chapter:
My life has a limit, but my knowledge is without limit. To drive the limited in search of the limitless, is fatal; and the knowledge of those who do this is fatally lost.

In striving for others, avoid fame. In striving for self, avoid disgrace. Pursue a middle course. Thus you will keep a sound body, and a sound mind, fulfil your duties, and work out your allotted span.

Prince Hui's cook was cutting up a bullock. Every blow of his hand, every heave of his shoulders, every tread of his foot, every thrust of his knee, every whshh of rent flesh, every chhk of the chopper, was in perfect harmony,—rhythmical like the dance of the Mulberry Grove, simultaneous like the chords of the Ching Shou.

"Well done!" cried the Prince. "Yours is skill indeed."

"Sire," replied the cook; "I have always devoted myself to Tao. It is better than skill. When I first began to cut up bullocks, I saw before me simply whole bullocks. After three years' practice, I saw no more whole animals.

And now I work with my mind and not with my eye. When my senses bid me stop, but my mind urges me on, I fall back upon eternal principles. I follow such openings or cavities as there may be, according to the natural constitution of the animal. I do not attempt to cut through joints: still less through large bones.

"A good cook changes his chopper once a year,—because he cuts. An ordinary cook, once a month,—because he hacks. But I have had this chopper nineteen years, and although I have cut up many thousand bullocks, its edge is as if fresh from the whetstone. For at the joints there are always interstices, and the edge of a chopper being without thickness, it remains only to insert that which is without thickness into such an interstice.

These words help to elucidate a much-vexed passage in ch. xliii of the Tao-Tê-Ching. See The Remains of Lao Tzŭ, p. 30.

By these means the interstice will be enlarged, and the blade will find plenty of room. It is thus that I have kept my chopper for nineteen years as though fresh from the whetstone.

"Nevertheless, when I come upon a hard part where the blade meets with a difficulty, I am all caution. I fix my eye on it. I stay my hand, and gently apply my blade, until with a hwah the part yields like earth crumbling to the ground. Then I take out my chopper, and stand up, and look around, and pause, until with an air of triumph I wipe my chopper and put it carefully away."

"Bravo!" cried the Prince. "From the words of this cook I have learnt how to take care of my life."

When Hsien, of the Kung-wên family, beheld a certain official, he was horrified, and said, "Who is that man? How came he to lose a foot? Is this the work of God, or of man?

"Why, of course," continued Hsien, "it is the work of God, and not of man. When God brought this man into the world, he wanted him to be unlike other men. Men always have two feet. From this it is clear that God and not man made him as he is.

It was by God's will that he took office with a view to personal aggrandisement. That he got into trouble and suffered the common punishment of loss of feet, cannot therefore be charged to man.

"Now, wild fowl get a peck once in ten steps, a drink once in a hundred. Yet they do not want to be fed in a cage. For although they would thus be able to command food, they would not be free."

And had our friend above kept out of the official cage he would still have been independent as the fowls of the air.

A disciple asked him saying, "Were you not our Master's friend?"

"I do," said Ch'in Shih. "I had believed him to be the man of all men, but now I know that he was not. When I went in to mourn, I found old persons weeping as if for their children, young ones wailing as if for their mothers. And for him to have gained the attachment of those people in this way, he too must have uttered words which should not have been spoken, and dropped tears which should not have been shed, thus violating eternal principles, increasing the sum of human emotion, and forgetting the source from which his own life was received. The ancients called such emotions the trammels of mortality. The Master came, because it was his time to be born; he went, because it was his time to die. For those who accept the phenomenon of birth and death in this sense, lamentation and sorrow have no place. The ancients spoke of death as of God cutting down a man suspended in the air. The fuel is consumed, but the fire may be transmitted, and we know not that it comes to an end."

The soul, according to Chuang Tzŭ, if duly nourished and not allowed to wear itself out with the body in the pursuits of mortality, may become immortal and return beatified to the Great Unknown whence it came.
