Still, whenever I come to a knotted place, I see the difficulty, grow wary and alert, my gaze settles, my movement slows, I ease the blade in delicately, and with a soft thud the whole thing falls apart like earth crumbling to the ground. Then I stand holding my knife, looking all around, savoring the moment, satisfied—then I wipe the blade and put it away." Lord Wenhui said: "Excellent! From Cook Ding's words I have learned how to nourish life."

Gongwen Xuan saw the Commander of the Right and was startled: "What kind of man is this? How did he lose a foot? Was it Heaven (tiān 天), or was it men?" The answer: "Heaven, not men. When Heaven gave me life it made me one-footed. A man's appearance is given by Heaven. So I know it was Heaven, not men."

The marsh pheasant takes a peck every ten steps, a drink every hundred, but it does not wish to be kept in a cage. There its spirit would be strong, but it would not be well.

When Lao Dan died, Qin Shi came to mourn, wailed three times, and left. A disciple asked: "Was he not your master's friend?" "He was." "Then is it right to mourn him like this?" "Yes. At first I took him to be that man, but now I do not. When I went in to mourn, there were old ones weeping for him as for their own child, young ones weeping as for their own mother. For them to have gathered so, there must have been those who spoke though not asked to speak, who wept though not asked to weep. This is to flee from Heaven and pile on excess feeling, forgetting what one has received—the ancients called it the punishment for fleeing Heaven. That he came was your master's timing; that he went was his following along. Rest in the timing and dwell in the following, and grief and joy cannot enter—the ancients called this being loosed from the bonds of the Lord." The fingers finish their work of adding kindling, but the fire passes on, and no one knows it will ever end.
abhyasa: When your blade (knife, pen, voice, attention) next meets resistance—in cutting, writing, speaking, or thinking—pause and let your hand go slack for three breaths. Feel where the thing you're working on already wants to separate, already has its own grain and spaces. Move only through those gaps, not against them. The resistance will tell you where not to press.

pratibha_layers.label: Original
pratibha_layers.body:
吾生也有涯，而知也無涯。
以有涯隨無涯，殆已！
已而為知者，殆而已矣！
為善無近名，為惡無近刑，緣督以為經，可以保身，可以全生，可以養親，可以盡年。
庖丁為文惠君解牛，手之所觸，肩之所倚，足之所履，膝之所踦，砉然響然，奏刀騞然，莫不中音，合於桑林之舞，乃中經首之會。
文惠君曰：「嘻，善哉！
技蓋至此乎？
」庖丁釋刀對曰：「臣之所好者道也，進乎技矣。
始臣之解牛之時，所見無非全牛者﹔三年之后，未嘗見全牛也﹔方今之時，臣以神遇而不以目視，官知止而神欲行。
依乎天理，批大卻，導大窾，因其固然。
技經肯綮之未嘗微礙，而況大軱乎！
良庖歲更刀，割也﹔族庖月更刀，折也﹔今臣之刀十九年矣，所解數千牛矣，而刀刃若新發於硎。
彼節者有閒，而刀刃者無厚，以無厚入有閒，恢恢乎其於游刃必有餘地矣。
是以十九年而刀刃若新發於硎。
雖然，每至於族，吾見其難為，怵然為戒，視為止，行為遲，動刀甚微，謋然已解，牛不知其死也，如土委地。
提刀而立，為之而四顧，為之躊躇滿志，善刀而藏之。
」文惠君曰：「善哉！
吾聞庖丁之言，得養生焉。
」公文軒見右師而驚曰：「是何人也？
惡乎介也？
天與？
其人與？
」曰：「天也，非人也。
天之生是使獨也，人之貌有與也。
以是知其天也，非人也。
」澤雉十步一啄，百步一飲，不蘄畜乎樊中。
神雖王，不善也。
老聃死，秦失弔之，三號而出。
弟子曰：「非夫子之友邪？
」曰：「然。
」「然則弔焉若此，可乎？
」曰：「然。
始也吾以為其人也，而今非也。
向吾入而弔焉，有老者哭之，如哭其子﹔少者哭之，如哭其母。
彼其所以會之，必有不蘄言而言，不蘄哭而哭者。
是遁天倍情，忘其所受，古者謂之遁天之刑。
適來，夫子時也﹔適去，夫子順也。
安時而處順，哀樂不能入也，古者謂是帝之縣解。
」指窮於為薪，火傳也，不知其盡也。

pratibha_layers.label: Pratibha Translation
pratibha_layers.body:
Cook Ding carves an ox for Lord Wenhui. Hand, shoulder, foot, knee, blade - every movement lands in rhythm, as if dance and music have entered the work.

The ruler says, "Excellent. Can skill really reach this level?"

Cook Ding sets down his knife and replies: "What I care for is Dao [*dào* 道], which goes beyond skill [*jì* 技]. At first I saw only whole oxen. After three years, I no longer saw the whole ox. Now I meet it with spirit [*shén* 神], not with the eyes. Sensory knowing comes to a stop; spirit-intent continues. I follow the natural pattern, guide the blade through the great openings, move along what is already so. I never force through tendon-knots - much less through heavy bone.

"A competent cook changes knives yearly because he cuts. An ordinary cook changes monthly because he hacks. I have used this blade for nineteen years on thousands of oxen, and its edge is still fresh. At the joints there are gaps; the blade has no thickness. Put what has no thickness into what has gaps, and there is ample room for the moving edge.

"Even so, when I reach a difficult place, I become fully careful. I steady attention, slow movement, and let the blade work subtly - then with a soft release, the part falls away like earth. I stand, look around, satisfied, wipe the blade, and store it."

Lord Wenhui says: "Excellent. From this cook's words I have learned how to nourish life."

pratibha_layers.label: Pratibha Commentary
pratibha_layers.body:
The claim is that true mastery is not increased force but refined non-forcing: action aligned with intrinsic pattern minimizes friction and preserves life-energy. The counterintuitive move is that expertise culminates in less assertion of the ego, not more. Early-stage skill stares at "the whole ox" and attacks it as a problem; mature skill perceives articulations, voids, and pathways already present. Cook Ding's phrase "spirit meets it" marks a shift from object-confrontation to field-participation.

Within Daoist tradition this is a paradigmatic illustration of *yangsheng* (nourishing life) and *wuwei*: one survives and flourishes not by withdrawing from complexity but by entering complexity at its natural seams. The knife image is philosophical, not merely artisanal. A thick self forcing thick intentions into dense situations dulls quickly; a "thin edge" self, attentive and unforced, moves through interstices. Even caution is integrated here - he slows down at difficult knots, which shows non-forcing is not carelessness but heightened responsiveness.

Existentially, the passage revises how to relate to strain. Most people alternate between brute push and collapse. Cook Ding offers a third mode: read the pattern, reduce unnecessary contact, and reserve decisive pressure for the exact point where the structure yields. The ruler learns "how to nourish life" because governance, relationships, and self-cultivation all fail when handled like hacking at bone. The text therefore teaches disciplined suppleness: precision over intensity, attunement over domination.

pratibha_layers.label: Practice (Abhyasa)
pratibha_layers.body: Choose one recurring task you usually "hack through," spend five minutes mapping its natural joints and transitions before starting, then perform it at 80% speed with full attention to where effort is actually needed and where you can move through existing openings.

items.definition: "to nourish life/vital living" -> in this passage, preserving one's edge through pattern-aligned engagement rather than depletion -> default translation "nourishment of the soul" can spiritualize the teaching and miss its concrete psychophysical pragmatics.

"heavenly pattern/principle" -> contextual meaning: the inherent structure of things that can be followed instead of overridden -> translated as "eternal principles," which can sound abstract-moral; here it means lived morphology, the actual grain of reality.
spirit, numinous awareness, finely responsive cognition -> Cook Ding's mode of knowing beyond ocular fixation -> "mind" alone is too cognitive; "spirit" here indicates vivid embodied intelligence.

literally "wandering blade" -> the easeful movement of the knife within available space, emblem of non-forced action -> translations that flatten this to "room for the blade" miss the improvisational freedom implied by *you* (to roam/wander).

items.resonance: "Yoga is skill in action" (*yogah karmasu kausalam*). Both texts define excellence as a quality of attuned action rather than mere output, and both link this to inner freedom from agitation.
items.divergence: The Gita situates skill in action within duty and offering to the divine, while Zhuangzi situates it in spontaneous conformity to pattern without duty-metaphysics.

items.citation: Epictetus, Enchiridion (discipline of assent and action)
items.resonance: Both traditions stress precision at the point of contact: do not hack at externals; work where agency truly operates.
items.divergence: Stoicism grounds this in rational governance of judgments (*prohairesis*), whereas Zhuangzi emphasizes fluid embodied responsiveness that can precede discursive judgment.

items.resonance: kitchen work as full-path practice parallels Cook Ding's ordinary labor becoming realization through total attention.
items.divergence: Dogen frames practice in explicit monastic-vow and Buddha-dharma context; Zhuangzi frames it as Daoist naturalness discovered in craft without institutional soteriology.

title: Man Among Men.
thesis: The philosophical claim is that transformation happens through emptied receptivity, not through more strategic intention.
source_excerpt: Yen Hui went to take leave of Confucius. A disciple of the Sage. Also known as Tzŭ Yüan. "Whither are you bound?" asked the Master. "I am going to the State of Wei," was the reply. translation_literal:
Yan Hui came to see Confucius and asked leave to travel. Confucius said, "Where are you going?" "To Wei." "To do what?" Yan Hui said, "I have heard that the ruler of Wei is young and headstrong. He treats his state carelessly and does not see his own faults. He wastes his people's lives so recklessly that the dead fill the marshes like heaps of cut reeds — the people have nowhere to turn. I once heard you, Master, say: 'Leave the well-governed state and go to the one in chaos; there are many sick at the doctor's gate.' I wish to take what I have learned and think out how to act, so that perhaps that state may be healed."

Confucius said, "Ah! You will only go there and be executed. The dào 道 does not want to be mixed up with other things; mixed, it multiplies; multiplied, it brings disturbance; disturbance brings anxiety, and anxiety brings no rescue. The perfected people of old first secured it in themselves, and only then in others. If what you hold in yourself is not yet settled, what leisure have you to correct the conduct of a tyrant?

"And do you understand how virtue (dé) gets dissipated and where cleverness comes from? Virtue is dissipated by the pursuit of reputation, and cleverness comes out of rivalry. Reputation is a thing by which people grind each other down; cleverness is a weapon of contention. Both are ill-omened tools, not the way to complete your conduct.

"Even if your virtue is deep and your sincerity solid, you have not yet touched the man's temper; even if you do not contend for reputation, you have not yet reached his heart. If you then force words of benevolence and righteousness, of standards and measuring-lines, before a tyrant, you are using another man's ugliness to show off your own beauty. This is called injuring people. He who injures people will surely be injured in return — you will likely be the one injured.

"Besides, if the ruler truly loved the worthy and hated the unworthy, what use would he have for you to make a difference? Better say nothing; for a king or lord will always exploit others and press his own quickness. Your eyes will be dazzled, your face forced into calm, your mouth busy defending yourself, your bearing bending to fit, and your heart will end up agreeing with him. This is fighting fire with fire, water with water — call it 'making more.' Once you begin to yield there is no end. And if you press your earnest words when he does not yet trust you, you will surely die before the tyrant.

"Long ago Jie killed Guan Longfeng, and Zhòu killed Prince Bigan. Both were men who cultivated themselves and bent down to comfort the ruler's people, and so, from below, went against their superiors. So their rulers, precisely because of their cultivation, destroyed them. These were men who loved reputation. Long ago Yao attacked Cong, Zhi, and Xu'ao, and Yu attacked You-hu. The states were laid waste, the rulers put to death — because their use of arms never stopped, their craving for gain never ceased. All these sought reputation and gain. Have you alone not heard of them? Reputation and gain — even the sages could not master them, much less you!

"Still, you must have some plan. Try telling me."

Yan Hui said, "If I am upright and empty, diligent and single-minded — will that do?" Confucius said, "No! How could it? The man is full of yang energy, high and overbearing, his moods unpredictable. Ordinary people do not dare oppose him, and he tramples on whatever others feel, seeking his own satisfaction. Even the slow, daily working of virtue cannot form in him — how much less some great transformation! He will hold fast and not change; he may agree outwardly but inwardly not even reflect. How could this work?"

"Then suppose I am straight within and yielding without, complete in myself while aligning with the ancients. Being straight within, I am a companion of tiān 天 (Heaven). One who is a companion of Heaven knows that the Son of Heaven and I are alike children of Heaven — so why should I care whether people approve or disapprove of my words? Such a one people call a child; this is to be a companion of Heaven. Yielding without, I am a companion of men. To lift the tablet, kneel, and bow — this is the etiquette of a minister. Everyone does it; dare I not? Doing what others do, no one can find fault with me — this is to be a companion of men. Complete in myself while aligning with the ancients, I am a companion of antiquity. Though my words are instruction, they aim at what is real, and they belong to the ancients, not to me. In this way, though I speak straight, I take no harm — this is to be a companion of antiquity. Would this do?"

Confucius said, "No! How could it? There is too much regulation, and no fitness. Though it is stiff and rigid, it commits no crime. Still, it stops at that — how could it reach transformation? You are still making a teacher of your own mind."

Yan Hui said, "I have nothing more to offer. May I ask the method?" Confucius said, "Fast, and I will tell you. Do you think it is easy to act with a purposeful mind? One who thinks it easy — bright Heaven will not agree." Yan Hui said, "My family is poor; I have gone months without drinking wine or eating meat or strong-smelling food. Can this count as fasting?" "That is the fasting for sacrifice, not the fasting of the heart-mind (xīn zhāi)." Yan Hui said, "May I ask about the fasting of the mind?" Confucius said, "Unify your will. Do not listen with your ears but with your mind; do not listen with your mind but with your qì 氣. Hearing stops at the ears; the mind stops at matching things. But qì is empty and waits upon all things. Only the dào 道 gathers in emptiness. This emptiness is the fasting of the mind."

Yan Hui said, "Before I received this, I was really Hui; now that I have received it, there has never been a Hui at all. Can this be called emptiness?" The Master said, "That's all of it! I tell you: you can enter and wander in his cage without being stirred by reputation. When he listens, sing out; when he does not, stop. Have no gate, no poison — dwell in unity and lodge in what cannot be helped, and you are nearly there. It is easy to walk leaving no tracks, but hard to walk without touching the ground. Working for man, it is easy to be false; working for Heaven, it is hard to be false. You have heard of flying with wings, but not of flying without wings; you have heard of knowing with knowledge..."
commentary:
This dialogue takes up the problem of the reformer who wants to enter the world of power and do good — 'man among men' — and shows how the usual equipment for that mission is precisely what destroys the mission. Yan Hui arrives armed with moral seriousness, a diagnosis of the tyrant, and a teaching he can apply. Confucius systematically strips each of these away. The passage dissolves the fixed distinction between the reformer's virtue and the tyrant's vice: as long as Yan Hui goes bearing his 'beauty' (his cultivation, his correct doctrine), he uses it to expose the ruler's 'ugliness,' and thereby becomes an aggressor who will provoke retaliation. Virtue that seeks recognition (dé dissipated into míng, reputation) and cleverness that arises from contention are not neutral tools — they are 'ill-omened weapons.' The self that shows up to fix another is already implicated in the same game of rivalry it means to correct.

Yan Hui offers three increasingly sophisticated strategies — inner emptiness, the triple stance of aligning with Heaven, men, and antiquity — and Confucius rejects each with the same devastating phrase: you are still 'making a teacher of your own mind' (shī xīn). Every strategy is still a fixed self deploying a technique. The turn comes with 'the fasting of the mind' (xīn zhāi). Ordinary fasting empties the stomach; this fasting empties the self. The progression — ear, to mind, to qì — moves from grasping (the ear catches sounds, the mind matches concepts) toward pure receptivity: qì is 'empty and waits upon all things.' Only in this emptiness does the dào gather. Yan Hui's breakthrough is not a better plan but the disappearance of the planner: 'there has never been a Hui at all.' The self/other distinction that made the mission dangerous simply drops out. Now he can enter the tyrant's 'cage' and respond — singing when heard, stopping when not — without staking his life on being recognized. The empty person leaves no tracks precisely because there is no fixed agent pressing an agenda. This is the Daoist reversal of the do-gooder: real efficacy in the world of men begins with the emptying of the meddling self.

Key Terms

**心齋 (xīn zhāi)** — 'Fasting of the heart-mind' — emptying the self of fixed intentions and concepts so one becomes purely receptive.
**氣 (qì)** — Vital breath-energy; here the mode of open, empty attention that 'waits upon all things,' beyond the grasping of ear and mind.
**德蕩乎名 (dé dàng hū míng)** — 'Virtue is dissipated by reputation' — moral cultivation leaks away when it becomes a bid for recognition.
practice: Try one conversation today as an exercise in the 'fasting of the mind.' Pick an interaction where you normally arrive with an agenda — a point to make, someone to correct, an impression to secure. Before it begins, drop the outcome you want. During the exchange, practice the three-stage listening: notice when you are merely hearing words (ears), then when you are matching them against your own concepts and rehearsing rebuttals (mind), and deliberately relax past both into simple receptivity — breathe, stay open, wait. Speak only when there is a genuine opening ('when he listens, sing out; when he does not, stop'), not to score points or be seen as right. Afterward, ask: how much of what I wanted to say was for the other person, and how much was to protect my own reputation? That honest look is the first taste of emptying the self.

」曰：「惡！

將執而不化，外合而內不訾，其庸詎可乎！

"I hear," answered Yen Hui, "that the Prince of Wei is of mature age, but of an unmanageable disposition. He behaves as if the State were of no account, and will not see his own faults. Consequently, the people perish; and their corpses lie about like so much undergrowth in a marsh. They are at extremities. And I have heard you, Sir, say that if a State is well governed it may be neglected; but that if it is badly governed, then we should visit it.

The science of medicine embraces many various diseases. I would test my knowledge in this sense, that perchance I may do some good to that State."

"Alas!" cried Confucius, "you will only succeed in bringing evil upon yourself. For Tao must not be distributed. If it is, it will lose its unity. If it loses its unity, it will be uncertain; and so cause mental disturbance,—from which there is no escape.

"The sages of old first got Tao for themselves, and then got it for others. Before you possess this yourself, what leisure have you to attend to the doings of wicked men? Besides, do you know what Virtue results in and where Wisdom ends? Virtue results in a desire for fame; Wisdom ends in contentions. In the struggle for fame men crush each other, while their wisdom but provokes rivalry. Both are baleful instruments, and may not be incautiously used.

"Besides, those who, before influencing by their own solid virtue and unimpeachable sincerity, and before reaching the heart by the example of their own disregard for name and fame, go and preach charity and duty to one's neighbour to wicked men,—only make these men hate them for their very goodness' sake. Such persons are called evil speakers. And those who speak evil of others are apt to be evil spoken of themselves. That, alas! will be your end.

"On the other hand, if the Prince loves the good and hates the bad, what object will you have in inviting him to change his ways? Before you have opened your mouth to preach, the Prince himself will have seized the opportunity to wrest the victory from you. Your eye will fall, your expression fade, your words will stick, your face will change, and your heart will die within you. It will be as though you took fire to quell fire, water to quell water, which is popularly known as 'pouring oil on the flames.' And if you begin with concessions, there will be no end to them. Neglect this sound advice, and you will be the victim of that violent man.

"Of old, Chieh murdered Kuan Lung Fêng, and Chou slew Prince Pi Kan. Their victims were both men who cultivated virtue themselves in order to secure the welfare of the people. But in doing this they offended their superiors; and therefore, because of that very moral culture, their superiors got rid of them, in order to guard their own reputations.

"Of old, Yao attacked the Ts'ung-chih and Hsü-ao countries, and Yü attacked the Yu-hu country. Homes were desolated and families destroyed by the slaughter of the inhabitants. Yet they fought without ceasing, and strove for victory to the last. These are instances known to all. Now if the Sages of old failed in their efforts against this love of fame, this desire for victory,—are you likely to succeed? But of course you have a scheme. Tell it to me."

"Gravity of demeanour," replied Yen Hui, "and dispassionateness; energy and singleness of purpose,—will this do?"

"Alas!" said Confucius, "that will not do. If you make a show of being perfect and obtrude yourself, the Prince's mood will be doubtful. Ordinarily, he is not opposed, and so he has come to take actual pleasure in trampling upon the feelings of others. And if he has thus failed in the practice of routine virtues, do you expect that he will take readily to higher ones? You may insist, but without result. Outwardly you will be right, but inwardly wrong. How then will you make him mend his ways?"

"Just so," replied Yen Hui. "I am inwardly straight, and outwardly crooked, completed after the models of antiquity.

"He who is inwardly straight is a servant of God. And he who is a servant of God knows that the Son of Heaven

and himself are equally the children of God. Shall then such a one trouble whether man visits him with evil or with good? Man indeed regards him as a child; and this is to be a servant of God.

"He who is outwardly crooked is a servant of man. He bows, he kneels, he folds his hands;—such is the ceremonial of a minister. What all men do, shall I dare not to do? What all men do, none will blame me for doing. This is to be a servant of man.

"He who is completed after the models of antiquity is a servant of the Sages of old. Although I utter the words of warning and take him to task, it is the Sages of old who speak, and not I. Thus my uprightness will not bring me into trouble, the servant of the Sages of old.—Will this do?"

(3) The responsibility rests, not with the mouthpiece, but with the authors of the doctrines enunciated.

"Alas!" replied Confucius, "No. Your plans are too many, and are lacking in prudence. However, your firmness will secure you from harm; but that is all. You will not influence him to such an extent that he shall seem to follow the dictates of his own heart."

"Then," said Yen Hui, "I am without resource, and venture to ask for a method."

Confucius said, "FAST.... Let me explain. You have a method, but it is difficult to practise. Those which are easy are not from God."

"Well," replied Yen Hui, "my family is poor, and for many months we have tasted neither wine nor flesh. Is not that fasting?"

"The fasting of religious observance it is," answered Confucius, "but not the fasting of the heart."

"And may I ask," said Yen Hui, "in what consists the fasting of the heart?"

The vital fluid which informs your whole being; in fact, "with your whole self."

But let hearing stop with the ears. Let the working of the mind stop with itself. Then the soul will be a negative existence, passively responsive to externals. In such a negative existence, only Tao can abide. And that negative state is the fasting of the heart."

"Then," said Yen Hui, "the reason I could not get the use of this method is my own individuality. If I could get the use of it, my individuality would have gone. Is this what you mean by the negative state?"

"Exactly so," replied the Master. "Let me tell you. If you can enter this man's domain without offending his amour propre, cheerful if he hears you, passive if he does not; without science, without drugs, simply living there in a state of complete indifference,—you will be near success. It is easy to stop walking: the trouble is to walk without touching the ground. As an agent of man, it is easy to deceive; but not as an agent of God. You have heard of winged creatures flying. You have never heard of flying without wings. You have heard of men being wise with wisdom. You have never heard of men wise without wisdom.

"Look at that window. Through it an empty room becomes bright with scenery; but the landscape stops outside. Were this not so, we should have an exemplification of sitting still and running away at one and the same time.

"In this sense, you may use your ears and eyes to communicate within, but shut out all wisdom from the mind.

And there where the supernatural

It was the instrument which Yü and Shun employed. It was the secret of the success of Fu Hsi and Chi Chü. Shall it not then be adopted by mankind in general?"

Tzŭ Kao, Duke of Shê,

being about to go on a mission to the Ch'i State, asked Confucius, saying, "The mission my sovereign is sending me on is a most important one. Of course, I shall be received with all due respect, but they will not take the same interest in the matter that I shall. And as an ordinary person cannot be pushed, still less a Prince, I am in a state of great alarm.

"Now you, Sir, have told me that in all undertakings great and small, Tao alone leads to a happy issue. Otherwise that, failing success, there is to be feared punishment from without, and with success, punishment from within; while exemption in case either of success or non-success falls only to the share of those who possess the virtue required.

I.e. those to whom the issue, as regards their own reward or punishment, is a matter of the completest indifference.

The term virtue, here as elsewhere unless specially notified, should be understood in the sense of exemplification of Tao.

"Well, I am not dainty with my food; neither am I always wanting to cool myself when hot. However, this morning I received my orders, and this evening I have been drinking iced water. I am so hot inside. Before I have put my hand to the business I am suffering punishment from within; and if I do not succeed I am sure to suffer punishment from without. Thus I get both punishments, which is really more than I can bear. Kindly tell me what there is to be done."

"There exist two sources of safety," Confucius replied. "One is Destiny: the other is Duty. A child's love for its parents is destiny. It is inseparable from the child's life. A subject's allegiance to his sovereign is duty. Beneath the canopy of heaven there is no place to which he can escape from it. These two sources of safety may be explained as follows. To serve one's parents without reference to place but only to the service, is the acme of filial piety. To serve one's prince without reference to the act but only to the service, is the perfection of a subject's loyalty. To serve one's own heart so as to permit neither joy nor sorrow within, but to cultivate resignation to the inevitable,—this is the climax of Virtue.

"Now a minister often finds himself in circumstances over which he has no control. But if he simply confines himself to his work, and is utterly oblivious of self, what leisure has he for loving life or hating death? And so you may safely go.

"But I have yet more to tell you. All intercourse, if personal, should be characterised by sincerity. If from a distance, it should be carried on in loyal terms. These terms will have to be transmitted by some one. Now the transmission of messages of good- or ill-will is the hardest thing possible. Messages of good-will are sure to be overdone with fine phrases; messages of ill-will with harsh ones. In each case the result is exaggeration, and a consequent failure to carry conviction, for which the envoy suffers. Therefore it was said in the Fa-yen,

'Confine yourself to simple statements of fact, shorn of all superfluous expression of feeling, and your risk will be small.'

"In trials of skill, at first all is friendliness; but at last it is all antagonism. Skill is pushed too far. So on festive occasions, the drinking which is in the beginning orderly enough, degenerates into riot and disorder. Festivity is pushed too far. It is in fact the same with all things: they begin with good faith and end with contempt. From small beginnings come great endings.

"Speech is like wind to wave. Action is liable to divergence from its true goal. By wind, waves are easily excited. Divergence from the true goal is fraught with danger. Thus angry feelings rise up without a cause. Specious words and dishonest arguments follow, as the wild random cries of an animal at the point of death. Both sides give way to passion. For where one party drives the other too much into a corner, resistance will always be provoked without apparent cause. And if the cause is not apparent, how much less will the ultimate effect be so?

"Travel beyond your instructions," is literally, "urge a settlement."

To pass the limit is to go to excess.'

"To deviate from, or to travel beyond instructions, may imperil the negotiation. A settlement to be successful must be lasting. It is too late to change an evil settlement once made.

"Therefore let yourself be carried along without fear, taking refuge in no alternative to preserve you from harm on either side. This is the utmost you can do. What need for considering your obligations? Better leave all to Destiny, difficult as this may be."

It is passing strange that this exposition of the laissez-aller inaction doctrine of Tao should be placed in the mouth of Confucius, who is thus made in some measure to discredit his own teachings. The commentators, however, see nothing anomalous in the position here assigned to the Sage.

Yen Ho

was about to become tutor to the eldest son of Prince Ling of the Wei State. Accordingly he observed to Chü Poh Yü,

"Here is a man whose disposition is naturally of a low order. To let him take his own unprincipled way is to endanger the State. To try to restrain him is to endanger one's personal safety. He has just wit enough to see faults in others, but not to see his own. I am consequently at a loss what to do."

"A good question indeed," replied Chü Poh Yü, "You must be careful, and begin by self-reformation. Outwardly you may adapt yourself, but inwardly you must keep up to your own standard. In this there are two points to be guarded against. You must not let the outward adaptation penetrate within, nor the inward standard manifest itself without. In the former case, you will fall, you will be obliterated, you will collapse, you will lie prostrate. In the latter case, you will be a sound, a name, a bogie, an uncanny thing. If he would play the child, do you play the child too. If he cast aside all sense of decorum, do you do so too. As far as he goes, do you go also. Thus you will reach him without offending him.

"Don't you know the story of the praying mantis? In its rage it stretched out its arms to prevent a chariot from passing, unaware that this was beyond its strength, so admirable was its energy! Be cautious. If you are always offending others by your superiority, you will probably come to grief.

"Do you not know that those who keep tigers do not venture to give them live animals as food, for fear of exciting their fury when killing the prey? Also, that whole animals are not given, for fear of exciting the tigers' fury when rending them? The periods of hunger and repletion are carefully watched in order to prevent such outbursts. The tiger is of a different species from man; but the latter too is manageable if properly managed, unmanageable if excited to fury.

"Those who are fond of horses surround them with various conveniences. Sometimes mosquitoes or flies trouble them; and then, unexpectedly to the animal, a groom will brush them off, the result being that the horse breaks his bridle, and hurts his head and chest. The intention is good, but there is a want of real care for the horse. Against this you must be on your guard."

A certain artisan was travelling to the Ch'i State. On reaching Ch'ü-yüan, he saw a sacred li tree,

large enough to hide an ox behind it, a hundred spans in girth, towering up ten cubits over the hill top, and carrying behind it branches, many tens of the smallest of which were of a size for boats. Crowds stood gazing at it, but our artisan took no notice, and went on his way without even casting a look behind. His apprentice however gazed his fill, and when he caught up his master, said, "Ever since I have handled an adze in your service, I have never seen such a splendid piece of timber as that. How was it that you, sir, did not care to stop and look at it?"

"It's not worth talking about," replied his master. "It's good for nothing. Make a boat of it,—'twould sink. A coffin,—'twould rot. Furniture,—'twould soon break down. A door,—'twould sweat. A pillar,—'twould be worm-eaten. It is wood of no quality, and of no use. That is why it has attained its present age."

When the artisan reached home, he dreamt that the tree appeared to him in a dream and spoke as follows:—"What is it that you compare me with? Is it with the more elegant trees?—The cherry-apple, the pear, the orange, the pumelo, and other fruit-bearers, as soon as their fruit ripens are stripped and treated with indignity. The great boughs are snapped off, the small ones scattered abroad. Thus do these trees by their own value injure their own lives. They cannot fulfil their allotted span of years, but perish prematurely in mid-career from their entanglement with the world around them. Thus it is with all things. For a long period my aim was to be useless. Many times I was in danger, but at length I succeeded, and so became useful as I am to-day. But had I then been of use, I should not now be of the great use I am. Moreover, you and I belong both to the same category of things. Have done then with this criticism of others. Is a good-for-nothing fellow whose dangers are not yet passed a fit person to talk of a good-for-nothing tree?"

When our artisan awaked and told his dream, his apprentice said, "If the tree aimed at uselessness, how was it that it became a sacred tree?"

"What you don't understand," replied his master, "don't talk about. That was merely to escape from the attacks of its enemies. Had it not become sacred, how many would have wanted to cut it down! The means of safety adopted were different from ordinary means,

and to test these by ordinary canons leaves one far wide of the mark."

Tzŭ Ch'i of Nan-poh

was travelling on the Shang mountain when he saw a large tree which astonished him very much. A thousand chariot teams could have found shelter under its shade.

"What tree is this?" cried Tzŭ Ch'i. "Surely it must have unusually fine timber." Then looking up, he saw that its branches were too crooked for rafters; while as to the trunk he saw that its irregular grain made it valueless for coffins. He tasted a leaf, but it took the skin off his lips; and its odour was so strong that it would make a man as it were drunk for three days together.

"Ah!" said Tzŭ Ch'i. "This tree is good for nothing, and that is how it has attained this size. A wise man might well follow its example."

In the State of Sung there is a place called Ching-shih, where thrive the beech, the cedar, and the mulberry. Such as are of a one-handed span or so in girth are cut down for monkey-cages. Those of two or three two-handed spans are cut down for the beams of fine houses. Those of seven or eight such spans are cut down for the solid sides of rich men's coffins.

To this day, the very best kinds of wood are still reserved for the "planks of old age."

Thus they do not fulfil their allotted span of years, but perish in mid-career beneath the axe. Such is the misfortune which overtakes worth.

For the sacrifices to the River God, neither bulls with white cheeks, nor pigs with large snouts, nor men suffering from piles, were allowed to be used. This had been revealed to the soothsayers, and these characteristics were consequently regarded as inauspicious. The wise, however, would regard them as extremely auspicious.

There was a hunchback named Su. His jaws touched his navel. His shoulders were higher than his head. His hair knot looked up to the sky. His viscera were upside down. His buttocks were where his ribs should have been. By tailoring, or washing, he was easily able to earn his living. By sifting rice he could make enough to support a family of ten.

When orders came down for a conscription, the hunchback stood unconcerned among the crowd. And similarly, in matters of public works, his deformity shielded him from being employed.

On the other hand, when it came to donations of grain, the hunchback received as much as three chung,

and of firewood, ten faggots. And if physical deformity was thus enough to preserve his body until its allotted end, how much more would not moral and mental deformity avail!

A moral and mental deviation would be still more likely to condemn a man to that neglect from his fellows which is so conducive to our real welfare.

When Confucius was in the Ch'u State, the eccentric Chieh Yü passed his door, saying, "O phœnix, O phœnix, how has thy virtue fallen!—

When you might be, or might have been, of use. The idea conveyed is that Confucianism was unsuited to its age. See Lun-yü, ch. xviii.

If Tao prevails on earth, prophets will fulfil their mission. If Tao does not prevail, they will but preserve themselves. At the present day they will but just escape.

"The honours of this world are light as feathers, yet none estimate them at their true value. The misfortunes of this life are weighty as the earth itself, yet none can keep out of their reach. No more, no more, seek to influence by virtue. Beware, beware, move cautiously on! O ferns, O ferns, wound not my steps! Through my tortuous journey wound not my feet! Hills suffer from the trees they produce. Fat burns by its own combustibility. Cinnamon trees furnish food: therefore they are cut down. The lacquer tree is felled for use. All men know the use of useful things; but they do not know the use of useless things."
translation:
Yan Hui came to see Confucius and asked leave to travel. Confucius said, "Where are you going?" "To Wei." "To do what?" Yan Hui said, "I have heard that the ruler of Wei is young and headstrong. He treats his state carelessly and does not see his own faults. He wastes his people's lives so recklessly that the dead fill the marshes like heaps of cut reeds — the people have nowhere to turn. I once heard you, Master, say: 'Leave the well-governed state and go to the one in chaos; there are many sick at the doctor's gate.' I wish to take what I have learned and think out how to act, so that perhaps that state may be healed."

Confucius said, "Ah! You will only go there and be executed. The dào 道 does not want to be mixed up with other things; mixed, it multiplies; multiplied, it brings disturbance; disturbance brings anxiety, and anxiety brings no rescue. The perfected people of old first secured it in themselves, and only then in others. If what you hold in yourself is not yet settled, what leisure have you to correct the conduct of a tyrant?

"And do you understand how virtue (dé) gets dissipated and where cleverness comes from? Virtue is dissipated by the pursuit of reputation, and cleverness comes out of rivalry. Reputation is a thing by which people grind each other down; cleverness is a weapon of contention. Both are ill-omened tools, not the way to complete your conduct.

"Even if your virtue is deep and your sincerity solid, you have not yet touched the man's temper; even if you do not contend for reputation, you have not yet reached his heart. If you then force words of benevolence and righteousness, of standards and measuring-lines, before a tyrant, you are using another man's ugliness to show off your own beauty. This is called injuring people. He who injures people will surely be injured in return — you will likely be the one injured.

"Besides, if the ruler truly loved the worthy and hated the unworthy, what use would he have for you to make a difference? Better say nothing; for a king or lord will always exploit others and press his own quickness. Your eyes will be dazzled, your face forced into calm, your mouth busy defending yourself, your bearing bending to fit, and your heart will end up agreeing with him. This is fighting fire with fire, water with water — call it 'making more.' Once you begin to yield there is no end. And if you press your earnest words when he does not yet trust you, you will surely die before the tyrant.

"Long ago Jie killed Guan Longfeng, and Zhòu killed Prince Bigan. Both were men who cultivated themselves and bent down to comfort the ruler's people, and so, from below, went against their superiors. So their rulers, precisely because of their cultivation, destroyed them. These were men who loved reputation. Long ago Yao attacked Cong, Zhi, and Xu'ao, and Yu attacked You-hu. The states were laid waste, the rulers put to death — because their use of arms never stopped, their craving for gain never ceased. All these sought reputation and gain. Have you alone not heard of them? Reputation and gain — even the sages could not master them, much less you!

"Still, you must have some plan. Try telling me."

Yan Hui said, "If I am upright and empty, diligent and single-minded — will that do?" Confucius said, "No! How could it? The man is full of yang energy, high and overbearing, his moods unpredictable. Ordinary people do not dare oppose him, and he tramples on whatever others feel, seeking his own satisfaction. Even the slow, daily working of virtue cannot form in him — how much less some great transformation! He will hold fast and not change; he may agree outwardly but inwardly not even reflect. How could this work?"

"Then suppose I am straight within and yielding without, complete in myself while aligning with the ancients. Being straight within, I am a companion of tiān 天 (Heaven). One who is a companion of Heaven knows that the Son of Heaven and I are alike children of Heaven — so why should I care whether people approve or disapprove of my words? Such a one people call a child; this is to be a companion of Heaven. Yielding without, I am a companion of men. To lift the tablet, kneel, and bow — this is the etiquette of a minister. Everyone does it; dare I not? Doing what others do, no one can find fault with me — this is to be a companion of men. Complete in myself while aligning with the ancients, I am a companion of antiquity. Though my words are instruction, they aim at what is real, and they belong to the ancients, not to me. In this way, though I speak straight, I take no harm — this is to be a companion of antiquity. Would this do?"

Confucius said, "No! How could it? There is too much regulation, and no fitness. Though it is stiff and rigid, it commits no crime. Still, it stops at that — how could it reach transformation? You are still making a teacher of your own mind."

Yan Hui said, "I have nothing more to offer. May I ask the method?" Confucius said, "Fast, and I will tell you. Do you think it is easy to act with a purposeful mind? One who thinks it easy — bright Heaven will not agree." Yan Hui said, "My family is poor; I have gone months without drinking wine or eating meat or strong-smelling food. Can this count as fasting?" "That is the fasting for sacrifice, not the fasting of the heart-mind (xīn zhāi)." Yan Hui said, "May I ask about the fasting of the mind?" Confucius said, "Unify your will. Do not listen with your ears but with your mind; do not listen with your mind but with your qì 氣. Hearing stops at the ears; the mind stops at matching things. But qì is empty and waits upon all things. Only the dào 道 gathers in emptiness. This emptiness is the fasting of the mind."

Yan Hui said, "Before I received this, I was really Hui; now that I have received it, there has never been a Hui at all. Can this be called emptiness?" The Master said, "That's all of it! I tell you: you can enter and wander in his cage without being stirred by reputation. When he listens, sing out; when he does not, stop. Have no gate, no poison — dwell in unity and lodge in what cannot be helped, and you are nearly there. It is easy to walk leaving no tracks, but hard to walk without touching the ground. Working for man, it is easy to be false; working for Heaven, it is hard to be false. You have heard of flying with wings, but not of flying without wings; you have heard of knowing with knowledge..."
abhyasa: Try one conversation today as an exercise in the 'fasting of the mind.' Pick an interaction where you normally arrive with an agenda — a point to make, someone to correct, an impression to secure. Before it begins, drop the outcome you want. During the exchange, practice the three-stage listening: notice when you are merely hearing words (ears), then when you are matching them against your own concepts and rehearsing rebuttals (mind), and deliberately relax past both into simple receptivity — breathe, stay open, wait. Speak only when there is a genuine opening ('when he listens, sing out; when he does not, stop'), not to score points or be seen as right. Afterward, ask: how much of what I wanted to say was for the other person, and how much was to protect my own reputation? That honest look is the first taste of emptying the self.

顏回見仲尼，請行。
曰：「奚之？
」曰：「將之衛。
」曰：「奚為焉？
」曰：「回聞衛君，其年壯，其行獨。
輕用其國，而不見其過。
輕用民死，死者以國量乎澤，若蕉，民其無如矣！
回嘗聞之夫子曰：'治國去之，亂國就之。
醫門多疾。
'愿以所聞，思其所行，庶幾其國有瘳乎！
」仲尼曰：「譆，若殆往而刑耳！
夫道不欲雜，雜則多，多則擾，擾則憂，憂而不救。
古之至人，先存諸己而后存諸人。
所存於己者未定，何暇至於暴人之所行！
且若亦知夫德之所蕩而知之所為出乎哉？
德蕩乎名，知出乎爭。
名也者，相軋也﹔知也者，爭之器也。
二者凶器，非所以盡行也。
且德厚信矼，未達人氣﹔名聞不爭，未達人心。
而強以仁義繩墨之言衒暴人之前者，是以人惡有其美也，命之曰菑人。
菑人者，人必反菑之。
若殆為人菑夫。
且苟為人悅賢而惡不肖，惡用而求有以異？
若唯無詔，王公必將乘人而鬥其捷。
而目將熒之，而色將平之，口將營之，容將形之，心且成之。
是以火救火，以水救水，名之曰益多。
順始無窮，若殆以不信厚言，必死於暴人之前矣！
且昔者桀殺關龍逢，紂殺王子比干，是皆修其身以下傴拊人之民，以下拂其上者也，故其君因其修以擠之。
是好名者也。
昔者堯攻叢、枝、胥、敖，禹攻有扈。
國為虛厲，身為刑戮。
其用兵不止，其求實無已，是皆求名實者也，而獨不聞之乎？
名實者，聖人之所不能勝也，而況若乎！
雖然，若必有以也，嘗以語我來。
」顏回曰「端而虛，勉而一，則可乎？
」曰：「惡！
惡可！
夫以陽為充孔揚，采色不定，常人之所不違，因案人之所感，以求容與其心。
名之曰日漸之德不成，而況大德乎！
將執而不化，外合而內不訾，其庸詎可乎！
」「然則我內直而外曲，成而上比。
內直者，與天為徒。
與天為徒者，知天子之與己，皆天之所子，而獨以己言蘄乎而人善之，蘄乎而人不善之邪？
若然者，人謂之童子，是之謂與天為徒。
外曲者，與人之為徒也。
擎跽曲拳，人臣之禮也。
人皆為之，吾敢不為邪？
為人之所為者，人亦無疵焉，是之謂與人為徒。
成而上比者，與古為徒。
其言雖教，適之實也，古之有也，非吾有也。
若然者，雖直而不病，是之謂與古為徒。
若是則可乎？
」仲尼曰：「惡！
惡可！
大多政法而不諜。
雖固亦無罪。
雖然，止是耳矣，夫胡可以及化！
猶師心者也。
」顏回曰：「吾無以進矣，敢問其方。
」仲尼曰：「齋，吾將語若。
有心而為之，其易邪？
易之者，皞天不宜。
」顏回曰：「回之家貧，唯不飲酒不茹葷者數月矣。
如此則可以為齋乎？
」曰：「是祭祀之齋，非心齋也。
」回曰：「敢問心齋。
」仲尼曰：「若一志，無聽之以耳而聽之以心﹔無聽之以心而聽之以氣。
耳止於聽，心止於符。
氣也者，虛而待物者也。
唯道集虛。
虛者，心齋也」顏回曰：「回之未始得使，實有回也﹔得使之也，未始有回也，可謂虛乎？
」夫子曰：「盡矣！
吾語若：若能入游其樊而無感其名，入則鳴，不入則止。
無門無毒，一宅而寓於不得已，則幾矣。
「絕跡易，無行地難。
為人使易以偽，為天使難以偽。

pratibha_layers.label: Pratibha Translation
pratibha_layers.body:
Yan Hui says, "I have reached my limit. Please give me a method."

Confucius says, "Fast. I will tell you. You have plans, but this cannot be done by planning."

Yan Hui says, "My household is poor. For months we have taken no wine and no rich food. Is that fasting?"

Confucius says, "That is ritual fasting, not heart-fasting."

Yan Hui asks, "What is heart-fasting?"

Confucius says, "Unify your intention. Do not listen with the ears; listen with the heart-mind. Do not listen with the heart-mind; listen with *qi*. Hearing stops at the ear. The heart-mind stops at signs. *Qi* is emptiness, waiting for things. Only Tao gathers in emptiness. That emptiness is heart-fasting."

pratibha_layers.label: Pratibha Commentary
pratibha_layers.body:
The philosophical claim is that transformation happens through emptied receptivity, not through more strategic intention. The counterintuitive move is sharp: Yan Hui asks for a method to influence a ruler, and Confucius answers with de-methodologizing the self that wants to influence. In ordinary discourse, "fasting" means deprivation from objects (food, wine, pleasure). In this passage, fasting is the suspension of appropriative cognition itself. That shift from external abstinence to internal de-cluttering is the hinge of the teaching.

In Daoist context, this is an early articulation of a non-coercive epistemology. The mind that rushes to classify, persuade, and impose cannot receive the pattern of the situation. "Listening with qi" names a more primordial responsiveness than argument and preference. The line "only Tao gathers in emptiness" is not metaphysical ornament; it is practical phenomenology: wherever the inner field is packed with opinion, Tao has no room to move as guidance.

Existentially, heart-fasting redefines effective action. It does not produce passivity, and it does not deny ethical stakes. It removes internal noise so action can arise from contact rather than projection. In relationships, leadership, or conflict, this means withholding the compulsion to win the frame before one has actually received what is present. Zhuangzi's wager is that genuine efficacy requires first becoming permeable. The one who is empty enough to receive is paradoxically the one most capable of precise response.

pratibha_layers.label: Practice (Abhyasa)
pratibha_layers.body: Before one difficult conversation today, sit for three minutes and notice each impulse to prepare your argument; with every impulse, exhale and silently say "empty," then enter the conversation with one task only: receive fully before speaking once.

items.definition: "heart-mind fasting" (*xīn* = heart-mind, *zhāi* = fasting/purification) -> in this passage, suspension of conceptual and egoic consumption -> default translation "fasting of the heart" can sound devotional; the operative meaning is cognitive de-appropriation so Tao can function through you.

breath-vitality, animating field, processive energy -> contextual meaning: pre-conceptual responsiveness that can receive situations before judgment hardens them -> translated as "soul" or "spirit" in older renderings, but that misses its embodied-process sense.

emptiness, openness, unoccupied capacity -> here the condition in which Tao "collects" or becomes effective -> "negative existence" in old translation sounds privative; xū is fertile openness, not nihilistic absence.

sign, token, match-mark -> in this context, the mind's tendency to stop at symbols and fixed interpretations -> default translations omit it, losing the warning that cognition often mistakes labels for living reality.

items.resonance: the mind is repeatedly returned to stillness and established in the Self through non-grasping discipline. Structurally, both passages interrupt discursivity to allow a deeper ordering principle to guide action.
items.divergence: The Gita stabilizes this process in Atman-realization and yogic concentration, while Zhuangzi emphasizes situational receptivity and unforced responsiveness without a fixed metaphysical witness.

items.citation: Vijnana Bhairava Tantra, dharana on the gap between breaths
items.resonance: both texts treat interior pause as operative, not empty in the trivial sense. The gap becomes the access-point for a wider intelligence than conceptual mind.
items.divergence: The VBT codifies explicit contemplative techniques tied to recognition of consciousness; Zhuangzi offers a behavioral-epistemic instruction embedded in political/ethical encounter.

items.resonance: both traditions train a pause between impression and reaction so freedom is exercised before compulsion.
items.divergence: Stoicism frames pause as rational assent-management by *prohairesis*; Zhuangzi frames it as emptying into Tao so action emerges from attunement rather than deliberate control.

translation_literal:
In Lu there was a man named Wang Tai who had lost a foot to punishment, yet the number of people who followed him as students rivaled those who followed Confucius. Chang Ji asked Confucius: "Wang Tai has had a foot cut off, yet his followers split Lu evenly with you. He does not lecture standing up, nor debate sitting down. People go to him empty and return full. Is there really such a thing as wordless teaching, a mind that reaches completion without any outward form? What kind of man is this?"

Confucius said: "That master is a sage. It is only that I have been slow and have not yet gone to him. I intend to make him my teacher — how much more should those less worthy than me! Why only the state of Lu? I would lead the whole world to follow him."

Chang Ji said: "He is a man missing a foot, yet he surpasses you, master — so he must be far beyond the ordinary man. If that is so, how uniquely does he use his mind?"

Confucius said: "Death and life are indeed great matters, yet they cannot alter him. Even if heaven and earth toppled and fell, he would not be lost along with them. He discerns what is without dependence and does not shift with things; he treats the transformations of things as their appointed course and holds fast to their source."

Chang Ji said: "What do you mean?"

Confucius said: "Looked at from the side of difference, the liver and gallbladder are as far apart as the states of Chu and Yue. Looked at from the side of sameness, the ten thousand things are all one. A man like this does not even bother with what suits the ears and eyes; he lets his mind wander in the harmony of virtue (dé 德). He sees things in their oneness and does not notice what is lost. He regards the loss of his foot as no more than the shedding of a clump of earth."

Chang Ji said: "He works on himself. Through knowing he grasps his mind, and through his mind he grasps his constant mind. But why should the world make him its center?"

Confucius said: "No one uses flowing water as a mirror; they mirror themselves in still water. Only what is still can still the multitude that seek stillness. Of things that receive their life from the earth, only the pine and cypress stand truly upright, staying green through winter and summer. Of those that receive their life from heaven, only Yao and Shun stood truly upright, at the head of all things. Fortunate enough to correct their own lives, they could correct the lives of the multitude. As for the proof of one who has preserved the origin, the reality of fearlessness — a single brave warrior may charge into an army of nine divisions. If a man seeking only fame and self-assurance can be like this, how much more one who takes heaven and earth for his office, holds all things in his storehouse, treats his six limbs as a mere lodging, regards eyes and ears as passing images, unifies all his knowing into one knowledge, and whose mind has never died! Such a man will choose his day and ascend into the far distance, and people will follow him. But why would he ever bother to make worldly things his business?"

Shen Tu Jia had lost a foot, and studied under Bo Hun Wu Ren together with Zi Chan of Zheng. Zi Chan said to Shen Tu Jia: "When I leave first, you stay behind; when you leave first, I stay behind." The next day, they were again sitting together in the same hall on the same mat. Zi Chan said: "When I leave first, you stay behind; when you leave first, I stay behind. Now I am about to leave — can you stay behind, or not? And when you see a high minister you don't get out of his way — do you take yourself for the equal of a minister?"

Shen Tu Jia said: "Within our master's gate is there really any such thing as 'the minister'? You are pleased with your ministerial rank and put others behind you. I have heard: 'If the mirror is bright, dust does not settle; if dust settles, it is not bright. Live long with a worthy man and you become free of fault.' Now you have come to take our master as the great thing, yet you still speak like this — is that not a fault?"

Zi Chan said: "You are already in such a state, yet you still contend with Yao over goodness. Reckon up your virtue — is it not enough to turn you back on yourself?"

Shen Tu Jia said: "Those who excuse their faults and claim they did not deserve to lose their footing are many; those who do not excuse their faults and admit they did not deserve to keep their footing are few. To know what cannot be helped and rest in it as one's destiny (mìng 命) — only the person of virtue can do that. Wandering within Yi the archer's range: the center of the field is where the arrow strikes; yet if you are not hit, that too is destiny. Many people with two whole feet have laughed at me for not having them. I used to flush with anger, but when I come to the master's place I let it all fall away and return to myself. I do not know whether the master has washed me clean with goodness, or whether I awakened on my own. I have wandered with the master nineteen years and he has never once been aware that I am a man without a foot. Now you and I wander within the realm of the inner form, and yet you seek me out in the realm of the outer body — is that not a fault?"

Zi Chan, startled, changed his expression and manner, and said: "Say no more."

In Lu there was a man named Shu Shan No-Toes, who had lost his toes. He came walking on his heels to see Confucius. Confucius said: "You were not careful, and so you fell into disaster before. Even coming now, what use is it?"

No-Toes said: "It was only that I did not understand my duties and treated my body lightly — that is how I lost my feet. Now I have come, and there is still something more honored than feet that survives, and this I am striving to keep whole. Heaven covers everything, earth carries everything; I took you, master, for heaven and earth — how could I have known you would be like this!"

Confucius said: "I have been narrow. Master, why not come in? Let me set out what I have learned." But No-Toes went out.

Confucius said: "Students, take this to heart! No-Toes is a man missing his toes, yet he still strives to learn in order to make up for the wrongs of his earlier conduct — how much more one whose virtue is whole!"

No-Toes told Lao Dan: "Kong Qiu — as for being the utmost person, he is not there yet, is he? Why does he keep coming so eagerly to study with you? He hankers after a reputation for the strange and the marvelous — does he not know that the utmost person takes such things as fetters and manacles on himself?"

Lao Dan said: "Why not simply make him treat death and life as one thread, the permissible and the impermissible as one string, and so loosen his fetters — might that be possible?"

No-Toes said: "It is heaven (tiān 天) that has punished him — how can it be loosened?"
commentary:
This chapter mounts a sustained assault on the distinction between whole and mutilated bodies, and beneath it, between outer form and inner power. Its heroes are all men who have suffered amputation as legal punishment — the most visibly "defective" and socially disgraced people imaginable — and each of them is presented as more complete than the intact. The Chinese word for their condition, wù 兀, literally means to have a foot chopped off; the chapter title, "the evidence of virtue complete," is deliberately ironic: the men whose bodies are conspicuously incomplete are the ones whose dé 德 is full.

The method throughout is to relocate the criterion of wholeness. Confucius, speaking uncharacteristically as a mouthpiece for Daoist insight, explains that Wang Tai neither teaches nor debates, yet transforms people, because he holds to "what does not depend on anything" (wú jiǎ 無假) and does not shift when things shift. The pivotal line is the double view: from the standpoint of difference, even organs inside one body — liver and gallbladder — are as remote as warring states; from the standpoint of sameness, the ten thousand things are one. A lost foot, seen this way, is like a clod of dirt falling away, not a diminishment of the self. The distinction whole/maimed is not refuted by argument but dissolved by shifting the vantage point from which the counting is done.

The still-water image sharpens this. Flowing water cannot reflect; only stillness reflects, and only what is itself still can arrest the restlessness of others. The sages and the pine and cypress are "upright" not because they conform to an external standard but because they hold their own source through winter and summer, life and death. This is the model of a wholeness that no punishment can reach.

The second dialogue turns the theme social. Zi Chan, a powerful minister, is embarrassed to share a mat with a one-footed convict and keeps trying to enforce a distinction of rank and body. Shen Tu Jia's rebuke is devastating: inside the master's gate there is no such thing as a "minister." He accepts his mutilation as mìng 命, destiny — the arrow that happens to strike within the archer's range. The luminous line is "you and I wander within the inner form, yet you seek me out in the outer body." Zi Chan's whole way of sorting people is exposed as a search in the wrong place.

The final movement is the sharpest. No-Toes goes to Confucius but finds him still fixated on carelessness and punishment — on the outer record — and leaves. His verdict, delivered to Laozi, is that Confucius chains himself with the pursuit of reputation for cleverness and marvels. The chapter ends on a startling reversal: the men society branded as punished are free, while the celebrated teacher is the one under a punishment that cannot be undone — 'heaven's punishment,' the self-imposed bondage of caring about how one appears. The truly mutilated man, it turns out, is the one whose body is whole but whose mind is fettered to distinctions.

Key Terms

**兀 wù** — Having a foot amputated as judicial punishment; the marked, disgraced bodily condition of the chapter's heroes.
**德 dé** — Inner power or virtue — here the wholeness that outer mutilation cannot touch.
**命 mìng** — Destiny or the appointed course of things; what cannot be helped and is to be rested in rather than resisted.
practice: Pick something you privately count as a defect or loss — a physical limitation, an aging feature, a failure on your record, a thing that draws pity or judgment. Spend five minutes deliberately looking at yourself, as Shen Tu Jia does, "within the inner form" rather than "outside" it: notice that the awareness reading these words, the mind that has wandered through your whole life, has not been amputated by that loss at all. Then, once today, when you catch yourself flushing at someone's judgment or your own comparison, try the shed-clod-of-earth move: let the feeling fall away rather than defending against it, and return to the plain fact of the mind that is still here. The point is not to pretend the loss didn't happen, but to stop making it the measure of who you are.
