translation_literal:
Nie Que questioned Wang Ni. Four times he asked, and four times Wang Ni said he did not know. At this Nie Que jumped up in delight and went to tell Pu Yizi. Pu Yizi said, "So now you finally understand? The lord Yu of the house of You never measured up to the great Tai. The lord Yu still hoarded benevolence in order to win people over; he did win them, but he never got outside the realm of judging others as 'not us.' The great Tai slept in easy calm and woke in simple ease. One moment he let himself be called a horse, the next a cow. His knowing was genuine and trustworthy, his virtue utterly true — yet he never entered into the realm of judging others as 'not us.'"

Jian Wu went to see the madman Jie Yu. Jie Yu said, "What did Zhongshi tell you the other day?" Jian Wu said, "He told me that when one governs people, one issues from oneself the rules, standards, principles, and measures — so who would dare not obey and be transformed?" Jie Yu said, "That is bogus virtue. Governing the world that way is like wading across the sea, chiseling out a river, or making a mosquito carry a mountain on its back. When the sage governs, does he govern externals? He sets himself right first, then acts; he simply makes sure a thing can actually be done. The bird flies high to escape the harm of arrows and nets; the little field mouse digs deep beneath the sacred mound to avoid the danger of being smoked out or dug up. Have even these two little creatures no sense?"

Tian Gen was wandering on the sunny side of Mount Yin. When he reached the Liao River, he happened to meet the Nameless Man and asked him, "Please tell me how to govern the world." The Nameless Man said, "Go away! You are a vulgar fellow — what an unpleasant thing to ask! I am just about to keep company with the Maker of Things; and when I tire of that, I ride the bird of light emptiness out beyond the six directions, roaming the land of Not-Anything-At-All, to dwell in the fields of boundless open space. Why do you come pestering my mind with this talk of governing the world?" Tian Gen asked again. The Nameless Man said, "Let your mind wander in the plain and simple; blend your qì 氣 with the vast stillness; follow the natural course of things and leave no room for private preference — then the world will be governed."

Yangzi Ju went to see Lao Dan and said, "Suppose there is a man here — quick and vigorous, strong and firm, seeing into things with piercing clarity, tireless in studying the dào 道. May such a one be ranked with the enlightened kings?" Lao Dan said, "To a sage, this is mere clerkishness and clever bondage — wearing out the body and alarming the heart. The tiger and leopard's markings bring on the hunter; the agile monkey and the dog-catching hound are what get them leashed. Can such a one be ranked with the enlightened kings?" Yangzi Ju looked uneasy and said, "May I ask about the governing of the enlightened king?" Lao Dan said, "The enlightened king's governing: his merit covers the world, yet seems not to come from himself; his transforming influence extends to the ten thousand things, yet the people do not depend on it. There is something there, but no name can be raised for it; he lets each thing delight in itself. He stands on the unfathomable and roams where there is Nothing."

In Zheng there was a shaman of spirit-power named Ji Xian. He knew whether people would die or live, survive or perish, meet fortune or disaster, live long or die young — naming the very year, month, week, and day, as though he were a god. When the people of Zheng saw him coming, they dropped everything and fled. Liezi went to see him and came home drunk with wonder. He told Huzi, "I used to think your dào 道 was the highest, but now here is something higher still!" Huzi said, "I have taught you the outer patterns of it, but not yet its substance — and you think you have really got the dào? A flock of hens with no cock — how will there be eggs? You take the dào and try to compete with the world, insisting on being believed, and so you let a man read your face. Try bringing him here; let him look at me."

The next day Liezi brought him to see Huzi. Coming out, the shaman said to Liezi, "Ah! Your master is a dead man. He won't live — not for another ten days. I saw something strange in him — I saw wet ashes." Liezi went in, tears soaking his collar, and told Huzi. Huzi said, "Just now I showed him the pattern of the earth — motionless growth, neither quaking nor still. He probably glimpsed my life-springs sealed shut. Try bringing him again."

The next day he brought him once more. Coming out, the shaman said, "How lucky your master is to have met me! He's recovering. He's fully alive again! I saw the sealed springs opening." Liezi went in and reported this. Huzi said, "Just now I showed him heaven-and-earth — where name and substance find no entry, and the life-spring rises up from the heels. He probably glimpsed the wholesome springs. Try bringing him again."

The next day he brought him once more. Coming out, the shaman said, "Your master is not steady; I can find nothing to read. Let him settle, and I'll read him again." Liezi went in and reported this. Huzi said, "Just now I showed him the great emptiness where nothing prevails — he probably glimpsed my balanced-qì springs. Where a whale wheels about, there is an abyss; where water stands still, there is an abyss; where water flows, there is an abyss. The abyss has nine names; I showed him three of them. Try bringing him again."

The next day he brought him once more. Before the shaman had even settled into place, he lost his composure and ran. Huzi said, "Go after him!" Liezi ran but could not catch him. He came back and reported, "He's vanished, he's gone, I couldn't catch him." Huzi said, "Just now I showed him what had not yet begun to come out of my source. I met him empty and yielding, wheeling with him, so that he could not tell who or what I was — I bent like grass with the wind, I flowed like the current, and that is why he fled."

After this Liezi realized he had never really begun to learn, and went home. For three years he did not go out. He cooked for his wife and fed the pigs as though feeding people. He took no side in affairs. He returned from carving and polishing back to the uncarved block, and stood alone, solid as a clod, amid all the tangle, sealed within it — and thus he stayed to the end.

Do not be a corpse for fame. Do not be a storehouse of schemes. Do not take on the burden of affairs. Do not be a master of knowledge.
commentary:
This chapter, traditionally titled "Fit for Emperors and Kings," strings together seven scenes that all worry the same knot: what governing really is. Its radical move is to dissolve the distinction between ruling others and being empty of self. Every image of the good ruler here turns out to be an image of a person who has stopped issuing anything from a fixed self.

The opening contrast sets the terms. Lord Yu still "hoards benevolence to win people" — his goodness is a strategy aimed at others, and precisely because it aims, it stays trapped in the division of us-and-them, self-and-not-self (the odd phrase 非人, judging what is 'not us'). The great Tai never even sorts people that way; he lets himself be called horse or cow without correcting the label, because he has no fixed self-image to defend. The paradox: the more genuinely one is oneself, the less one insists on a self. This is why Nie Que jumps for joy at four answers of "I don't know" — not-knowing is the doorway out of the self that governs.

Jie Yu then attacks conventional statecraft directly. Imposing rules "out of oneself" onto others is described as physically absurd — a mosquito hauling a mountain. Real order isn't projected outward (治外, governing externals); it starts with getting oneself right, after which action follows naturally. Even the high-flying bird and the deep-burrowing mouse know how to look after themselves; the officious ruler knows less than a field mouse.

The long Huzi story is the passage's masterpiece of dissolving distinctions. Ji Xian the face-reader can name your death to the day — but only because there is a fixed, readable self there to name. Huzi defeats him not by resistance but by showing successive faces: sealed earth, opening life, balanced emptiness, and finally "what has not yet begun to come out of my source." At that last showing there is nothing to read, no fixed configuration, no self that persists across the moments — so the diviner, whose whole art depends on a stable object, panics and runs. Life and death, fortune and doom, the whole grid the shaman trades in, collapses when confronted with someone who is genuinely empty and flowing, "bending like grass, flowing like water." The self that could be diagnosed has dissolved.

The closing lines gather this into practice: don't be a corpse where fame is stored, a warehouse of plots, a load-bearer for tasks, a proprietor of knowledge. These are four ways of being a fixed something for others to grip — exactly what Huzi refused to be, and what makes both a person and a ruler graspable, readable, and finally exhausted. To govern well, in this text, is to become ungraspable in the good sense: present, responsive, and empty of the rigid self that everyone else is busy defending.

Key Terms

**非人 fēi rén** — Literally 'not-human/not-us' — the mental sorting of others into a category outside oneself; the division the sage never enters.
**無何有之鄉 wú hé yǒu zhī xiāng** — The 'land of not-anything-at-all' — Zhuangzi's image for open, unconditioned space beyond fixed things and roles.
**朴 pǔ** — The uncarved block — original simplicity one returns to after dropping the 'carving and polishing' of cultivated self-image.
practice: When someone calls you by a label or role today — competent, helper, leader, whatever — let yourself be called that without internal correction or defense, as the great Tai let himself be called horse or cow. Notice the urge to clarify, explain, or adjust how they see you, and instead exhale it away. Let the label pass through you like wind through empty space.

齧缺問於王倪，四問而四不知。
齧缺因躍而大喜，行以告蒲衣子。
蒲衣子曰：「而乃今知之乎？
有虞氏不及泰氏。
有虞氏，其猶藏仁以要人，亦得人矣，而未始出於非人。
泰氏，其臥徐徐，其覺于于。
一以己為馬，一以己為牛。
其知情信，其德甚真，而未始入於非人。
」肩吾見狂接輿。
狂接輿曰：「日中始何以語女？
」肩吾曰：「告我君人者以己出經式義度，人孰敢不聽而化諸！
」狂接輿曰：「是欺德也。
其於治天下也，猶涉海鑿河，而使蚊負山也。
夫聖人之治也，治外夫？
正而後行，確乎能其事者而已矣。
且鳥高飛以避矰弋之害，鼷鼠深穴乎神丘之下，以避熏鑿之患，而曾二虫之無知？
」天根游於殷陽，至蓼水之上，適遭無名人而問焉，曰：「請問為天下。
」無名人曰：「去！
汝鄙人也，何問之不豫也！
予方將與造物者為人，厭，則又乘夫莽眇之鳥，以出六極之外，而游無何有之鄉，以處壙垠之野。
汝又何帠以治天下感予之心為？
」又復問，無名人曰：「汝游心於淡，合氣於漠，順物自然而無容私焉，而天下治矣。
」陽子居見老聃，曰：「有人於此，嚮疾強梁，物徹疏明，學道不卷，如是者，可比明王乎？
」老聃曰：「是於聖人也，胥易技係，勞形怵心者也。
且也虎豹之文來田，猿狙之便來藉。
如是者，可比明王乎？
」陽子居蹴然曰：「敢問明王之治。
」老聃曰：「明王之治：功蓋天下而似不自己，化貸萬物而民弗恃。
有莫舉名，使物自喜。
立乎不測，而游於無有者也。
」鄭有神巫曰季咸，知人之死生存亡、禍福壽夭，期以歲月旬日若神。
鄭人見之，皆棄而走。
列子見之而心醉，歸，以告壺子，曰：「始吾以夫子之道為至矣，則又有至焉者矣。
」壺子曰：「吾與汝既其文，未既其實。
而固得道與？
眾雌而無雄，而又奚卵焉！
而以道與世亢，必信，夫故使人得而相汝。
嘗試與來，以予示之。
」明日，列子與之見壺子。
出而謂列子曰：「嘻！
子之先生死矣！
弗活矣！
不以旬數矣！
吾見怪焉，見濕灰焉。
」列子入，泣涕沾襟以告壺子。
壺子曰：「鄉吾示之以地文，萌乎不震不止，是殆見吾杜德機也。
嘗又與來。
」明日，又與之見壺子。
出而謂列子曰：「幸矣！
子之先生遇我也，有瘳矣！
全然有生矣！
吾見其杜權矣！
」列子入，以告壺子。
壺子曰：「鄉吾示之以天壤，名實不入，而機發於踵。
是殆見吾善者機也。
嘗又與來。
」明日，又與之見壺子。
出而謂列子曰：「子之先生不齊，吾無得而相焉。
試齊，且復相之。
」列子入，以告壺子。
壺子曰：「吾鄉示之以太沖莫勝，是殆見吾衡氣機也。
鯢桓之審為淵，止水之審為淵，流水之審為淵。
淵有九名，此處三焉。
嘗又與來。
」明日，又與之見壺子。
立未定，自失而走。
壺子曰：「追之！
」列子追之不及。
反，以報壺子曰：「已滅矣，已失矣，吾弗及已。
」壺子曰：「鄉吾示之以未始出吾宗。
吾與之虛而委蛇，不知其誰何，因以為弟靡，因以為波流，故逃也。
」然後列子自以為未始學而歸。
三年不出，為其妻爨，食豕如食人，於事無與親。
雕琢復朴，塊然獨以其形立。
紛而封哉，一以是終。
無為名尸，無為謀府，無為事任，無為知主。

anchor_chapter:
Yeh Ch'üeh asked Wang I

four questions, none of which he could answer. Thereat the former was greatly delighted,

For now he discovered that ignorance is true knowledge:—an explanation which I adopt only for want of a better.

Shun was all for charity in his zeal for mankind; but although he succeeded in government, he himself never rose above the level of artificiality. Now T'ai Huang was peaceful when asleep and inactive when awake. At one time he would think himself a horse; at another, an ox.

His wisdom was substantial and above suspicion. His virtue was genuine indeed. And yet he never sank to the level of artificiality."

Chien Wu meeting the eccentric Chieh Yü, the latter enquired, saying, "What did Jih Chung Shih teach you?"

"He taught me," replied Chien Wu, "about the laws and regulations which princes evolve, and which he said none would venture not to hear and obey."

"That is a false teaching indeed," replied Chieh Yü. "To attempt to govern mankind thus,—as well try to wade through the sea, to hew a passage through a river, or make a mosquito fly away with a mountain!

"The government of the truly wise man has no concern with externals. He first perfects himself, and then by virtue thereof he is enabled to accomplish what he wants.

"The bird flies high to avoid snare and dart. The mouse burrows down below the hill to avoid being smoked or cut out of its nest. Is your wit below that of these two creatures?"

That you should be unable to devise means of avoiding the artificial restraints of princes. Better than coercing into goodness is letting men be good of their own accord.

T'ien Kên

was travelling on the south of the Yin mountain. He had reached the river Liao when he met a certain Sage to whom he said, "I beg to ask about the government of the empire."

"Begone!" cried the Sage. "You are a low fellow, and your question is ill timed. God has just turned me out a man. That is enough for me. Borne on light pinions I can soar beyond the cardinal points, to the land of nowhere, in the domain of nothingness. And you come to worry me with government of the empire!"

But T'ien Kên enquired a second time, and the Sage replied, "Resolve your mental energy into abstraction, your physical energy into inaction. Allow yourself to fall in with the natural order of phenomena, without admitting the element of self,—and the empire will be governed."

Yang Tzŭ Chü went to see Lao Tzŭ, and said, "Suppose a man were ardent and courageous, acquainted with the order and principles of things, and untiring in the pursuit of Tao—would he be accounted a wise ruler?"

"From the point of view of a truly wise man," replied Lao Tzŭ, "such a one would be a mere handicraftsman, wearing out body and mind alike. The tiger and the pard suffer from the beauty of their skins. The cleverness of the monkey, the tractability of the ox, bring them both to the tether. It is not on such grounds that a ruler may be accounted wise."

"But in what, then," cried Yang Tzŭ Chü, "does the government of a wise man consist?"

"The goodness of a wise ruler," answered Lao Tzŭ, "covers the whole empire, yet he himself seems to know it not. It influences all creation, yet none is conscious thereof. It appears under countless forms, bringing joy to all things. It is based upon the baseless, and travels through the realms of Nowhere."

In the State of Chêng there was a wonderful magician, named Chi Han. He knew all about birth and death, gain and loss, misfortune and happiness, long life and short life,—predicting events to a day with supernatural accuracy. The people of Chêng used to flee at his approach; but Lieh Tzŭ

went to see him, and became so infatuated that on his return he said to Hu Tzŭ,

"I used to look upon your Tao as perfect. Now I know something more perfect still."

"So far," replied Hu Tzŭ, "I have only taught you the ornamentals, not the essentials, of Tao; and yet you think you know all about it. Without cocks in your poultry-yard, what sort of eggs do the hens lay? If you go about trying to force Tao down people's throats, you will be simply exposing yourself. Bring your friend with you, and let me show myself to him."

So next day Lieh Tzŭ went with Chi Han to see Hu Tzŭ, and when they came out Chi Han said, "Alas! your teacher is doomed. He cannot live. I hardly give him ten days. I am astonished at him. He is but wet ashes."

Lieh Tzŭ went in and wept bitterly, and told Hu Tzŭ; but the latter said, "I showed myself to him just now as the earth shows us its outward form, motionless and still, while production is all the time going on. I merely prevented him from seeing my pent-up energy

within. Bring him again."

Next day the interview took place as before; but as they were leaving Chi Han said to Lieh Tzŭ, "It is lucky for your teacher that he met me. He is better. He will recover. I saw he had recuperative power."

Lieh Tzŭ went in and told Hu Tzŭ; whereupon the latter replied, "I showed myself to him just now as heaven shows itself in all its dispassionate grandeur, letting a little energy run out of my heels. He was thus able to detect that I had some. Bring him here again."

Next day a third interview took place, and as they were leaving, Chi Han said to Lieh Tzŭ, "Your teacher is never one day like another. I can tell nothing from his physiognomy. Get him to be regular, and I will then examine him again."

This being repeated to Hu Tzŭ as before, the latter said, "I showed myself to him just now in a state of harmonious equilibrium. Where the whale disports itself,—is the abyss. Where water is at rest,—is the abyss. Where water is in motion,—is the abyss. The abyss has nine names. These are three of them."

Alluding to three phases of Tao as manifested at the three interviews above described, Tao being the abyss.

Next day the two went once more to see Hu Tzŭ; but Chi Han was unable to stand still, and in his confusion turned and fled.

"Pursue him!" cried Hu Tzŭ; whereupon Lieh Tzŭ ran after him, but could not overtake him, so he returned and told Hu Tzŭ that the fugitive had disappeared.

"I showed myself to him just now," said Hu Tzŭ, "as Tao appeared before time was. I was to him as a great blank, existing of itself. He knew not who I was. His face fell. He became confused. And so he fled."

Upon this Lieh Tzŭ stood convinced that he had not yet acquired any real knowledge, and at once set to work in earnest, passing three years without leaving the house. He helped his wife to cook the family dinner, and fed his pigs just like human beings. He discarded the artificial and reverted to the natural. He became merely a shape. Amidst confusion,

See ch. i. In the old funeral rites of China, a boy was made to sit speechless and motionless as a corpse, for the reason assigned in the text.

By Inaction, one can become the centre of thought, the focus of responsibility, the arbiter of wisdom. Full allowance must be made for others, while remaining unmoved oneself. There must be a thorough compliance with divine principles, without any manifestation thereof.

All of which may be summed up in the one word passivity. For the perfect man employs his mind as a mirror. It grasps nothing: it refuses nothing. It receives, but does not keep. And thus he can triumph over matter, without injury to himself.

The ruler of the southern sea was called Shu. The ruler of the northern sea was called Hu. The ruler of the central zone was called Hun Tun.

This term is generally used to denote the condition of matter before separation and subdivision into the phenomena of the visible universe.

Shu and Hu often met on Hun Tun's territory, and being always well treated by him, determined to repay his kindness.

They said, "All men have seven holes,—for seeing, hearing, eating, and breathing. Hun Tun alone has none. We will bore some for him."

Illustrating the perils of action. "The empire," says Lao Tzŭ, "is a divine trust, and may not be ruled. He who rules, ruins. He who holds by force, loses."

"Men's actions," says Emerson, "are too strong for them."

Huzi said, "I have taught you the outer patterns of it, but not yet its substance — and you think you have really got the dào? A flock of hens with no cock — how will there be eggs? You take the dào and try to compete with the world, insisting on being believed, and so you let a man read your face. Try bringing him here; let him look at me."

The next day Liezi brought him to see Huzi. Coming out, the shaman said to Liezi, "Ah! Your master is a dead man. He won't live — not for another ten days. I saw something strange in him — I saw wet ashes." Liezi went in, tears soaking his collar, and told Huzi. Huzi said, "Just now I showed him the pattern of the earth — motionless growth, neither quaking nor still. He probably glimpsed my life-springs sealed shut. Try bringing him again."

The next day he brought him once more. Coming out, the shaman said, "How lucky your master is to have met me! He's recovering. He's fully alive again! I saw the sealed springs opening." Liezi went in and reported this. Huzi said, "Just now I showed him heaven-and-earth — where name and substance find no entry, and the life-spring rises up from the heels. He probably glimpsed the wholesome springs. Try bringing him again."

The next day he brought him once more. Coming out, the shaman said, "Your master is not steady; I can find nothing to read. Let him settle, and I'll read him again." Liezi went in and reported this. Huzi said, "Just now I showed him the great emptiness where nothing prevails — he probably glimpsed my balanced-qì springs. Where a whale wheels about, there is an abyss; where water stands still, there is an abyss; where water flows, there is an abyss. The abyss has nine names; I showed him three of them. Try bringing him again."

The next day he brought him once more. Before the shaman had even settled into place, he lost his composure and ran. Huzi said, "Go after him!" Liezi ran but could not catch him. He came back and reported, "He's vanished, he's gone, I couldn't catch him." Huzi said, "Just now I showed him what had not yet begun to come out of my source. I met him empty and yielding, wheeling with him, so that he could not tell who or what I was — I bent like grass with the wind, I flowed like the current, and that is why he fled."

After this Liezi realized he had never really begun to learn, and went home. For three years he did not go out. He cooked for his wife and fed the pigs as though feeding people. He took no side in affairs. He returned from carving and polishing back to the uncarved block, and stood alone, solid as a clod, amid all the tangle, sealed within it — and thus he stayed to the end.

Do not be a corpse for fame. Do not be a storehouse of schemes. Do not take on the burden of affairs. Do not be a master of knowledge.
abhyasa: When someone calls you by a label or role today — competent, helper, leader, whatever — let yourself be called that without internal correction or defense, as the great Tai let himself be called horse or cow. Notice the urge to clarify, explain, or adjust how they see you, and instead exhale it away. Let the label pass through you like wind through empty space.

pratibha_layers.label: Original
pratibha_layers.body:
齧缺問於王倪，四問而四不知。
齧缺因躍而大喜，行以告蒲衣子。
蒲衣子曰：「而乃今知之乎？
有虞氏不及泰氏。
有虞氏，其猶藏仁以要人，亦得人矣，而未始出於非人。
泰氏，其臥徐徐，其覺于于。
一以己為馬，一以己為牛。
其知情信，其德甚真，而未始入於非人。
」肩吾見狂接輿。
狂接輿曰：「日中始何以語女？
」肩吾曰：「告我君人者以己出經式義度，人孰敢不聽而化諸！
」狂接輿曰：「是欺德也。
其於治天下也，猶涉海鑿河，而使蚊負山也。
夫聖人之治也，治外夫？
正而後行，確乎能其事者而已矣。
且鳥高飛以避矰弋之害，鼷鼠深穴乎神丘之下，以避熏鑿之患，而曾二虫之無知？
」天根游於殷陽，至蓼水之上，適遭無名人而問焉，曰：「請問為天下。
」無名人曰：「去！
汝鄙人也，何問之不豫也！
予方將與造物者為人，厭，則又乘夫莽眇之鳥，以出六極之外，而游無何有之鄉，以處壙垠之野。
汝又何帠以治天下感予之心為？
」又復問，無名人曰：「汝游心於淡，合氣於漠，順物自然而無容私焉，而天下治矣。
」陽子居見老聃，曰：「有人於此，嚮疾強梁，物徹疏明，學道不卷，如是者，可比明王乎？
」老聃曰：「是於聖人也，胥易技係，勞形怵心者也。
且也虎豹之文來田，猿狙之便來藉。
如是者，可比明王乎？
」陽子居蹴然曰：「敢問明王之治。
」老聃曰：「明王之治：功蓋天下而似不自己，化貸萬物而民弗恃。
有莫舉名，使物自喜。
立乎不測，而游於無有者也。
」鄭有神巫曰季咸，知人之死生存亡、禍福壽夭，期以歲月旬日若神。
鄭人見之，皆棄而走。
列子見之而心醉，歸，以告壺子，曰：「始吾以夫子之道為至矣，則又有至焉者矣。
」壺子曰：「吾與汝既其文，未既其實。
而固得道與？
眾雌而無雄，而又奚卵焉！
而以道與世亢，必信，夫故使人得而相汝。
嘗試與來，以予示之。
」明日，列子與之見壺子。
出而謂列子曰：「嘻！
子之先生死矣！
弗活矣！
不以旬數矣！
吾見怪焉，見濕灰焉。
」列子入，泣涕沾襟以告壺子。
壺子曰：「鄉吾示之以地文，萌乎不震不止，是殆見吾杜德機也。
嘗又與來。
」明日，又與之見壺子。
出而謂列子曰：「幸矣！
子之先生遇我也，有瘳矣！
全然有生矣！
吾見其杜權矣！
」列子入，以告壺子。
壺子曰：「鄉吾示之以天壤，名實不入，而機發於踵。
是殆見吾善者機也。
嘗又與來。
」明日，又與之見壺子。
出而謂列子曰：「子之先生不齊，吾無得而相焉。
試齊，且復相之。
」列子入，以告壺子。
壺子曰：「吾鄉示之以太沖莫勝，是殆見吾衡氣機也。
鯢桓之審為淵，止水之審為淵，流水之審為淵。
淵有九名，此處三焉。
嘗又與來。
」明日，又與之見壺子。
立未定，自失而走。
壺子曰：「追之！
」列子追之不及。
反，以報壺子曰：「已滅矣，已失矣，吾弗及已。
」壺子曰：「鄉吾示之以未始出吾宗。
吾與之虛而委蛇，不知其誰何，因以為弟靡，因以為波流，故逃也。
」然後列子自以為未始學而歸。
三年不出，為其妻爨，食豕如食人，於事無與親。
雕琢復朴，塊然獨以其形立。
紛而封哉，一以是終。
無為名尸，無為謀府，無為事任，無為知主。

pratibha_layers.label: Pratibha Translation
pratibha_layers.body:
Carpenter Qing carves a bell-stand. When it is complete, those who see it think it must be the work of spirits.

The ruler asks, "What technique produced this?"

Qing replies, "I am only a craftsman, yet there is one thing. Before I begin, I do not let my vitality be scattered. I fast my mind into stillness. After three days, reward and rank disappear. After five days, praise and blame disappear. After seven days, even awareness of my limbs and body falls away.

"Then court concerns are absent, and my skill is gathered into one point. External noise drops out. I enter the mountain forest and observe the natural form of the wood. If the shape is there, I see the completed stand first and only then put hand to tool. If not, I leave it.

"I match my natural capacity with the natural grain of the wood. That is why the work seems more than human."

pratibha_layers.label: Pratibha Commentary
pratibha_layers.body:
The philosophical claim is that highest craft is a relation, not an imposition: form emerges when human attention and material pattern converge. The counterintuitive move is that technical mastery does not begin with adding techniques but with subtracting motivations that fragment perception - reward-seeking, reputation management, fear of judgment. Qing's staged emptying (three days, five days, seven days) is an ontology of preparation: by removing social overlays, he becomes able to perceive latent form in the wood itself.

In Daoist terms, this is *wuwei* inside skilled action. He is not passive and he is not anti-technology; he is anti-forcing. The phrase "matching heaven with heaven" (or natural with natural) expresses non-dual craftsmanship: human capacity is itself natural when de-distorted, so it can meet material nature without violence. The resulting object appears "supernatural" only because most action is burdened by egoic friction.

Existentially, this passage reorients work in every field. Burnout often comes from crafting under the demand to perform identity, not from the task itself. Qing shows another sequence: quiet the gain-loss mind, perceive what the situation asks, then act minimally and precisely. This is not mystification of labor; it is de-noising of labor. The more accurately you perceive the grain, the less force you waste. True excellence is therefore inseparable from inner economy.

pratibha_layers.label: Practice (Abhyasa)
pratibha_layers.body: Before your next focused work block, spend seven minutes in silence and deliberately set aside three motives in sequence (reward, recognition, fear), then begin only after you can name one concrete "grain" in the task you will follow instead of force.

items.definition: to fast/purify/even out -> in this passage, progressive simplification of motive-structure before action -> rendered as "quiescence" in older translation, but qí is active inner discipline that prepares non-forced precision.

quieted heart-mind -> contextual meaning: stable attentional field that can receive material pattern without projecting ambition -> default "absolute quiescence" can sound inert; this is alert stillness.

natural endowment/nature-given pattern -> here the intrinsic grain and form latent in the wood -> "natural constitution" is close, but the term also implies cosmological fit, not only physical structure.

items.term: yǐ tiān hé tiān (以天合天)
items.definition: "use the natural to join the natural" -> the core craft formula: de-distorted human capacity aligns with material nature -> translation as "supernatural" misses that the point is radical naturalness, not occult intervention.

items.resonance: both texts insist that quality of mind and quality of action are inseparable in ordinary work, and that precision emerges from wholehearted, undistracted presence.
items.divergence: Dogen frames this in explicit Zen monastic vows and Buddha-way realization, while Zhuangzi frames it in Daoist spontaneity and non-coercive fit with material pattern.

items.resonance: action is performed with inward evenness and without clinging to result; excellence appears as "skill in action."
items.divergence: The Gita roots this in disciplined duty and offering to the divine, whereas Qing roots it in de-socialized attentional clarity and direct responsiveness to the thing itself.

items.resonance: both articulate that deep skill involves dialogue with materials rather than domination by abstract plan.
items.divergence: Sennett remains in sociological and practical terms; Zhuangzi radicalizes the account into a spiritual anthropology of de-centered agency.

title: Joined Toes.
thesis: The claim is that freedom is a physiological-ethical integration: ontology, affect, and breath are not separate domains.
source_excerpt: Joined toes and extra fingers are an addition to nature, though, functionally speaking, superfluous. Wens and tumours are an addition to the bodily form, though, as far as nature is concerned, superfluous. And similarly, to include charity and duty to one's neighbour among the functions of man's organism, is not true Tao. The whole of this chapter is a violent tirade against the leading doctrines of Confucianism. For just as joined toes are but useless lumps of flesh, and extra fingers but useless excrescences, so are any artificial additions to our internal economy but harmful adjuncts to real charity and duty to one's neighbour, Which are the outcome of Tao. and are moreover prejudicial to
translation_literal:
Webbed toes and branching fingers—these sprout from our nature! Yet people make a show of virtue over them. Warts and tumors hanging from the body—these emerge from our form! Yet people treat them as part of their nature. Those who multiply methods of humaneness and righteousness and put them to use—do these lodge in the five organs? Yet this is not the straightness of dào and dé.

So webbing at the feet is just connected flesh serving no use; branching at the hands is just extra digits serving no use. Those who multiply webbing and branching through the five organs' patterns—these twist into the conduct of humaneness and righteousness, multiplying the uses of cleverness. So those webbed in perception jumble the five colors, corrupt patterns and designs—the dazzle of blue and yellow, the gleam of woven silk—is this not so? This is Li Zhu! Those multiplied in hearing jumble the five tones, corrupt the six pitches—the sounds of metal and stone, silk and bamboo, the Yellow Bell and Great Tube—is this not so? This is Shi Kuang! Those branching in humaneness pluck up virtue, block nature to gather fame—causing all under heaven to work like bellows to serve a law they cannot reach—is this not so? This is Zeng and Shi. Those webbed in argument pile tiles, knot rope, hide phrases, let their hearts wander between hardness-whiteness and sameness-difference, wearing out their steps in useless words—is this not so? This is Yang and Mo.

All these follow the path of multiplying webbing and branching—not the utmost straightness of all under heaven. Those who are truly straight do not lose the pattern of their life-nature. So when joined, there is no webbing; when branched, there is no limping. The long is not excess, the short is not lack. This is why the mallard's leg, though short, if lengthened brings worry; the crane's leg, though long, if shortened brings sorrow. So what nature makes long should not be cut, what nature makes short should not be extended—there is no way to remove worry.

Is humaneness and righteousness perhaps not human feeling? Why does the humane person have such worry? When toes are webbed, cutting them brings tears; when fingers branch, biting them brings cries. One has surplus in number, one has lack in number—both bring the same worry. Now the humane people of this age stare with furrowed brows, worrying over the world's troubles; the non-humane person cuts through life-nature's pattern and gorges on wealth and rank. So is humaneness and righteousness perhaps not human feeling?

From the Three Dynasties onward, why is all under heaven so clamorous? When something waits for hook and plumb line to be set straight, this carves away its nature. When something waits for rope and glue to be fixed, this invades its dé. Bending and twisting ritual and music, nodding and bowing with humaneness and righteousness to comfort the hearts of all under heaven—this loses what is constant. All under heaven has what is constant: the bent does not need the hook, the straight does not need the rope, the round does not need the compass, the square does not need the square. Attachment and separation do not need glue, binding does not need cord. So all under heaven naturally generates, yet we do not know how it generates; all alike obtain, yet we do not know how they obtain. So past and present are not two—this cannot be diminished.

Why then must humaneness and righteousness stick like glue and cord, wandering between dào and dé, causing all under heaven to be confused? Small confusion easily turns direction; great confusion easily turns nature. How do we know this is so? Since the Yao clan first drew in humaneness and righteousness to disturb all under heaven, all under heaven has rushed to serve humaneness and righteousness. Is this not exchanging their nature for humaneness and righteousness? Let us test this: from the Three Dynasties onward, all under heaven has not failed to exchange things for their nature! The small person sacrifices the body for profit; the scholar sacrifices the body for name; the minister sacrifices the body for family; the sage sacrifices the body for all under heaven. So these several kinds—their affairs differ, their reputations have different names, yet in harming nature by making the body a sacrifice, they are one.

Zang and Gu, two people herding sheep together, both lost their sheep. Asked what Zang was doing, he held a book and read strategy. Asked what Gu was doing, he gambled and played. Two people with different affairs, yet equally they lost the sheep. Bo Yi died for name at the foot of Shouyang Mountain; Robber Zhi died for profit at the top of Dongling. Two people dying for different things, yet equally they damaged life and harmed nature. Why must Bo Yi be right and Robber Zhi be wrong? All under heaven sacrifices itself. Those who sacrifice themselves to humaneness and righteousness—the vulgar call them gentlemen; those who sacrifice themselves to goods and wealth—the vulgar call them small people. If the sacrifice is one, then there are gentlemen and there are small people; if they damage life and harm nature, then Robber Zhi is already Bo Yi—how can we distinguish gentleman from small person between them?

Those who bind their nature to humaneness and righteousness—even if penetrating like Zeng and Shi, this is not what I call storage. Those who bind their nature to the five flavors—even if penetrating like Yu Er, this is not what I call storage. Those who bind their nature to the five tones—even if penetrating like Shi Kuang, this is not what I call hearing. Those who bind their nature to the five colors—even if penetrating like Li Zhu, this is not what I call sight. What I call storage is not what humaneness and righteousness speak of—it is simply being stored in one's dé. What I call storage is not what humaneness and righteousness speak of—it is simply letting life-nature's pattern do its work. What I call hearing is not hearing that—it is simply self-hearing. What I call sight is not seeing that—it is simply self-sight.

Not to see from oneself but to see another, not to get from oneself but to get another—this is getting another's getting while not getting one's own getting, fitting into another's fitting while not fitting into one's own fitting. Those who fit into another's fitting while not fitting into one's own fitting—whether Robber Zhi or Bo Yi, both are equally twisted and perverse. I am ashamed before dào and dé, and therefore...
commentary:
This passage demolishes the distinction between 'useful' and 'useless,' 'natural' and 'cultivated,' by showing that all deliberate cultivation—whether of virtue, skill, or morality—is itself a deformity. The webbed toe and branching finger are the opening image: extra digits that serve no function, yet people treat them as extensions of their nature. Zhuangzi then extends this logic to humaneness and righteousness: they too are 'extra digits' grafted onto human nature, and the more we cultivate them, the more we distort ourselves.

The passage's central paradox lies in the collapse of moral hierarchy. Bo Yi and Robber Zhi both 'sacrifice' themselves—one for name, one for profit—yet the vulgar world calls one a gentleman and the other a criminal. But if both damage life and harm nature equally, the distinction evaporates. The world's judgment rests on which idol you serve, not on whether you serve an idol at all. This is the 'great confusion' that 'easily turns nature.'

The resolution comes near the end: true storage (臧, cáng) is not binding oneself to humaneness and righteousness, but simply 'being stored in one's dé'—allowing one's nature to work without external measures, hooks, ropes, or glue. True hearing is 'self-hearing,' true sight is 'self-sight.' The constant pattern (常然) of all under heaven generates itself; we do not need ritual, music, or moral codes to make it work. When we impose these external tools, we do not straighten what is crooked—we carve away what is naturally whole.

The passage dissolves the distinction between moral and immoral action by showing both spring from the same root: the binding of nature to external standards. It also dissolves the distinction between natural and artificial by revealing that all cultivation—even the most refined—is a kind of deformity, a webbing or branching that serves no genuine function.

Key Terms

**dào 道** — The way, the path, the constant unfolding of what is—not a moral code but the natural functioning of all things.
**dé 德** — Virtue, potency, or integrity—not moral achievement but the intrinsic power of a thing to be itself without external constraint.
**xìng 性** — Nature, inborn pattern, the original endowment of each being—what is damaged when we bind ourselves to external standards.
practice: Throughout today, each time you catch yourself justifying an action as 'virtuous' or 'necessary,' pause and ask: what would happen if I simply stopped? Not in judgment, but as an experiment—let the justification drop like a weight from your hand, and notice what remains of the impulse itself.
sanskrit_devanagari:
駢拇枝指，出乎性哉！
而侈於德。
附贅縣疣，出乎形哉！
而侈於性。
多方乎仁義而用之者，列於五藏哉！
而非道德之正也。
是故駢於足者，連無用之肉也；
枝於手者，樹無用之指也；
多方駢枝於五藏之情者，淫僻於仁義之行，而多方於聰明之用也。
是故駢於明者，亂五色，淫文章，青黃黼黻之煌煌非乎？
而離朱是已！
多於聰者，亂五聲，淫六律，金石絲竹黃鐘大呂之聲非乎？
而師曠是已！
枝於仁者，擢德塞性以收名聲，使天下簧鼓以奉不及之法非乎？
而曾、史是已。
駢於辯者，累瓦結繩竄句，游心於堅白同異之間，而敝跬譽無用之言非乎？
而楊墨是已。
故此皆多駢旁枝之道，非天下之至正也。
彼正正者，不失其性命之情。
故合者不為駢，而枝者不為跂；
長者不為有餘，短者不為不足。
是故鳧脛雖短，續之則憂；
鶴脛雖長，斷之則悲。
故性長非所斷，性短非所續，無所去憂也。
意仁義其非人情乎！
彼仁人何其多憂也？
且夫駢於拇者，決之則泣；
枝於手者，齕之則啼。
二者，或有餘於數，或不足於數，其於憂一也。
今世之仁人，蒿目而憂世之患；
不仁之人，決性命之情而饕貴富。
故意仁義其非人情乎！
自三代以下者，天下何其囂囂也？
且夫待鉤繩規矩而正者，是削其性也；
待繩約膠漆而固者，是侵其德者也；
屈折禮樂，呴俞仁義，以慰天下之心者，此失其常然也。
天下有常然，常然者，曲者不以鉤，直者不以繩，圓者不以規，方者不以矩，附離不以膠漆，約束不以纆索。
故天下誘然皆生，而不知其所以生；
同焉皆得，而不知其所以得。
故古今不二，不可虧也。
則仁義又奚連連如膠漆纆索而游乎道德之間為哉！
使天下惑也！
夫小惑易方，大惑易性，何以知其然邪？
自虞氏招仁義以撓天下也，天下莫不奔命於仁義。
是非以仁義易其性與？
故嘗試論之，自三代以下者，天下莫不以物易其性矣！
小人則以身殉利；
士則以身殉名；
大夫則以身殉家；
聖人則以身殉天下。
故此數子者，事業不同，名聲異號，其於傷性以身為殉，一也。
臧與穀，二人相與牧羊，而俱亡其羊。
問臧奚事，則挾策讀書；
問穀奚事，則博塞以游。
二人者，事業不同，其於亡羊均也。
伯夷死名於首陽之下，盜跖死利於東陵之上。
二人者，所死不同，其於殘生傷性均也。
奚必伯夷之是而盜跖之非乎？
天下盡殉也。
彼其所殉仁義也，則俗謂之君子；
其所殉貨財也，則俗謂之小人。
其殉一也，則有君子焉，有小人焉；
若其殘生損性，則盜跖亦伯夷已，又惡取君子小人於其間哉！

anchor_chapter:
Joined toes and extra fingers are an addition to nature, though, functionally speaking, superfluous. Wens and tumours are an addition to the bodily form, though, as far as nature is concerned, superfluous. And similarly, to include charity and duty to one's neighbour among the functions of man's organism, is not true Tao.

For just as joined toes are but useless lumps of flesh, and extra fingers but useless excrescences, so are any artificial additions to our internal economy but harmful adjuncts to real charity and duty to one's neighbour,

People with extra keenness of vision muddle themselves over the five colours, exaggerate the value of shades, and of distinctions of greens and yellows for sacrificial robes. Of such was Li Chu.

People with extra keenness of hearing muddle themselves over the five notes, exaggerate the tonic differences of the six pitch-pipes, and the various timbres of metal, stone, silk, and bamboo, of the Huang-chung, and of the Ta-lü. Of such was Shih K'uang.

The blind musician mentioned in ch. ii. The Huang-chung and the Ta-lü were two of the twelve bamboo tubes, or pitch-pipes, on which ancient Chinese music was based. Six were male or positive, and six female or negative. Hence they are spoken of collectively as six.

People who graft on charity, force themselves to display this virtue in order to gain reputation and to enjoy the applause of the world for that which is of no account. Of such were Tsêng and Shih.

Tsêng Shên, a famous disciple of Confucius, and Shih Yu, both noted for their high moral characters.

People who refine in argument do but pile up tiles or knot ropes in their maunderings over the hard and white, the like and the unlike, wearing themselves out over mere useless terms. Of such were Yang and Mih.

Yang Chu, a philosopher of the fourth century B.C., whose "selfish" system was condemned by Mencius; and Mih Tzŭ, already mentioned in ch. ii.

He who would attain to such perfection never loses sight of the natural conditions of his existence. With him the joined is not united, nor the separated apart, nor the long in excess, nor the short wanting. For just as a duck's legs, though short, cannot be lengthened without pain to the duck, and a crane's legs, though long, cannot be shortened without misery to the crane, so that which is long in man's moral nature cannot be cut off, nor that which is short be lengthened. All sorrow is thus avoided.

Intentional charity and intentional duty to one's neighbour are surely not included in our moral nature. Yet what sorrow these have involved. Divide your joined toes and you will howl: bite off your extra finger and you will scream. In one case there is too much, in the other too little; but the sorrow is the same. And the charitable of the age go about sorrowing over the ills of the age, while the non-charitable cut through the natural conditions of things in their greed after place and wealth. Surely then intentional charity and duty to one's neighbour are not included in our moral nature. Yet from the time of the Three Dynasties downwards what a fuss has been made about them!

Those who cannot make perfect without arc, line, compasses, and square, injure the natural constitution of things. Those who require cords to bind and glue to stick, interfere with the natural functions of things. And those who seek to satisfy the mind of man by hampering with ceremonies and music and preaching charity and duty to one's neighbour, thereby destroy the intrinsicality of things.

For such intrinsicality does exist, in this sense:—Things which are curved require no arcs; things which are straight require no lines; things which are round require no compasses; things which are rectangular require no squares; things which stick require no glue; things which hold together require no cords. And just as all things are produced, and none can tell how they are produced, so do all things possess their own intrinsic qualities and none can tell how they possess them. From time immemorial this has always been so, without variation. Why then should charity and duty to one's neighbour be as it were glued or corded on, and introduced into the domain of Tao, to give rise to doubt among mankind?

How do we know this? By the fact that ever since the time when Shun bid for charity and duty to one's neighbour in order to secure the empire, men have devoted their lives to the pursuit thereof. Is it not then charity and duty to one's neighbour which change the nature of man?

Therefore I have tried to show that from the time of the Three Dynasties it has always been the external which has changed the nature of man. If a mean man, he will die for gain. If a superior man, he will die for fame. If a man of rank, he will die for his ancestral honours. If a Sage, he will die for the world. The pursuits and ambitions of these men differ, but the injury to their natures involved in the sacrifice of their lives is the same.

Tsang and Ku were shepherds, both of whom lost their flocks. On inquiry, it appeared that Tsang had been engaged in reading, while Ku had gone to take part in some trials of strength. Their occupations had been different, but the result was in each case loss of the sheep.

Their deaths were not the same, but the injury to their lives and natures was in each case the same. How then can we applaud the former and blame the latter?

And so, if a man dies for charity and duty to his neighbour the world calls him a noble fellow; but if he dies for gain, the world calls him a low fellow. The dying being the same, one is nevertheless called noble and the other low. But in point of injury to life and nature, the robber Chê and Poh I are one. Where then does the distinction of noble and low come in?

Were a man to apply himself to charity and duty towards his neighbour until he were the equal of Tsêng or Shih, this would not be what I mean by perfection. Or to flavours, until he were the equal of Yü Erh.

Or to sounds, until he were the equal of Shih K'uang. Or to colours, until he were the equal of Li Chu. What I mean by perfection is not what is meant by charity and duty to one's neighbour. It is found in the cultivation of Tao. And those whom I regard as cultivators of Tao are not those who cultivate charity and duty to one's neighbour. They are those who yield to the natural conditions of things. What I call perfection of hearing is not hearing others but oneself. What I call perfection of vision is not seeing others but oneself.

A saying attributed by Han Fei Tzŭ to Lao Tzŭ:—"To see oneself is to be clear of sight." See The Remains of Lao Tzŭ, p. 18.

For a man who sees not himself but others, takes not possession of himself but of others, thus taking what others should take and not what he himself should take.

Instead of being himself, he in fact becomes some one else. And if a man thus becomes some one else instead of himself, this is a fatal error of which both the robber Chê and Poh I can be equally guilty.

And so, conscious of my own deficiency in regard to Tao, I do not venture at my best to practise the principles of charity and duty to my neighbour, nor at my worst to fall into the fatal error above-mentioned.
translation:
Webbed toes and branching fingers—these sprout from our nature! Yet people make a show of virtue over them. Warts and tumors hanging from the body—these emerge from our form! Yet people treat them as part of their nature. Those who multiply methods of humaneness and righteousness and put them to use—do these lodge in the five organs? Yet this is not the straightness of dào and dé.

So webbing at the feet is just connected flesh serving no use; branching at the hands is just extra digits serving no use. Those who multiply webbing and branching through the five organs' patterns—these twist into the conduct of humaneness and righteousness, multiplying the uses of cleverness. So those webbed in perception jumble the five colors, corrupt patterns and designs—the dazzle of blue and yellow, the gleam of woven silk—is this not so? This is Li Zhu! Those multiplied in hearing jumble the five tones, corrupt the six pitches—the sounds of metal and stone, silk and bamboo, the Yellow Bell and Great Tube—is this not so? This is Shi Kuang! Those branching in humaneness pluck up virtue, block nature to gather fame—causing all under heaven to work like bellows to serve a law they cannot reach—is this not so? This is Zeng and Shi. Those webbed in argument pile tiles, knot rope, hide phrases, let their hearts wander between hardness-whiteness and sameness-difference, wearing out their steps in useless words—is this not so? This is Yang and Mo.

All these follow the path of multiplying webbing and branching—not the utmost straightness of all under heaven. Those who are truly straight do not lose the pattern of their life-nature. So when joined, there is no webbing; when branched, there is no limping. The long is not excess, the short is not lack. This is why the mallard's leg, though short, if lengthened brings worry; the crane's leg, though long, if shortened brings sorrow. So what nature makes long should not be cut, what nature makes short should not be extended—there is no way to remove worry.

Is humaneness and righteousness perhaps not human feeling? Why does the humane person have such worry? When toes are webbed, cutting them brings tears; when fingers branch, biting them brings cries. One has surplus in number, one has lack in number—both bring the same worry. Now the humane people of this age stare with furrowed brows, worrying over the world's troubles; the non-humane person cuts through life-nature's pattern and gorges on wealth and rank. So is humaneness and righteousness perhaps not human feeling?

From the Three Dynasties onward, why is all under heaven so clamorous? When something waits for hook and plumb line to be set straight, this carves away its nature. When something waits for rope and glue to be fixed, this invades its dé. Bending and twisting ritual and music, nodding and bowing with humaneness and righteousness to comfort the hearts of all under heaven—this loses what is constant. All under heaven has what is constant: the bent does not need the hook, the straight does not need the rope, the round does not need the compass, the square does not need the square. Attachment and separation do not need glue, binding does not need cord. So all under heaven naturally generates, yet we do not know how it generates; all alike obtain, yet we do not know how they obtain. So past and present are not two—this cannot be diminished.

Why then must humaneness and righteousness stick like glue and cord, wandering between dào and dé, causing all under heaven to be confused? Small confusion easily turns direction; great confusion easily turns nature. How do we know this is so? Since the Yao clan first drew in humaneness and righteousness to disturb all under heaven, all under heaven has rushed to serve humaneness and righteousness. Is this not exchanging their nature for humaneness and righteousness? Let us test this: from the Three Dynasties onward, all under heaven has not failed to exchange things for their nature! The small person sacrifices the body for profit; the scholar sacrifices the body for name; the minister sacrifices the body for family; the sage sacrifices the body for all under heaven. So these several kinds—their affairs differ, their reputations have different names, yet in harming nature by making the body a sacrifice, they are one.

Zang and Gu, two people herding sheep together, both lost their sheep. Asked what Zang was doing, he held a book and read strategy. Asked what Gu was doing, he gambled and played. Two people with different affairs, yet equally they lost the sheep. Bo Yi died for name at the foot of Shouyang Mountain; Robber Zhi died for profit at the top of Dongling. Two people dying for different things, yet equally they damaged life and harmed nature. Why must Bo Yi be right and Robber Zhi be wrong? All under heaven sacrifices itself. Those who sacrifice themselves to humaneness and righteousness—the vulgar call them gentlemen; those who sacrifice themselves to goods and wealth—the vulgar call them small people. If the sacrifice is one, then there are gentlemen and there are small people; if they damage life and harm nature, then Robber Zhi is already Bo Yi—how can we distinguish gentleman from small person between them?

Those who bind their nature to humaneness and righteousness—even if penetrating like Zeng and Shi, this is not what I call storage. Those who bind their nature to the five flavors—even if penetrating like Yu Er, this is not what I call storage. Those who bind their nature to the five tones—even if penetrating like Shi Kuang, this is not what I call hearing. Those who bind their nature to the five colors—even if penetrating like Li Zhu, this is not what I call sight. What I call storage is not what humaneness and righteousness speak of—it is simply being stored in one's dé. What I call storage is not what humaneness and righteousness speak of—it is simply letting life-nature's pattern do its work. What I call hearing is not hearing that—it is simply self-hearing. What I call sight is not seeing that—it is simply self-sight.

Not to see from oneself but to see another, not to get from oneself but to get another—this is getting another's getting while not getting one's own getting, fitting into another's fitting while not fitting into one's own fitting. Those who fit into another's fitting while not fitting into one's own fitting—whether Robber Zhi or Bo Yi, both are equally twisted and perverse. I am ashamed before dào and dé, and therefore...
abhyasa: Throughout today, each time you catch yourself justifying an action as 'virtuous' or 'necessary,' pause and ask: what would happen if I simply stopped? Not in judgment, but as an experiment—let the justification drop like a weight from your hand, and notice what remains of the impulse itself.

pratibha_layers.body:
駢拇枝指，出乎性哉！
而侈於德。
附贅縣疣，出乎形哉！
而侈於性。
多方乎仁義而用之者，列於五藏哉！
而非道德之正也。
是故駢於足者，連無用之肉也；
枝於手者，樹無用之指也；
多方駢枝於五藏之情者，淫僻於仁義之行，而多方於聰明之用也。
是故駢於明者，亂五色，淫文章，青黃黼黻之煌煌非乎？
而離朱是已！
多於聰者，亂五聲，淫六律，金石絲竹黃鐘大呂之聲非乎？
而師曠是已！
枝於仁者，擢德塞性以收名聲，使天下簧鼓以奉不及之法非乎？
而曾、史是已。
駢於辯者，累瓦結繩竄句，游心於堅白同異之間，而敝跬譽無用之言非乎？
而楊墨是已。
故此皆多駢旁枝之道，非天下之至正也。
彼正正者，不失其性命之情。
故合者不為駢，而枝者不為跂；
長者不為有餘，短者不為不足。
是故鳧脛雖短，續之則憂；
鶴脛雖長，斷之則悲。
故性長非所斷，性短非所續，無所去憂也。
意仁義其非人情乎！
彼仁人何其多憂也？
且夫駢於拇者，決之則泣；
枝於手者，齕之則啼。
二者，或有餘於數，或不足於數，其於憂一也。
今世之仁人，蒿目而憂世之患；
不仁之人，決性命之情而饕貴富。
故意仁義其非人情乎！
自三代以下者，天下何其囂囂也？
且夫待鉤繩規矩而正者，是削其性也；
待繩約膠漆而固者，是侵其德者也；
屈折禮樂，呴俞仁義，以慰天下之心者，此失其常然也。
天下有常然，常然者，曲者不以鉤，直者不以繩，圓者不以規，方者不以矩，附離不以膠漆，約束不以纆索。
故天下誘然皆生，而不知其所以生；
同焉皆得，而不知其所以得。
故古今不二，不可虧也。
則仁義又奚連連如膠漆纆索而游乎道德之間為哉！
使天下惑也！
夫小惑易方，大惑易性，何以知其然邪？
自虞氏招仁義以撓天下也，天下莫不奔命於仁義。
是非以仁義易其性與？
故嘗試論之，自三代以下者，天下莫不以物易其性矣！
小人則以身殉利；
士則以身殉名；
大夫則以身殉家；
聖人則以身殉天下。
故此數子者，事業不同，名聲異號，其於傷性以身為殉，一也。
臧與穀，二人相與牧羊，而俱亡其羊。
問臧奚事，則挾策讀書；
問穀奚事，則博塞以游。
二人者，事業不同，其於亡羊均也。
伯夷死名於首陽之下，盜跖死利於東陵之上。
二人者，所死不同，其於殘生傷性均也。
奚必伯夷之是而盜跖之非乎？
天下盡殉也。
彼其所殉仁義也，則俗謂之君子；
其所殉貨財也，則俗謂之小人。
其殉一也，則有君子焉，有小人焉；
若其殘生損性，則盜跖亦伯夷已，又惡取君子小人於其間哉！

pratibha_layers.label: Pratibha Translation
pratibha_layers.body:
The true persons of old do not resist little losses, do not glorify success, and do not construct plans as identity. So when they miss, they do not brood; when they attain, they do not become self-congratulatory.

They sleep without dream-turbulence and wake without anxious residue. They eat without compulsive preference. Their breathing is deep and whole: true persons breathe from the heels, ordinary people only from the throat.

They do not cling to life and do not recoil from death. They do not celebrate coming-into-being, nor struggle against return. They come lightly and go lightly. They do not forget their beginning, and they do not force their ending. They receive what comes and release what passes. This is called not using the mind to damage Tao, and not using the human to overrule the natural.

pratibha_layers.label: Pratibha Commentary
pratibha_layers.body:
The claim is that freedom is a physiological-ethical integration: ontology, affect, and breath are not separate domains. The counterintuitive move is the line about breathing "from the heels." Taken literally, it sounds absurd; read structurally, it names total-organismic participation rather than superficial, threat-driven respiration. Zhuangzi ties existential fixation (on gain/loss, life/death, success/failure) to shallow breathing and contracted awareness. To de-contract one is to de-contract all.

Within Daoist tradition, the *zhenren* (true person) is not morally heroic in the conventional sense but unentangled. Their non-attachment is not indifference to life; it is refusal to convert life-events into ego drama. "Not using the human to overrule the natural" identifies the core error: compulsive intervention by a mind that distrusts process. The true person does less psychic violence to what already moves by its own rhythm.

Existentially, this passage reframes anxiety management. We often attack anxiety cognitively while leaving the organism in chronic throat-breath, vigilance, and narrative acceleration. Zhuangzi's image suggests a different sequence: broaden breath, soften evaluative grasping, and identity pressure lessens. One does not become passive; one becomes less brittle. The teaching is radical because it dissolves prestige around constant self-manufacture. To come and go lightly is not laziness - it is fidelity to a deeper continuity than personal storyline.

pratibha_layers.label: Practice (Abhyasa)
pratibha_layers.body: Three times today, when you notice yourself rehearsing gain/loss scenarios, stop for ten breaths into the lower body (long exhale, relaxed throat), and on each exhale silently repeat: "Do not force what is already moving."

items.definition: "true person / realized person" -> in this passage, one whose psychophysical life is aligned with Tao rather than managed by egoic control -> default "pure man" imports moral purity language and misses processual integration.

"breathes from the heels" -> contextual meaning: whole-body, non-contracted respiration and awareness -> literal readings become occult or anatomical; the phrase points to depth and totality of embodied presence.

items.term: bù yǐ xīn juān dào (不以心捐道)
items.definition: "do not let the heart-mind damage/abandon Tao" -> names conceptual interference as a mode of self-injury -> older translations soften this into piety; the original carries diagnostic force about cognitive violence.

items.term: bù yǐ rén zhù tiān (不以人助天)
items.definition: "do not use the human to 'help' heaven/nature" -> in context, do not overmanage process through anxious control -> default renderings can sound fatalistic; the point is calibrated non-interference, not helplessness.

items.resonance: the steady one is not agitated in sorrow, not elated in gain, and remains free from compulsive attachment and aversion. Structurally, both portray equanimity as embodied non-reactivity rather than concept-only discipline.
items.divergence: The Gita frames stability within devotion, duty, and Self-knowledge; Zhuangzi frames it as natural process alignment and de-intensification of selfing.

items.resonance: both traditions link breath refinement with transformation of mental fluctuation and perceptual clarity.
items.divergence: Patanjali formalizes a staged technical system; Zhuangzi gives a poetic anthropological image without codifying practice mechanics.

items.resonance: both counsel non-grasping relation to beings rather than constant calculative control.
items.divergence: Heidegger's project is a modern philosophical critique of technological enframing; Zhuangzi's is a cosmological-ethical invitation grounded in Daoist naturalism.

title: Horses' Hoofs.
thesis: The claim is that survivability often depends on strategic illegibility to systems of extraction.
source_excerpt: Horses have hoofs to carry them over frost and snow; hair, to protect them from wind and cold. They eat grass and drink water, and fling up their heels over the champaign. Such is the real nature of horses. Palatial dwellings are of no use to them. One day Poh Loh A Chinese Rarey, of somewhat legendary character. appeared, saying, "I understand the management of horses." So he branded them, and clipped them, and pared their hoofs, and put halters on them, tying them up by the head and shackling them by the feet, and disposing them in stables, with the result that two or three in every ten died. Then he kept them hungry and thirsty, trotting them and galloping them, and grooming, and trimming
translation_literal:
A horse's hooves can tread on frost and snow; its coat can withstand wind and cold. It eats grass, drinks water, and lifts its legs to prance about — this is the true nature of a horse. Even if you gave it grand terraces and stately halls, it would have no use for them.

Then along came Bo Le, who said, "I am skilled at managing horses." He singed them, clipped them, pared their hooves, branded them. He bound them with halters and hobbles, penned them in stables and stalls — and two or three horses in ten died. He starved them, made them thirst, drove them at a gallop, raced them, drilled them into formation. In front they suffered the torment of bit and ornament; behind, the threat of whip and crop — and now more than half the horses were dead.

The potter says, "I am skilled at working clay: the round pieces match my compass, the square ones match my square." The carpenter says, "I am skilled at working wood: the curved pieces match my hook, the straight ones answer to my line." But is it the nature of clay and wood to want to match compass and square, hook and line? Yet generation after generation they praise them, saying, "Bo Le was skilled at managing horses; the potter and carpenter are skilled at working clay and wood." This is exactly the error of those who would govern the world.

My thought is that one truly skilled at governing the world does not act this way. The people have a constant nature: they weave and clothe themselves, they plow and feed themselves — this is called their shared virtue (dé 德). They are unified and not factional; call this the freedom given by tiān 天 (Heaven). So in an age of utmost virtue, people walked with a steady, solid gait, and their gaze was calm and undistracted. In those times there were no trails cut through the mountains, no boats or bridges on the marshes. The ten thousand things lived together in their communities, their settlements joined side by side. Birds and beasts formed their flocks and herds; grasses and trees grew to their full length. And so you could lead the birds and beasts about on a tether, and climb up to peer into the nest of a magpie. In this age of utmost virtue, people dwelt alongside the birds and beasts and lived clustered together with all the ten thousand things. How could anyone then know the difference between the noble and the petty? All alike were without cunning, so their virtue did not depart from them; all alike were without desire, and this is called uncarved simplicity. In such uncarved simplicity the people's nature was fulfilled.

Then the sages arrived. They limped and strained to produce "benevolence" (rén 仁), stood on tiptoe reaching for "righteousness" (yì 義), and the world began to doubt. They sprawled out extravagant "music," fussed and picked over "ritual," and the world began to split apart. If the plain wood were not carved up, who would make the sacrificial goblet? If the white jade were not cut, who would make the ceremonial tablets? If the dào 道 and dé 德 were not cast aside, what use would there be for benevolence and righteousness? If nature and feeling were not abandoned, what use for ritual and music? If the five colors were not confused, who would need patterns and ornament? If the five notes were not disordered, who would need to tune the six pitch-pipes? To carve up the plain wood into vessels — that is the craftsman's crime. To destroy the dào and dé to make benevolence and righteousness — that is the sages' error.

As for horses: living on open land they eat grass and drink water; when pleased they rub their necks together, when angry they turn their backs and kick. That is the whole of a horse's knowledge! But burden it with crossbar and yoke, line it up with the moon-shaped brow-piece, and now the horse learns to break the shaft, to slip the yoke, to butt the cover, to spit out the bit, to steal the reins. So when a horse's cunning grows until it acts like a thief, that is Bo Le's crime.

In the time of He Xu, the people stayed at home not knowing what they were doing, went out not knowing where they were going, filled their mouths with food and were happy, drummed their bellies and roamed at ease. That was the whole of what the people could do! Then the sages arrived, bending and twisting people into ritual and music in order to correct the shape of the world, dangling benevolence and righteousness overhead to comfort the world's heart — and only then did the people begin to strain on tiptoe after knowledge, scrambling and competing to chase profit, and it could not be stopped. This too is the sages' error.
commentary:
This chapter builds its whole argument on a single fixed distinction it wants to dissolve: the divide between *skill* and *harm*, between *cultivating* something and *ruining* it. The horse trainer Bo Le is celebrated precisely as an expert — and the passage forces us to see that his expertise is a kind of slow slaughter. The rhetorical gut-punch is arithmetic: two or three in ten die, then more than half. The praise-word 'skilled' (善) and the death-count sit right next to each other, and the reader is meant to feel the contradiction. What looks like improvement is really the imposition of an alien standard — compass, square, hook, plumb-line — onto something that had its own completeness.

The deeper move is the collapse of the distinction between *raw* and *finished*. Our habit is to see the uncarved block, the untooled horse, the unlettered people, as incomplete — waiting for the artisan or sage to complete them. Zhuangzi reverses the vector: the goblet is not a gift added to the wood, it is a wound inflicted on the wood; the sacrificial jade tablet is what remains after the jade has been mutilated. The list of counterfactuals ('if the plain wood were not carved up... if the dào were not cast aside...') is one sustained proof that all our prized cultural achievements — ritual, music, virtue-as-doctrine, refined art — are subtractions dressed as additions. Each one presupposes a prior wholeness it has already broken.

Crucially, the horse's newfound *cunning* — learning to bite through the bit, steal the reins, break the shaft — is not evidence of the horse's badness but of Bo Le's. Constraint *manufactures* the resistance it then claims to be correcting. This is the passage's sharpest political insight: the sage who governs by ritual, knowledge, and moral distinction generates the very competitiveness and profit-chasing he was supposed to cure. 'It could not be stopped' — because the mechanism is self-amplifying. Once you install a standard for the noble versus the petty, people begin straining on tiptoe (踶跂) toward it, and desire replaces contentment. The distinction between the well-governed and the unruly turns out to be produced by the act of governing itself.

The He Xu people who eat, drum their bellies, and wander 'not knowing where they are going' are not primitives to be pitied — they embody 素樸 (unworked plainness), a fullness that needs no cutting. Zhuangzi is not offering a nostalgic historical program; the 'age of utmost virtue' is a philosophical mirror held up so we can see what our supposed refinements have cost. The distinction between civilized and wild, cultivated and coarse, dissolves the moment you notice that the tools of civilization are also its wounds.

Key Terms

**素樸 (sù pǔ)** — Undyed silk and uncarved wood; the state of natural, unworked wholeness before any 'improvement' cuts into it.
**天放 (tiān fàng)** — The 'release/freedom of Heaven' — living according to one's given nature, unified and unfactional, not steered by imposed rules.
**踶跂 (dì qì)** — Straining on tiptoe; the strenuous, unnatural reaching after moral ideals and status that Zhuangzi says the sages' teachings induce.
practice: The next time you find yourself correcting, training, or optimizing something — a child's posture, a plant's growth, your own morning routine — pause and watch what dies in the correction. Name one small thing that was alive in the raw state and is now gone. Whisper it aloud: 'I have made it match my compass.'

anchor_chapter:
Horses have hoofs to carry them over frost and snow; hair, to protect them from wind and cold. They eat grass and drink water, and fling up their heels over the champaign. Such is the real nature of horses. Palatial dwellings are of no use to them.

One day Poh Loh

appeared, saying, "I understand the management of horses."

So he branded them, and clipped them, and pared their hoofs, and put halters on them, tying them up by the head and shackling them by the feet, and disposing them in stables, with the result that two or three in every ten died. Then he kept them hungry and thirsty, trotting them and galloping them, and grooming, and trimming, with the misery of the tasselled bridle before and the fear of the knotted whip behind, until more than half of them were dead.

The potter says, "I can do what I will with clay. If I want it round, I use compasses; if rectangular, a square."

The carpenter says, "I can do what I will with wood. If I want it curved, I use an arc; if straight, a line."

But on what grounds can we think that the natures of clay and wood desire this application of compasses and square, of arc and line? Nevertheless, every age extols Poh Loh for his skill in managing horses, and potters and carpenters for their skill with clay and wood. Those who govern the empire make the same mistake.

The people have certain natural instincts;—to weave and clothe themselves, to till and feed themselves. These are common to all humanity, and all are agreed thereon. Such instincts are called "Heaven-sent."

And so in the days when natural instincts prevailed, men moved quietly and gazed steadily. At that time, there were no roads over mountains, nor boats, nor bridges over water. All things were produced, each for its own proper sphere. Birds and beasts multiplied; trees and shrubs grew up. The former might be led by the hand; you could climb up and peep into the raven's nest. For then man dwelt with birds and beasts, and all creation was one. There were no distinctions of good and bad men. Being all equally without knowledge, their virtue could not go astray. Being all equally without evil desires, they were in a state of natural integrity, the perfection of human existence.

But when Sages appeared, tripping people over charity and fettering with duty to one's neighbour, doubt found its way into the world. And then with their gushing over music and fussing over ceremony, the empire became divided against itself.

Were the natural integrity of things left unharmed, who could make sacrificial vessels? Were white jade left unbroken, who could make the regalia of courts? Were Tao not abandoned, who could introduce charity and duty to one's neighbour? Were man's natural instincts his guide, what need would there be for music and ceremonies? Were the five colours not confused, who would practise decoration? Were the five notes not confused, who would adopt the six pitch-pipes?

Destruction of the natural integrity of things, in order to produce articles of various kinds,—this is the fault of the artisan. Annihilation of Tao in order to practise charity and duty to one's neighbour,—this is the error of the Sage.

Horses live on dry land, eat grass and drink water. When pleased, they rub their necks together. When angry, they turn around and kick up their heels at each other. Thus far only do their natural dispositions carry them. But bridled and bitted, with a plate of metal on their foreheads, they learn to cast vicious looks, to turn the head to bite, to resist, to get the bit out of the mouth or the bridle into it. And thus their natures become depraved,—the fault of Poh Loh.

In the days of Ho Hsü

the people did nothing in particular when at rest, and went nowhere in particular when they moved. Having food, they rejoiced; having full bellies, they strolled about. Such were the capacities of the people. But when the Sages came to worry them with ceremonies and music in order to rectify the form of government, and dangled charity and duty to one's neighbour before them in order to satisfy their hearts,—then the people began to develop a taste for knowledge and to struggle one with the other in their desire for gain. This was the error of the Sages.

The simplicity of style, and general intelligibility of this chapter have raised doubts as to its genuineness. But as Lin Hsi Chung justly observes, its sympathetic tone in relation to dumb animals, stamps it, in spite of an undue proportion of word to thought, as beyond reach of the forger's art.
translation:
A horse's hooves can tread on frost and snow; its coat can withstand wind and cold. It eats grass, drinks water, and lifts its legs to prance about — this is the true nature of a horse. Even if you gave it grand terraces and stately halls, it would have no use for them.

Then along came Bo Le, who said, "I am skilled at managing horses." He singed them, clipped them, pared their hooves, branded them. He bound them with halters and hobbles, penned them in stables and stalls — and two or three horses in ten died. He starved them, made them thirst, drove them at a gallop, raced them, drilled them into formation. In front they suffered the torment of bit and ornament; behind, the threat of whip and crop — and now more than half the horses were dead.

The potter says, "I am skilled at working clay: the round pieces match my compass, the square ones match my square." The carpenter says, "I am skilled at working wood: the curved pieces match my hook, the straight ones answer to my line." But is it the nature of clay and wood to want to match compass and square, hook and line? Yet generation after generation they praise them, saying, "Bo Le was skilled at managing horses; the potter and carpenter are skilled at working clay and wood." This is exactly the error of those who would govern the world.

Birds and beasts formed their flocks and herds; grasses and trees grew to their full length. And so you could lead the birds and beasts about on a tether, and climb up to peer into the nest of a magpie. To destroy the dào and dé to make benevolence and righteousness — that is the sages' error.

As for horses: living on open land they eat grass and drink water; when pleased they rub their necks together, when angry they turn their backs and kick. That is the whole of a horse's knowledge! But burden it with crossbar and yoke, line it up with the moon-shaped brow-piece, and now the horse learns to break the shaft, to slip the yoke, to butt the cover, to spit out the bit, to steal the reins. In the time of He Xu, the people stayed at home not knowing what they were doing, went out not knowing where they were going, filled their mouths with food and were happy, drummed their bellies and roamed at ease. That was the whole of what the people could do! Then the sages arrived, bending and twisting people into ritual and music in order to correct the shape of the world, dangling benevolence and righteousness overhead to comfort the world's heart — and only then did the people begin to strain on tiptoe after knowledge, scrambling and competing to chase profit, and it could not be stopped. pratibha_layers.label: Pratibha Translation
pratibha_layers.body:
Master Carpenter Shi sees the great shrine-oak and dismisses it: unusable timber, unfit for boat, coffin, furniture, door, or pillar. "Exactly why it has lived so long," he says.

That night the tree appears in his dream and rebukes his metric. Fruit trees are cut, stripped, and broken precisely because they are immediately useful. "I sought long to be unusable," the tree says. "Had I been conventionally useful, I would never have attained this magnitude."

When the apprentice objects that the tree's sacred status itself is a use, the master clarifies: its mode of safety is unlike ordinary utility. It survives by escaping extractive categories.

pratibha_layers.label: Pratibha Commentary
pratibha_layers.body:
The claim is that survivability often depends on strategic illegibility to systems of extraction. The counterintuitive move is not merely "useless things last longer"; it is that refusal of dominant utility criteria can become an affirmative design principle for life. The tree is not inertly lucky - it actively "seeks" non-capture over time. Zhuangzi turns what looks like deficiency into adaptive intelligence.

In Daoist context, this deepens the earlier gourd/tree motif by adding dream-voice and temporal strategy. Immediate utility serves short-cycle economies; non-extractability serves long-cycle flourishing. The artisan's first judgment is technically correct yet existentially narrow. The dream destabilizes professional expertise when it absolutizes its own frame. A carpenter's measure can evaluate boards, but cannot by itself evaluate lives.

Existentially, this passage speaks to modern optimization culture. Individuals and communities are pressured to maximize legibility, output, and market-use. Zhuangzi asks what must remain unoptimized if anything is to endure. "Sacredness" here can be read as social shielding around what should not be consumed. The teaching is not anti-skill; it is anti-totalization of one skill's metric over all values. To preserve life, one sometimes must be deliberately unprofitable to predatory systems.

pratibha_layers.label: Practice (Abhyasa)
pratibha_layers.body: Identify one capability you habitually over-offer to gain approval, set a clear boundary around one instance of that offering this week, and observe whether the protected space increases depth, longevity, or integrity in your work.

items.definition: "not timber / not fit material" -> in this passage, non-extractable being that escapes instrumental capture -> translated as "worthless wood," which misses the strategic and protective function of non-fit.

items.term: wú suǒ kě yòng (無所可用)
items.definition: "nothing available for immediate use" -> contextual meaning: refusal of narrow deployability -> literal "good for nothing" obscures Zhuangzi's inversion that this is precisely what enables greater life-use.

shrine/community-sacred tree -> marks a social-ritual buffer that can protect what economics would otherwise consume -> reducing it to "sacred tree" can hide its institutional role as a protective designation.
"great use" -> long-horizon, ecosystemic, existential value beyond short-term extraction -> default "use" collapses scales; the passage contrasts immediate utility with enduring significance.

items.resonance: both challenge the assumption that what is most economically efficient is most life-giving, and both defend forms of value that resist extraction.
items.divergence: Gandhi grounds critique in moral-politico program and collective resistance; Zhuangzi offers imagistic-philosophical strategy centered on ontological non-capture.

items.resonance: both distinguish human-scale flourishing from systems that turn persons and things into mere inputs.
items.divergence: Illich theorizes institutional design explicitly; Zhuangzi dramatizes the insight through parable and dream speech, leaving implementation open and plural.

items.resonance: as Buddhism uses expedient forms to liberate, Zhuangzi uses non-useful form to protect being from instrumental violence.
items.divergence: Mahayana upaya is pedagogical and compassion-driven; Zhuangzi's non-use strategy is ecological-existential and often non-programmatic.
