translation:
Zeyang traveled to Chu, and Yi Jie spoke of him to the king, but the king would not grant him an audience. Yi Jie went home. Peng Yang (Zeyang) went to Wang Guo and said: "Sir, why not mention me to the king?" Wang Guo said: "I am not as good at this as Gong Yuexiu." Peng Yang asked: "What kind of man is Gong Yuexiu?" He replied: "In winter he spears turtles in the river; in summer he rests at the mountain's edge. When someone passes and asks about it, he says, 'This is my dwelling.' Now if even Yi Jie could not manage the introduction, how much less could I! And I am not even Yi Jie's equal. As for Yi Jie's character — he has no inner virtue (dé 德) but plenty of cleverness. He does not restrain himself, and so he lets his connections work their spell on him, rigidly, blindly stumbling about in the domain of wealth and rank. He does not help others through virtue but helps them dissolve it. A freezing man borrows spring for warmth; a man overheated wishes back the cold winds of winter. Now the King of Chu, as a man, is imposing in bearing and severe. Toward crime he is unforgiving as a tiger. Only a flatterer or a man of upright virtue could ever bend him. So the sage: in poverty he makes his household forget its want; in success he makes lords and dukes forget their rank and salary, humbling them. Toward things he takes joy in them; toward people he delights in their free flow while keeping his own integrity. So sometimes without speaking he pours harmony (hé 和) into others, and simply standing beside a person he transforms them — the natural rightness between father and son. Thus he returns to stillness. Dwelling there, he unifies whatever he touches. His distance from the common human mind is that great. That is why I said, 'Wait for Gong Yuexiu.'"

The sage penetrates all entanglements, comprehending everything as a single body, yet does not know that it is so — this is his nature (xìng 性). He returns to his destiny and moves and acts, taking tiān 天 (heaven, the natural) as his teacher, and people follow along and give him names. To worry over knowledge, when one's actions never last more than a moment — if these have their stopping point, what can one do about it! A person born beautiful — others hand him a mirror; if he is not told, he does not know he is more beautiful than others. Whether he knows it or not, whether he hears of it or not, his delight in it never ceases, and others' fondness for it never ceases — this is nature. The sage's love for people — others give it a name; if he is not told, he does not know he loves people. Whether he knows it or not, whether he hears it or not, his love for people never ceases, and people's ease in him never ceases — this is nature. The old homeland, the old city — to gaze at it fills one with gladness. Even if nine parts in ten are overgrown with hills, weeds, and trees, still one feels glad — how much more when one sees what one has seen and hears what one has heard, raised up like a tower a hundred feet high among the crowds!

Ranxiang Shi grasped the hub of the ring (the pivot) and let things complete themselves accordingly; with things he had no end and no beginning, no measure of time. Daily changing along with things, he was the one thing that did not change. Why ever let go of this! One who takes tiān as teacher yet fails to truly take tiān as teacher will perish along with things — how then can he make anything his real work? The sage has never had a 'heaven,' never had a 'human,' never had a 'beginning,' never had 'things.' He walks together with the world and does not stop; his conduct is complete and does not leak away. His merging with things — how does he do it?

Tang got Menyin Dengheng as his tutor; he followed the teacher without being fenced in by him, and attained self-completion. He held office under a name, but the name proved excessive to the method, and so he got a double view. Confucius exhausted his deliberations and made this his teaching. Rongcheng Shi said: "Take away the days and there is no year; take away the inner and there is no outer."

King Ying of Wei made a pact with Marquis Mou of Qi, and Marquis Mou broke it. King Ying, enraged, was about to send an assassin. Gongsun Yan, the 'Rhinoceros-Head' general, heard of it and was ashamed. He said: "You are lord of ten thousand chariots, yet you would take revenge like a common man. Give me two hundred thousand armored troops and I will attack Qi for you, capture its people, seize its cattle and horses, make its ruler burn with fever until it breaks out on his back, and then I will tear his state from him. When Tian Ji flees, I will strike his back and break his spine." Ji Zi heard this and was ashamed. He said: "To build a wall a hundred feet high, and then, once it is built, to tear it down again — this is the torment of the laborers. Now for seven years no troops have been raised — this is the foundation of your reign. Yan is a troublemaker; do not listen to him." Huazi heard this and was disgusted. He said: "One who eloquently urges attacking Qi is a troublemaker; one who eloquently urges not attacking is also a troublemaker; and one who says 'those who argue for attacking or not attacking are troublemakers' is himself yet another troublemaker." The king said: "Then what should I do?" He said: "Just seek the dào 道, that is all!"

Huizi heard of this and presented Dai Jinren. Dai Jinren said: "There is a creature called the snail — do you know it, my lord?" "Yes." "On the snail's left horn there is a kingdom called Chu; on its right horn a kingdom called Man. From time to time they battle over territory, corpses pile up by the tens of thousands, and the pursuit of the routed lasts fifteen days before they turn back." The king said: "Bah! Empty talk!" He said: "Let me make it real for you, my lord. In your mind, do the four directions and up and down have any limit?" The king said: "No limit." He said: "And knowing how to let the mind roam in the limitless, when you turn back to the lands one can actually reach and travel, don't they seem barely to exist at all?" The king said: "Yes." He said: "Among the reachable lands is Wei; within Wei is Liang; within Liang is the king. Between the king and the ruler of Man, is there any difference?" The king said: "No difference." The guest left, and the king sat dazed as if he had lost something. The guest gone, Huizi came in. The king said: "That guest — he is a great man..."

則陽游於楚，夷節言之於王，王未之見。
夷節歸。
彭陽見王果曰：「夫子何不譚我於王？
」王果曰：「我不若公閱休。
」彭陽曰：「公閱休奚為者邪？
」曰：「冬則擉鱉於江，夏則休乎山樊。
有過而問者，曰：「此予宅也。
」夫夷節已不能，而況我乎！
吾又不若夷節。
夫夷節之為人也，無德而有知，不自許，以之神其交，固，顛冥乎富貴之地。
非相助以德，相助消也。
夫凍者假衣於春，暍者反冬乎冷風。
夫楚王之為人也，形尊而嚴。
其於罪也，無赦如虎。
非夫佞人正德，其孰能橈焉﹗故聖人，其窮也，使家人忘其貧；
其達也，使王公忘爵祿而化卑。
其於物也，與之為娛矣；
其於人也，樂物之通而保己焉。
故或不言而飲人以和，與人並立而使人化，父子之宜。
彼其乎歸。
居，而一間其所施。
其於人心者，若是其遠也。
故曰「待公閱休」。
」聖人達綢繆，周盡一體矣，而不知其然，性也。
復命搖作而以天為師，人則從而命之也。
憂乎知而所行恆無幾時，其有止也，若之何！
生而美者，人與之鑑，不告則不知其美於人也。
若知之，若不知之，若聞之，若不聞之，其可喜也終無已，人之好之亦無已，性也。
聖人之愛人也，人與之名，不告則不知其愛人也。
若知之，若不知之，若聞之，若不聞之，其愛人也終無已，人之安之亦無已，性也。
舊國舊都，望之暢然。
雖使丘陵草木之緡入之者十九，猶之暢然，況見見聞聞者也，以十仞之臺縣眾閒者也。
冉相氏得其環中以隨成，與物無終無始，無幾無時。
日與物化者，一不化者也。
闔嘗舍之！
夫師天而不得師天，與物皆殉，其以為事也，若之何？
夫聖人未始有天，未始有人，未始有始，未始有物，與世偕行而不替，所行之備而不洫，其合之也，若之何？
湯得其司御門尹登恆為之傅之，從師而不囿；
得其隨成。
為之司其名；
之名嬴法，得其兩見。
仲尼之盡慮，為之傅之。
容成氏曰：「除日無歲，無內無外。
」魏瑩與田侯牟約，田侯牟背之，魏瑩怒，將使人剌之。
犀首公孫衍聞而恥之，曰：「君為萬乘之君也，而以匹夫從讎。
衍請受甲二十萬，為君攻之，虜其人民，係其牛馬，使其君內熱發於背，然後拔其國。
忌也出走，然後抶其背，折其脊。
」季子聞而恥之，曰：「築十仞之城，城者既十仞矣，則又壞之，此胥靡之所苦也。
今兵不起七年矣，此王之基也。
衍亂人，不可聽也。
」華子聞而醜之，曰：「善言伐齊者，亂人也；
善言勿伐者，亦亂人也；
謂「伐之與不伐亂人也」者，又亂人也。
」君曰：「然則若何？
」曰：「君求其道而已矣﹗」惠之聞之，而見戴晉人。
戴晉人曰：「有所謂蝸者，君知之乎？
」曰：「然。
」「有國於蝸之左角者，曰觸氏；
有國於蝸之右角者，曰蠻氏，時相與爭地而戰，伏尸數萬，逐北旬有五日而後反。
」君曰：「噫！
其虛言與？
」曰：「臣請為君實之。
君以意在四方上下，有窮乎？
」君曰：「無窮。
」曰：「知游心於無窮，而反在通達之國，若存若亡乎？
」君曰：「然。
」曰：「通達之中有魏，於魏中有梁，於梁中有王，王與蠻氏，有辯乎？
」君曰：「無辯。
」客出而君惝然若有亡也。
客出，惠子見。

pratibha_layers.body: When Tsê Yang visited the Ch'u State, I Chieh Upon I Chieh's return, Tsê Yang went to see Wang Kuo, "I am not so fitted for that," replied Wang Kuo, "as Kung Yüeh Hsiu." "In winter," said Wang Kuo, "he catches turtles on the river. In summer, he reposes in some mountain copse. If any passers-by ask of him, he tells them, "This is my home." Where I Chieh could not succeed, still less should I. I am not equal even to him. "He is a man without virtue, but possessed of knowledge. Were it not for an air of arrogance, he would be very popular with his superiors. But help without virtue is a hindrance. Shivering people borrowing clothes in the coming spring! Hot people thinking of last winter's icy blast! "The prince of Ch'u is dignified and severe. In punishing, he is merciless as a tiger. Only a very practised or a very perfect man could influence him. "The true Sage, when in obscurity, causes those around him to forget their poverty. When in power, he causes princes to forget ranks and emoluments, and to become as though of low estate. He rejoices exceedingly in all creation. He exults to see Tao diffused among his fellow-men, while suffering no loss himself. "Thus, although silent, he can instil peace; and by his mere presence cause men to be to each other as father and son. From his very return to passivity comes this active influence for good. So widely does he differ in heart from ordinary men. Wherefore I said, 'Wait for Kung Yüeh Hsiu.' "The true Sage is free from all embarrassments. All things are to him as One. Yet he knows not that this is so. It is simply nature. In the midst of action he remains the same. He makes God his guide, and men make him theirs. He grieves that wisdom carries one but a short distance, and at times comes altogether to a deadlock. "To a beauty, mankind is the mirror in which she sees herself. If no one tells her she is beautiful, she does not know that she is so. But whether she knows it or whether she does not know it, whether she hears it or whether she does not hear it, her joy will never cease, neither will mankind ever cease to take pleasure therein. It is nature. "The love of a Sage for his fellows likewise finds expression among mankind. Were he not told so, he would not know that he loved his fellows.

德 “potency, virtue, obtained power” — how the Way is efficacious in a particular being -> in this passage (tsê Yang.), inner potency that shows as unforced efficacy rather than moral display -> trap: Victorian “virtue” as propriety; dé is charismatic power of alignment, not rule-keeping

translation_literal:
External things cannot be counted on. So Long Feng was executed, Bi Gan was cut down, Ji Zi feigned madness, E Lai died, and the tyrants Jie and Zhou were destroyed. Every ruler wants his ministers loyal, yet loyalty does not guarantee trust: thus Wu Yun's body was thrown into the river, and Chang Hong died in Shu, where his blood, stored three years, turned to green jade. Every parent wants a filial child, yet filial devotion does not guarantee love: thus Xiao Ji grieved and Zeng Shen sorrowed.

Rub wood against wood and it kindles; hold metal beside fire and it melts. When yīn and yáng run crosswise, heaven and earth are shaken; then come thunder and lightning, fire within water, burning even the great locust tree. There is a grief that traps you on both sides with nowhere to flee. Restless and unformed, the heart hangs suspended between heaven and earth, oppressed and sunk in dull knots. Gain and loss grind against each other and kindle much fire; the crowd burns up its inner harmony. The cool moon cannot overcome that fire, and so, all at once, one collapses and the dào runs out.

Zhuang Zhou's household was poor, so he went to borrow grain from the Marquis Overseer of the River. The Marquis said, 'Fine. When I collect the taxes from my fief I'll lend you three hundred pieces of gold. Will that do?' Zhuang Zhou flushed with anger and said, 'Yesterday as I came, something called out to me in the middle of the road. I looked back and saw a carp in the wheel-rut. I asked, "Carp! What are you doing there?" It answered, "I am a wave-official of the Eastern Sea. Can you spare a dipperful of water to keep me alive?" I said, "Fine. I'm on my way to visit the kings of Wu and Yue in the south; I'll divert the waters of the West River to meet you. Will that do?" The carp flushed with anger and said, "I've lost my usual element and have nowhere to be. All I need is a dipper or so of water to live. But you talk like that — you might as well look for me at the dried-fish market!"'

Prince Ren made an enormous hook and a thick black line, baited it with fifty bullocks, squatted on Mount Kuaiji, and cast into the Eastern Sea. Day after day he fished, and for a whole year caught nothing. Then a great fish took the bait, dragging the huge hook under, plunging down, thrashing and rearing its fins, throwing up white waves like mountains. The sea shook, the sound like gods and demons, terrifying for a thousand miles. Prince Ren landed this fish, sliced and dried it, and from the river eastward, from Cangwu northward, everyone had their fill of it. Ever after, the small-minded storytellers all pass the tale around in amazement. But someone who shoulders a little rod and line and trots off to ditches and gutters after minnows will have a hard time catching a great fish. Those who dress up petty sayings to court the county magistrates are just as far from great attainment. So one who has never heard of Prince Ren's manner is far indeed from being fit to help run the world.

Some Confucians were robbing a tomb, quoting the Odes and the Rites. The senior scholar called down, 'Dawn is breaking in the east — how goes the work?' The junior scholar said, 'I haven't got the burial robes off yet, but there's a pearl in the mouth. The Odes say: "Green, green the grain, growing on the slope. In life he gave no charity — why in death should he hold a pearl?"' They grabbed the corpse's temple-hair, pressed down its chin, and while one pried at the cheeks with a metal mallet, they eased the jaws apart — 'Careful not to damage the pearl in the mouth!'

A disciple of Lao Laizi went out gathering firewood and met Confucius. Returning, he reported: 'There's a man over there — long above, short below, hunched in the back, ears set far back, and a gaze as though he's managing the whole world. I don't know whose son he is.' Lao Laizi said, 'That's Qiu. Call him here.' When Confucius came, Lao Laizi said, 'Qiu, drop that self-importance of yours and that clever look, and you'll become a noble person.' Confucius bowed and stepped back, changed his expression uneasily, and asked, 'Can my work still make progress?' Lao Laizi said, 'You cannot bear the harm of one age, and so you set loose calamity for ten thousand ages. Is this mere stinginess, or does your plan simply fall short? To grant favors so as to make people happy, taking that as your glory — this is a lifelong disgrace, the conduct of mediocre folk. They pull one another along by reputation, bind one another with hidden schemes. Rather than praise Yao and condemn Jie, better to forget both and shut off your praising. What runs backward always does harm; every stirring is deviation. The sage hesitates before undertaking anything, and so he always succeeds. But you — how can you keep carrying this burden and priding yourself on it to the end?'

Lord Yuan of Song, at midnight, dreamed of a man with loose hair peering in at his side door, who said, 'I come from the Zailu deep. As envoy of the Clear River I was going to the place of the Earl of the River, but a fisherman, Yu Ju, has caught me.' Lord Yuan woke and had a diviner interpret it. The diviner said, 'This is a sacred turtle.' The lord asked, 'Is there a fisherman named Yu Ju?' His attendants said, 'There is.' The lord said, 'Order Yu Ju to attend court.' The next day Yu Ju came. The lord asked, 'What have you caught?' He answered, 'My net took a white turtle, five feet across.' The lord said, 'Present your turtle.' When it arrived, the lord twice wished to kill it and twice wished to spare it. Uncertain, he had it divined: 'Kill the turtle for divination — auspicious.' So the turtle was gutted; drilled seventy-two times, and not one prophecy failed.

Confucius said, 'The sacred turtle could appear in Lord Yuan's dream, but could not escape Yu Ju's net. Its knowledge could yield seventy-two flawless prophecies, but could not escape the disaster of being gutted. So it is: knowledge has its limits, and even the divine has what it cannot reach. Even the highest knowledge can be outmaneuvered by ten thousand schemers. A fish does not fear the net but fears the pelican. Discard petty knowledge and great knowledge shines; discard being good and you'll become good of yourself. An infant is born without a great teacher yet learns to speak — because it lives among those who speak.' Huizi said to...
commentary:
This chapter opens with a blunt thesis — 外物不可必, 'external things cannot be counted on' — and then dissolves several fixed distinctions we cling to for security. The opening catalogue of loyal ministers who were executed and filial sons who suffered demolishes the assumption that virtue reliably produces reward. Loyalty and betrayal, devotion and abandonment: the moral bookkeeping we trust does not balance. Zhuangzi is not preaching cynicism but puncturing the illusion of control over outcomes.

The borrowed-grain fable sharpens this into the distinction between timely and untimely help. The Marquis offers a grand future payment; the carp needs a cupful now. Aid that arrives on the giver's schedule, scaled to the giver's grandeur, is worthless to the one actually gasping in the rut. The story quietly collapses the difference between generosity and neglect: a promise magnificent in scale but wrong in timing is functionally the dried-fish market.

The Prince Ren fable and the tomb-robbing Confucians turn the lens on scale and pretense. Great fishing requires great patience and a willingness to wait a year; petty minnow-hunters cannot even imagine it. Meanwhile the tomb-robbers recite the Odes to sanctify grave-robbery — scholarship weaponized to strip a corpse. Here the fixed distinction between the learned and the base dissolves: quoting scripture while prying open a dead man's jaw shows how 'usefulness' and virtue-language get hollowed into tools.

The turtle story is the philosophical hinge. The sacred turtle is knowing enough to appear in a king's dream, yet not knowing enough to dodge one fisherman's net; its divinatory power is flawless, yet it cannot foresee its own gutting. This dissolves the distinction between wisdom and vulnerability, between the sacred and the caught. Confucius' concluding lines — discard petty knowledge and great knowledge shines, discard 'being good' and you become good — point past the whole apparatus of calculation. The infant learning speech simply by living among speakers is the model: not strategic mastery but responsive immersion. Contingency (外物) can't be mastered by more cleverness; it can only be met by dropping the grasping self that keeps score.

Key Terms

**外物 wài wù** — 'External things' — circumstances and outcomes outside the self, which cannot be relied upon or controlled.
**道盡 dào jìn** — 'The dào runs out' — the exhaustion or collapse of one's vital way when the heart burns itself up in gain-and-loss calculation.
**小知 / 大知 xiǎo zhī / dà zhī** — 'Petty knowledge' versus 'great knowledge' — strategic cleverness that entraps, versus the open awareness that shines only when scheming is set aside.
practice: Today, notice one situation where you are waiting for the 'right-sized' response before acting — waiting until you have more time, more money, more expertise before you help someone or address a real need. Then do the small, immediate, unimpressive thing instead: give the cupful of water now, not the diverted river later. Send the one-line message, make the small payment, offer the ten minutes you actually have. Watch how the mind resists because the gesture feels too minor to matter. That resistance is exactly the Marquis-of-the-River reflex — grandeur postponing usefulness. The carp only needed a dipper.

anchor_chapter:
Contingencies are uncertain. Hence the decapitation of Lung Fêng, the disembowelment of Pi Kan, the enthusiasm of Chi Tzŭ, the death of Wu Lai, the flights of Chieh and Chou.

No sovereign but would have loyal ministers; yet loyalty does not necessarily inspire confidence. Hence Wu Yüan found a grave in the river;

and Ch'ang Hung perished in Shu, his blood, after being preserved three years, turning into green jade.

No parent but would have filial sons; yet filial piety does not necessarily inspire love. Hence Hsiao Chi sorrowed, and Tsêng Shên grieved.

The first, prince of the House of Yin, was turned out of doors by his stepmother. The second, one of the disciples of Confucius and a rare pattern of filial piety, grieved because his mother was too old to hit him hard enough. See p. 100.

Wood rubbed with wood produces fire. Metal exposed to fire will liquefy. If the Positive and Negative principles operate inharmoniously, heaven and earth are greatly disturbed. Thunder crashes, and with rain comes lightning, scorching up the tall locust-trees. One fears lest sky and land should collapse and leave no escape. Unable to lie perdu, the heart feels as though suspended between heaven and earth.

So in the struggle between peace and unrest, the friction between good and evil, much fire is evolved which consumes the inner harmony of man. But the mind is unable to resist fire. It is destroyed, and with it Tao comes to an end.

"Yes," said the prince. "I am just about collecting the revenue of my fief, and will then lend you three hundred ounces of silver. Will that do?"

At this Chuang Tzŭ flushed with anger and said, "Yesterday, as I was coming along, I heard a voice calling me. I looked round, and in the cart-rut I saw a stickleback.

"'I am a denizen of the eastern ocean,' replied the stickleback. 'Pray, Sir, a pint of water to save my life.'

"'Yes,' said I. 'I am just going south to visit the princes of Wu and Yüeh. I will bring you some from the west river. Will that do?'

"At this the stickleback flushed with anger and said, 'I am out of my element. I have nowhere to go. A pint of water would save me. But to talk to me like this,—you might as well put me in a dried-fish shop at once.'"

Jên Kung Tzŭ

got a huge hook on a big line, which he baited with fifty oxen. He squatted down at Kuei-chi, and cast into the eastern ocean. Every day he fished, but for a whole year he caught nothing. Then came a great fish which swallowed the bait, and dragging the huge hook dived down below. This way and that way it plunged about, erecting the dorsal fin. The white waves rolled mountain high. The great deep was shaken up. The noise was like that of so many devils, terrifying people for many miles around.

But when Jên Kung Tzŭ had secured his fish, he cut it up and salted it. And from Chih-ho eastwards, and from Ts'ang-wu northwards, there was none but ate his fill of that fish. Even among succeeding generations, gobemouches of the day recounted the marvellous tale.

To take a rod and line, and go to a pool, and catch small fry is a very different thing from catching big fish. And by means of a little show of ability to secure some small billet is a very different thing from really pushing one's way to the front. So that those who do not imitate the example of Jên Kung Tzŭ will be very far from becoming leaders in their generation.

When some Confucianists were opening a grave in accordance with their Canons of Poetry and Rites, the master shouted out, "Day is breaking. How are you getting on with the work?"

"Not got off the burial-clothes yet," answered an apprentice. "There is a pearl in the mouth."

Now the Canon of Poetry says—

The greenest corn
Grows over graves.
In life, no charity;
In death, no pearl.
So seizing the corpse's brow with one hand, and forcing down its chin with the other, these Confucianists proceed to tap its cheeks with a metal hammer, in order to make the jaws open gently and not injure the pearl!

The above, pronounced by Lin Hsi Chung to be spurious, is aimed at the Confucianists, who are ready to commit any outrage on natural feeling so long as there is no violation of the details of their own artificial system.

A disciple of Lao Lai Tzŭ

while out gathering fuel, chanced to meet Confucius. On his return, he said, "There is a man over there with a long body and short legs, round shoulders and drooping ears. He looks as though he were sorrowing over mankind. I know not who he can be."

"It is Confucius!" cried Lao Lai Tzŭ. "Bid him come hither."

When Confucius arrived, Lao Lai Tzŭ addressed him as follows:—

"Ch'iu! Get rid of your dogmatism and your specious knowledge, and you will be really a superior man."

Confucius bowed and was about to retire, when suddenly his countenance changed and he enquired, "Shall I then be able to enter upon Tao?"

"The wounds of one generation being too much," answered Lao Lai Tzŭ, "you would take to yourself the sorrows of all time. Are you not weary? Is your strength equal to the task?

"To employ goodness as a passport to influence through the gratification of others, is an everlasting shame. Yet this is the common way of all, to lure people by fame, to bind them by ties of gratification.

"Better than extolling Yao and cursing Chieh is oblivion of both, keeping one's praises to oneself. These things react injuriously on self; the agitation of movement results in deflection.

"The true Sage is a passive agent. If he succeeds, he simply feels that he was provided by no effort of his own with the energy necessary to success."

Prince Yüan of Sung dreamed one night that a man with dishevelled hair peeped through a side door and said, "I have come from the waters of Tsai-lu. I am a marine messenger attached to the staff of the River God. A fisherman, named Yü Ch'ieh, has caught me."

When the prince awaked, he referred his dream to the soothsayers, who said, "This is a divine tortoise."

"Is there any fisherman," asked the prince, "whose name is Yü Ch'ieh?"

Being told there was, the prince gave orders for his appearance at court; and the next day Yü Ch'ieh had an audience.

"Fisherman," said the prince, "what have you caught?"

"I have netted a white tortoise," replied the fisherman, "five feet in semi-circumference."

"Bring your tortoise," said the prince. But when it came, the prince could not make up his mind whether to kill it or keep it alive. Thus in doubt, he had recourse to divination, and received the following response:—

So the tortoise was despatched. After which, out of seventy-two omens taken, not a single one proved false.

"A divine tortoise," said Confucius, "can appear to prince Yüan in a dream, yet it cannot escape the net of Yü Ch'ieh. Its wisdom can yield seventy-two faultless omens, yet it cannot escape the misery of being cut to pieces. Truly wisdom has its limits; spirituality, that which it cannot reach.

"In spite of the highest wisdom, there are countless snares to be avoided; If a fish has not to fear nets, there are always pelicans. Get rid of small wisdom, and great wisdom will shine upon you. Put away goodness and you will be naturally good. A child does not learn to speak because taught by professors of the art, but because it lives among people who can themselves speak."

Hui Tzŭ said to Chuang Tzŭ, "Your theme, Sir, is the useless."

"For instance, the earth is of huge proportions, yet man uses of it only as much as is covered by the sole of his foot. By and by, he turns up his toes and goes beneath it to the Yellow Spring. Has he any further use for it?"

"Could a man transcend the limits of the human," said Chuang Tzŭ, "would he not do so? Unable to do so, how should he succeed?

"The determination to retire, to renounce the world,—such alas! is not the fruit of perfect wisdom or immaculate virtue. From cataclysms ahead, these do not turn back; nor do they heed the approach of devouring flame. Although there are class distinctions of high and low, these are but for a time, and under the changed conditions of a new sphere are unknown.

"Wherefore it has been said, 'The perfect man leaves no trace behind.'

"For instance, to glorify the past and to condemn the present has always been the way of the scholar.

Yet if Hsi Wei Shih and individuals of that class

were caused to re-appear in the present day, which of them but would accommodate himself to the age?

"Only the perfect man can transcend the limits of the human and yet not withdraw from the world, live in accord with mankind and yet suffer no injury himself. Of the world's teachings he learns nothing. He has that within which makes him independent of others.

"If the eye is unobstructed, the result is sight. If the ear is unobstructed the result is hearing. If the nose is unobstructed, the result is sense of smell. If the mouth is unobstructed, the result is sense of taste. If the mind is unobstructed, the result is wisdom. If wisdom is unobstructed, the result is Tê.

"Tao may not be obstructed. To obstruct is to strangle. This affects the base, and all evils spring into life.

"All sentient beings depend upon breath. If this does not reach them in sufficient quantity, it is not the fault of God. God supplies it day and night without cease, but man stops the passage.

"Man has for himself a spacious domain. His mind may roam to heaven. If there is no room in the house, the wife and her mother-in-law run against one another. If the mind cannot roam to heaven, the faculties will be in a state of antagonism. Those who would benefit mankind from deep forests or lofty mountains are simply unequal to the strain upon their higher natures.

"Ill-regulated virtue ends in reputation. Ill-regulated reputation ends in notoriety. Scheming leads to confusion. Knowledge begets contentions. Obstinacy produces stupidity. Organised government is for the general good of all.

"Spring rains come in due season, and plants and shrubs burst up from the earth. Weeding and tending do not begin until such plants and shrubs have reached more than half their growth, and without being conscious of the fact.

"Repose gives health to the sick. Rubbing the eyelids removes the wrinkles of old age. Quiet will dispel anxieties. These remedies however are the resource only of those who need them. Others who are free from such ills pay no attention thereto.

"That which the true Sage marvels at in the empire, claims not the attention of the Divine man. That which the truly virtuous man marvels at in his own sphere, claims not the attention of the true Sage. That which the superior man marvels at in his State, claims not the attention of the truly virtuous man. How the mean man adapts himself to his age, claims not the attention of the superior man.

"The keeper of the Yen gate,

having maltreated himself severely in consequence of the death of his parents, received a high official post.

"Yao offered the empire to Hsü Yu, but Hsü Yu fled. T'ang offered it to Wu Kuang, but Wu Kuang declined with anger.

"When Chi T'o heard of Hsü Yu's flight, he took all his disciples with him and jumped into the river K'uan;

upon which the various feudal princes mourned for three years,

"The raison d'être of a fish-trap is the fish. When the fish is caught, the trap may be ignored. The raison d'être of a rabbit-snare is the rabbit. When the rabbit is caught the snare may be ignored. The raison d'être of language is an idea to be expressed. When the idea is expressed, the language may be ignored. But where shall I find a man to ignore language, with whom I may be able to converse?"
abhyasa: Today, notice one situation where you are waiting for the 'right-sized' response before acting — waiting until you have more time, more money, more expertise before you help someone or address a real need. Then do the small, immediate, unimpressive thing instead: give the cupful of water now, not the diverted river later. Send the one-line message, make the small payment, offer the ten minutes you actually have. Watch how the mind resists because the gesture feels too minor to matter. That resistance is exactly the Marquis-of-the-River reflex — grandeur postponing usefulness. The carp only needed a dipper.
practice_provenance: Practice re-authored for form diversity, grounded in the passage.
translation:
External things cannot be counted on. So Long Feng was executed, Bi Gan was cut down, Ji Zi feigned madness, E Lai died, and the tyrants Jie and Zhou were destroyed. Every ruler wants his ministers loyal, yet loyalty does not guarantee trust: thus Wu Yun's body was thrown into the river, and Chang Hong died in Shu, where his blood, stored three years, turned to green jade. Every parent wants a filial child, yet filial devotion does not guarantee love: thus Xiao Ji grieved and Zeng Shen sorrowed.

Rub wood against wood and it kindles; hold metal beside fire and it melts. When yīn and yáng run crosswise, heaven and earth are shaken; then come thunder and lightning, fire within water, burning even the great locust tree. There is a grief that traps you on both sides with nowhere to flee. Restless and unformed, the heart hangs suspended between heaven and earth, oppressed and sunk in dull knots. Gain and loss grind against each other and kindle much fire; the crowd burns up its inner harmony. The cool moon cannot overcome that fire, and so, all at once, one collapses and the dào runs out.

Zhuang Zhou's household was poor, so he went to borrow grain from the Marquis Overseer of the River. The Marquis said, 'Fine. When I collect the taxes from my fief I'll lend you three hundred pieces of gold. Will that do?' Zhuang Zhou flushed with anger and said, 'Yesterday as I came, something called out to me in the middle of the road. I looked back and saw a carp in the wheel-rut. I asked, "Carp! What are you doing there?" It answered, "I am a wave-official of the Eastern Sea. Can you spare a dipperful of water to keep me alive?" I said, "Fine. I'm on my way to visit the kings of Wu and Yue in the south; I'll divert the waters of the West River to meet you. Will that do?" The carp flushed with anger and said, "I've lost my usual element and have nowhere to be. All I need is a dipper or so of water to live. But you talk like that — you might as well look for me at the dried-fish market!"'

Prince Ren made an enormous hook and a thick black line, baited it with fifty bullocks, squatted on Mount Kuaiji, and cast into the Eastern Sea. Day after day he fished, and for a whole year caught nothing. Then a great fish took the bait, dragging the huge hook under, plunging down, thrashing and rearing its fins, throwing up white waves like mountains. The sea shook, the sound like gods and demons, terrifying for a thousand miles. Prince Ren landed this fish, sliced and dried it, and from the river eastward, from Cangwu northward, everyone had their fill of it. Ever after, the small-minded storytellers all pass the tale around in amazement. But someone who shoulders a little rod and line and trots off to ditches and gutters after minnows will have a hard time catching a great fish. Those who dress up petty sayings to court the county magistrates are just as far from great attainment. So one who has never heard of Prince Ren's manner is far indeed from being fit to help run the world.

Some Confucians were robbing a tomb, quoting the Odes and the Rites. The senior scholar called down, 'Dawn is breaking in the east — how goes the work?' The junior scholar said, 'I haven't got the burial robes off yet, but there's a pearl in the mouth. The Odes say: "Green, green the grain, growing on the slope. In life he gave no charity — why in death should he hold a pearl?"' They grabbed the corpse's temple-hair, pressed down its chin, and while one pried at the cheeks with a metal mallet, they eased the jaws apart — 'Careful not to damage the pearl in the mouth!'

A disciple of Lao Laizi went out gathering firewood and met Confucius. Returning, he reported: 'There's a man over there — long above, short below, hunched in the back, ears set far back, and a gaze as though he's managing the whole world. I don't know whose son he is.' Lao Laizi said, 'That's Qiu. Call him here.' When Confucius came, Lao Laizi said, 'Qiu, drop that self-importance of yours and that clever look, and you'll become a noble person.' Confucius bowed and stepped back, changed his expression uneasily, and asked, 'Can my work still make progress?' Lao Laizi said, 'You cannot bear the harm of one age, and so you set loose calamity for ten thousand ages. Is this mere stinginess, or does your plan simply fall short? To grant favors so as to make people happy, taking that as your glory — this is a lifelong disgrace, the conduct of mediocre folk. They pull one another along by reputation, bind one another with hidden schemes. Rather than praise Yao and condemn Jie, better to forget both and shut off your praising. What runs backward always does harm; every stirring is deviation. The sage hesitates before undertaking anything, and so he always succeeds. But you — how can you keep carrying this burden and priding yourself on it to the end?'

Lord Yuan of Song, at midnight, dreamed of a man with loose hair peering in at his side door, who said, 'I come from the Zailu deep. As envoy of the Clear River I was going to the place of the Earl of the River, but a fisherman, Yu Ju, has caught me.' Lord Yuan woke and had a diviner interpret it. The diviner said, 'This is a sacred turtle.' The lord asked, 'Is there a fisherman named Yu Ju?' His attendants said, 'There is.' The lord said, 'Order Yu Ju to attend court.' The next day Yu Ju came. The lord asked, 'What have you caught?' He answered, 'My net took a white turtle, five feet across.' The lord said, 'Present your turtle.' When it arrived, the lord twice wished to kill it and twice wished to spare it. Uncertain, he had it divined: 'Kill the turtle for divination — auspicious.' So the turtle was gutted; drilled seventy-two times, and not one prophecy failed.

Confucius said, 'The sacred turtle could appear in Lord Yuan's dream, but could not escape Yu Ju's net. Its knowledge could yield seventy-two flawless prophecies, but could not escape the disaster of being gutted. So it is: knowledge has its limits, and even the divine has what it cannot reach. Even the highest knowledge can be outmaneuvered by ten thousand schemers. A fish does not fear the net but fears the pelican. Discard petty knowledge and great knowledge shines; discard being good and you'll become good of yourself. An infant is born without a great teacher yet learns to speak — because it lives among those who speak.' Huizi said to...

pratibha_layers.body:
外物不可必，故龍逢誅，比干戮，箕子狂，惡來死，桀、紂亡。
人主莫不欲其臣之忠，而忠未必信，故伍員流於江，萇弘死於蜀，藏其血三年而化為碧。
人親莫不欲其子之孝，而孝未必愛，故孝己憂而曾參悲。
木與木相摩則然，金與火相守則流，陰陽錯行，則天地大駭，於是乎有雷有霆，水中有火，乃焚大槐。
有甚憂兩陷而無所逃。
螴蜳不得成，心若縣於天地之間，慰暋沈屯，利害相摩，生火甚多，眾人焚和，月固不勝火，於是乎有僓然而道盡。
莊周家貧，故往貸粟於監河侯。
監河侯曰：「諾，我將得邑金，將貸子三百金，可乎？
」莊周忿然作色曰：「周昨來，有中道而呼者。
周顧視車轍中，有鮒魚焉。
周問之曰：「鮒魚來﹗子何為者耶？
」對曰：「我，東海之波臣也。
君豈有斗升之水而活我哉？
」周曰：「諾，我且南游吳越之王，激西江之水而迎子，可乎？
」鮒魚忿然作色曰：「吾失我常與，我無所處。
我得斗升之水然活耳。
君乃言此，曾不如早索我於枯魚之肆﹗」」任公子為大鉤巨緇，五十犗以為餌，蹲乎會稽，投竿東海，旦旦而釣，期年不得魚。
已而大魚食之，牽巨鉤陷，沒而下，騖揚而奮鬐，白波若山，海水震蕩，聲侔鬼神，憚赫千里。
任公子得若魚，離而腊之，自制河以東，蒼梧已北，莫不厭若魚者。
已而後世輇才諷說之徒，皆驚而相告也。
夫揭竿累，趣灌瀆，守鯢鮒，其於得大魚難矣，飾小說以干縣令，其於大達亦遠矣，是以未嘗聞任氏之風俗，其不可與經於世亦遠矣！
儒以︽詩︾、︽禮︾發冢。
大儒臚傳曰：「東方作矣，事之何若？
」小儒曰：「未解裙襦，口中有珠。
」︽詩︾固有之曰：「青青之麥，生於陵陂。
生不布施，死何含珠為？
」接其鬢，壓其顪，儒以金椎控其頤，徐別其頰，無傷口中珠﹗」老萊子之弟子出薪，遇仲尼，反以告，曰：「有人於彼，修上而趨下，末僂而後耳，視若營四海，不知其誰氏之子。
」老萊子曰：「是丘也，召而來。
」仲尼至。
曰：「丘，去汝躬矜與汝容知，斯為君子矣。
」仲尼揖而退，蹙然改容而問曰：「業可得進乎？
」老萊子曰：「夫不忍一世之傷而驁萬世之患，抑固窶邪，亡其略弗及邪？
惠以歡為驁，終身之醜，中民之行進焉耳，相引以名，相結以隱。
與其譽堯而非桀，不如兩忘而閉其所譽。
反無非傷也。
動無非邪也。
聖人躊躇以興事，以每成功。
奈何哉其載焉終矜爾！
」宋元君夜半而夢人被髮闚阿門，曰：「予自宰路之淵，予為清江使河伯之所，漁者余且得予。
」元君覺，使人占之，曰：「此神龜也。
」君曰：「漁者有余且乎？
」左右曰：「有。
」君曰：「令余且會朝。
」明日，余且朝。
君曰：「漁何得？
」對曰：「且之網得白龜焉，箕圓五尺。
」君曰：「獻若之龜。
」龜至，君再欲殺之，再欲活之，心疑，卜之，曰：「殺龜以卜吉。
」乃刳龜，七十二鑽而無遺筴。
仲尼曰：「神龜能見夢於元君，而不能避余且之網；
知能七十二鑽而無遺筴，不能避刳腸之患。
如是，則知有所困，神有所不及也。
雖有至知，萬人謀之。
魚不畏網而畏鵜鶘。
去小知而大知明，去善而自善矣。
嬰兒生無石師而能言，與能言者處也。
」惠子謂

pratibha_layers.body: Contingencies are uncertain. Hence the decapitation of Lung Fêng, the disembowelment of Pi Kan, the enthusiasm of Chi Zi, the death of Wu Lai, the flights of Chieh and Chou. No sovereign but would have loyal ministers; yet loyalty does not necessarily inspire confidence. Hence Wu Yüan found a grave in the river; and Ch'ang Hung perished in Shu, his blood, after being preserved three years, turning into green jade. No parent but would have filial sons; yet filial piety does not necessarily inspire love. Hence Hsiao Chi sorrowed, and Tsêng Shên grieved. The first, prince of the House of Yin, was turned out of doors by his stepmother. The second, one of the disciples of Confucius and a rare pattern of filial piety, grieved because his mother was too old to hit him hard enough. See p. 100. Wood rubbed with wood produces fire. Metal exposed to fire will liquefy. If the Positive and Negative principles operate inharmoniously, heaven and earth are greatly disturbed. Thunder crashes, and with rain comes lightning, scorching up the tall locust-trees. One fears lest sky and land should collapse and leave no escape. Unable to lie perdu, the heart feels as though suspended between heaven and earth. So in the struggle between peace and unrest, the friction between good and evil, much fire is evolved which consumes the inner harmony of man. But the mind is unable to resist fire. It is destroyed, and with it Tao comes to an end. "Yes," said the prince. "I am just about collecting the revenue of my fief, and will then lend you three hundred ounces of silver. Will that do?" At this Zhuang Zi flushed with anger and said, "Yesterday, as I was coming along, I heard a voice calling me. I looked round, and in the cart-rut I saw a stickleback. "'I am a denizen of the eastern ocean,' replied the stickleback. 'Pray, Sir, a pint of water to save my life.' "'Yes,' said I. 'I am just going south to visit the princes of Wu and Yüeh. I will bring you some from the west river. Will that do?' "At this the stickleback flushed with anger and said, 'I am out of my element. I have nowhere to go. A pint of water would save me.

Pratibha treats the chapter as a philosophical movement: read the anchor appendix for the full Victorian translation, then the Pratibha translation for a modern, source-honest excerpt. Full chapter text remains in the public-domain appendix for philological comparison; the display layers do not reproduce Giles wholesale.

items.definition: 道 “path/way” and “to speak/guide” — course that can be walked and barely named -> in this passage (contingencies.), the nameless source-and-course that lets beings move by their own measure -> trap: a deity named Tao, a lifestyle brand, or a fixed doctrine one can possess

無用 “without use” — the great use of the useless -> in this passage (contingencies.), uselessness as survival and freedom: what cannot be extracted escapes the axe -> trap: mere inefficiency; Zhuangzi’s wúyòng is strategic non-instrumentality

自然 “self-so” — thus-of-itself, not “picturesque nature” -> in this passage (contingencies.), spontaneous so-ness: things unfolding without forced contrivance -> trap: Romantic wilderness aesthetics; zìrán is ontological non-forcing, not scenery

無 “without” + 為 “contrived doing” — action without aggressive interference -> in this passage (contingencies.), unforced congruence with conditions: skill that does not obstruct the work -> trap: “non-action” as passivity; wúwéi can be highly skilled activity without strain

pratibha_layers.label: Practice (Abhyasa)
pratibha_layers.body: Sit for 3 minutes with natural breathing. At each inhale and exhale, notice awareness before naming experience.

items.resonance: Both texts refuse a single fixed stance toward reality: Chuang Tzu's contingencies resist certainty, while the Isavasya Upanishad warns that exclusive fixation on either manifest or unmanifest leads to darkness. Each demands a both/and awareness rather than either/or commitment.
items.divergence: The Upanishad frames the problem as metaphysical error (darkness from wrong view), while Chuang Tzu treats contingency as the nature of existence itself, requiring adaptive responsiveness rather than corrected doctrine.

items.citation: Tao Te Ching — Living Soft, Dead Hard
items.resonance: Both passages invert conventional expectation about a binary state: Chuang Tzu's contingencies undermine certainty about what will occur, while the Tao Te Ching reverses the assumed relationship between life (softness) and death (hardness), revealing hidden structural opposites.
items.divergence: The Tao Te Ching uses the life/death reversal to teach a practical principle of yielding strength, whereas Chuang Tzu's contingencies emphasize the radical unpredictability that resists any fixed principle.

title: Language.
thesis: Chapter 27 (Language.) in Giles's 1889 rendering.
source_excerpt: Of language put into other people's mouths, nine tenths will succeed. Of language based upon weighty authority, seven tenths. But language which flows constantly over, as from a full goblet, is in accord with God. The natural overflowings of the heart. When language is put into other people's mouths, outside support is sought. Just as a father does not negotiate his son's marriage; for any praise he could bestow would not have the same value as praise by an outsider. Thus, the fault is not mine, but that of others. Who will not believe the original speaker. To that which agrees with our own opinions we assent; from that which does not we dissent. We regard that which agrees with our own opin
translation_literal:
Nine out of ten of my words are put in the mouths of others; seven out of ten carry weight because they are borrowed from the honored; the goblet-words (zhī yán 卮言) pour out fresh each day, harmonized by the whetstone of tiān 天. Nine in ten spoken through others—one borrows an outside voice to make the point. A father does not act as matchmaker for his own son; better that another praise the boy than his father. This is not my fault; it is how people are: what agrees with them they accept, what differs from them they oppose; what matches their view they call right, what departs from it they call wrong.

Seven in ten that carry weight are meant to stop dispute—these are the words of elders. But if a man is ahead only in years and has no grasp of the warp and weft, the root and branch fitting to his age, then he is not really 'ahead.' A person with nothing to place him ahead of others lacks the way of a human being; and a person without the human way is simply called a stale relic.

The goblet-words pour out fresh each day, harmonized by the whetstone of tiān, spreading out endlessly, and so one lives out one's years. When nothing is said, things are level and equal; but that equality plus speech is no longer equal, and speech plus that equality is no longer equal. So it is said: 'Say nothing.' Yet to speak the unspoken—you may speak all your life and never have really spoken; you may say nothing all your life and never have failed to speak.

There is a reason things are acceptable, and a reason they are not; a reason they are so, and a reason they are not so. Why so? Because they are made so. Why not so? Because they are made not so. Why acceptable? Because accepted. Why unacceptable? Because rejected. Every thing has its 'so,' every thing has its 'acceptable.' No thing is not so; no thing is not acceptable. Without goblet-words pouring fresh each day, harmonized by the whetstone of tiān, who could last long? All the ten-thousand things are seeds, handing on their differing forms in turn; beginning and end are like a ring whose sequence no one can trace. This is called the leveling wheel of tiān (tiān jūn 天均), which is the whetstone of tiān.

Zhuangzi said to Huizi: 'Confucius at sixty had changed sixty times. What he first held as right he came in the end to reject—so who knows whether what he now calls right is not the same as what he called wrong at fifty-nine?' Huizi said: 'Confucius worked hard at his purpose and put knowledge to use.' Zhuangzi said: 'Confucius gave that up—he simply never spoke of it. Confucius said: We receive our talents from the great root and recover our spirit to live. Our singing should fit the pitch, our words fit the standard. When profit and duty are laid out before people, and likes and dislikes, right and wrong are used, one only subdues their mouths. To make people submit in their hearts, not daring to stand against you, and so establish the settledness of the world—enough, enough! I could never reach that.'

Zengzi served in office twice and his heart changed twice. He said: 'When I served while my parents lived, three fu of grain made my heart glad; later, serving for three thousand zhong that they never reached, my heart grieved.' A disciple asked Confucius: 'Can someone like Zeng be called free of any attachment that binds him?' He said: 'He was already bound. One truly unattached—could he feel such grief? Such a one would watch three fu and three thousand zhong the way you watch sparrows and mosquitoes passing before your eyes.'

Yancheng Ziyou said to Dongguo Ziqi: 'Since I heard your words: after one year I grew wild and plain, after two I followed along, after three I broke through, after four I became just a thing among things, after five they came to me, after six the spirit entered, after seven tiān was complete in me, after eight I no longer knew death from life, after nine—the great marvel. Life is doing; death is loss. Do you hold that death has a cause, while living-yang has none? Is that really so? Where is the fitting? Where is the unfitting? Tiān has its cycles of number, earth has its human holdings—where should I seek it? No one knows where it ends; how then can there be no fate? No one knows where it begins; how then can there be fate? Since things respond to one another, how can there be no ghosts? Since nothing determines the response, how can there be ghosts?'

The penumbras—the fringe-shadows—asked the Shadow: 'A moment ago you bowed, now you look up; a moment ago your hair was bound, now it hangs loose; a moment ago you sat, now you stand; a moment ago you walked, now you stop—why?' The Shadow said: 'So restless and fussy—why keep asking these little questions! I do these things but don't know why. I am like a cicada's husk, a snake's cast skin—resembling the thing but not it. In firelight and sunlight I gather; in shade and night I fade. Do I depend on that body of yours? And it, in turn, depends on something! When it comes I come with it, when it goes I go with it, when it surges I surge with it. Surging like that—what is there to ask about!'

Yangzi Ju was heading south to Pei; Laozi was traveling west into Qin. They arranged to meet at the outskirts, and at Liang, Yangzi met him. Midway Laozi looked up to the sky and sighed: 'At first I thought you could be taught; now I see you cannot.' Yangzi Ju said nothing. At the lodging he brought water, towel, and comb, took off his shoes outside the door, and crawled forward on his knees: 'Earlier I wished to ask you, master, but you were traveling and had no leisure, so I did not dare. Now you have leisure—may I ask the reason?' Laozi said: 'That haughty stare, that glaring look of yours—who could live with you? The purest white looks soiled; abundant virtue looks lacking.' When he had first arrived, the guests at the inn had welcomed him with ceremony, the host carried his mat, the hostess carried towel and comb, guests gave up their seats, the man at the stove yielded his place. When he returned, the guests fought with him for the mat!
commentary:
This chapter is Zhuangzi's own account of how he uses language—and it turns out to be an account of how to unfix every fixed thing. He names three modes: words lodged in others' mouths (yù yán), weighted words borrowed from the revered (zhòng yán), and 'goblet-words' (zhī yán) that pour out and empty themselves each day. The image is a tipping vessel that fills, spills, and rights itself—speech that never hardens into a permanent position because it keeps emptying. Ordinary speech traps us: we call 'right' whatever agrees with us and 'wrong' whatever differs, and even the authority of age is empty if it is mere seniority without substance. So the passage attacks the fixed distinction between right and wrong (shì/fēi) itself. Everything is 'so' from some standpoint and 'not so' from another; every position has a reason behind it. There is no view from nowhere—except the shifting, self-emptying view of goblet-words tuned to the tiān jūn, the leveling wheel of heaven where beginning and end circle like a ring with no traceable order.

The stories that follow dissolve one boundary after another. Confucius 'changed sixty times' by sixty—so which of his selves was the true one? The self is not fixed but a running sequence. Zengzi's shifting heart, glad over a little grain when his parents lived and grieved over vast wealth after, shows how attachment persists even when its object changes—the boundary between attachment and freedom is subtler than it looks. Then comes the dialogue of the Shadow and its own fringe-shadows: the shadow bows and rises and doesn't know why, because it depends on the body, which depends on something else, which depends on something else again—there is no final ground on which anything stands independently. The chain of dependence has no first link. And finally Yangzi Ju: when he traveled full of self-importance, people deferred and cleared away from him; after Laozi punctured his haughtiness, people jostled him for the mat—which is the mark of success. Losing your special status is exactly the arrival. Being fought with over a seat means you have become one among the crowd, no longer setting yourself apart. The dissolved distinction here is self/other: the sage does not stand out, and precisely by not standing out he lives freely among people.

Key Terms

**卮言 zhī yán** — 'Goblet-words'—speech modeled on a self-emptying tipping vessel; fluid, non-fixed language that never hardens into a permanent position.
**天倪 tiān ní** — The 'whetstone/differentiation of tiān'—the natural leveling boundary that harmonizes opposites rather than fixing them into right and wrong.
**天均 tiān jūn** — The 'leveling wheel of heaven'—the equalizing rotation in which beginning and end, this and that, circle endlessly like a ring with no traceable order.
practice: Try the 'goblet' exercise with one opinion you hold strongly today. State it plainly to yourself: 'X is right / Y is wrong.' Then deliberately fill in the sentence Zhuangzi hands you: 'It is so because it is made so; it is acceptable because it is accepted.' Ask honestly: from what standpoint, whose interest, what history, does my 'so' arise? Then set the opinion down—don't argue against it, just let the vessel tip and empty—and notice you can pick it up again later if it's still useful. Do this once with something small (a food preference, a judgment about a coworker) so the stakes are low enough to actually let go. The goal is not to become someone with no views, but someone whose views pour fresh and don't calcify into the fixed self that others must defer to or fight.

anchor_chapter:
Of language put into other people's mouths, nine tenths will succeed. Of language based upon weighty authority, seven tenths. But language which flows constantly over, as from a full goblet, is in accord with God.

When language is put into other people's mouths, outside support is sought. Just as a father does not negotiate his son's marriage; for any praise he could bestow would not have the same value as praise by an outsider. Thus, the fault is not mine, but that of others.

To that which agrees with our own opinions we assent; from that which does not we dissent. We regard that which agrees with our own opinion as right. We regard that which differs from our opinion as wrong. Language based on weighty authority is used to bar further argument. The authorities are our superiors, our elders in years. But if they lack the requisite knowledge and experience, being our superiors only in the sense of age, then they are not our superiors. And if men are not the superiors of their fellows, no one troubles about them. And those about whom no one troubles are merely stale.

Because it spreads out on all sides, it endures for all time. Without language, contraries are identical. The identity is not identical with its expression: the expression is not identical with its identity. Therefore it has been said, Language not expressed in language is not language. Constantly spoken, it is as though not spoken. Constantly unspoken, it is not as though not spoken.

From the subjective point of view, there are possibilities and impossibilities, there are suitabilities and unsuitabilities. This results from the natural affinity of things for what they are and their natural antagonism to what they are not. For all things have their own particular constitutions and potentialities. Nothing can exist without these.

But for language that constantly flows over, as from a full goblet, and is in accord with God, how should the permanent be attained?

All things spring from germs. Under many diverse forms these things are ever being reproduced. Round and round, like a wheel, no part of which is more the starting-point than any other. This is called the equilibrium of God. And he who holds the scales is God.

Alluding to the Identity-philosophy, which means, in the words of Emerson, "that nature iterates her means perpetually on successive planes.... The whole art of the plant is still to repeat leaf on leaf without end."

Chuang Tzŭ said to Hui Tzŭ, "When Confucius reached his sixtieth year he changed his opinions. What he had previously regarded as right, he ultimately came to regard as wrong. But who shall say whether the right of to-day may not be as wrong as the wrong of the previous fifty-nine years?"

"He was a persevering worker," replied Hui Tzŭ, "and his wisdom increased day by day."

"Confucius," replied Chuang Tzŭ, "discarded both perseverance and wisdom, but did not attempt to formulate the doctrine in words. He said, 'Man has received his talents from God, together with a soul to give them life. He should speak in accordance with established laws. His words should be in harmony with fixed order. Personal advantage and duty to one's neighbour lie open before us. Likes and dislikes, rights and wrongs, are but as men choose to call them. But to bring submission into men's hearts, so that they shall not be stiff-necked, and thus fix firmly the foundations of the empire,—to that, alas! I have not attained.'"

"From the above," says Lin Hsi Chung, "we may see that Hui Tzŭ, though skilled in winning debates was unskilled in winning hearts."

"As long as my parents were alive," said he, "I was happy on a small salary. When I had a large salary, but my parents were no more, I was sad."

A disciple said to Confucius, "Can we call Tsêng Tzŭ a man without cares to trouble him?"

"He had cares to trouble him," replied Confucius. "Can a man who has no cares to trouble him feel grief? His small salary and his large salary were to him like a heron or a mosquito flying past."

Yen Ch'êng Tzŭ Yu said to Tung Kuo Tzŭ Chi,

"One year after receiving your instructions I became naturally simple. After two years, I could adapt myself as required. After three years, I understood. After four years, my intelligence developed. After five years, it was complete. After six years, the spirit entered into me. After seven, I knew God. After eight, life and death existed for me no more. After nine, perfection.

"Life has its distinctions; but in death we are all made equal. That death should have an origin, but that life should have no origin,—can this be so? What determines its presence in one place, its absence in another?

Earth has yielded up its secrets to man. But where to seek whence am I?

"Not knowing the hereafter, how can we deny the operation of Destiny? Not knowing what preceded birth, how can we assert the operation of Destiny? When things turn out as they ought, who shall say that the agency is not supernatural? When things turn out otherwise, who shall say that it is?"

The various Penumbræ said to the Umbra, "Before you were looking down, now you are looking up. Before you had your hair tied up, now it is all loosed. Before you were sitting, now you have got up. Before you were moving, now you are stopping still. How is this?"

I do these things, but I do not know why. I am like the scaly back of the cicada, the shell of the locust,—apparently independent, but not really so. By firelight or in daylight I am seen: in darkness or by night I am gone. And if I am dependent on these, how much more are they dependent on something else? When they come, I come with them. When they go, I go with them. When they live, I live with them. But who it is that gives the life, how shall we seek to know?"

Yang Tzŭ Chü

went southwards to P'ei, and when Lao Tzŭ was travelling westwards to Ch'in, hastened to receive him outside the city. Arriving at the bridge, he met Lao Tzŭ; and the latter standing in the middle of the road, looked up to heaven and said with a sigh, "At first, I thought you could be taught. I think so no more."

Yang Tzŭ Chü made no reply, but when they reached the inn, handed Lao Tzŭ water for washing and rinsing, and a towel and comb. He then removed his own boots outside the door, and crawling on his knees into the Master's presence, said, "I have been wishing to ask for instruction, Sir, but as you were travelling and not at leisure, I did not venture. You are now, Sir, at leisure. May I enquire the reason of what you said?"

"You have an overbearing look," said Lao Tzŭ. "Who would live with such a man? He who is truly pure behaves as though he were sullied. He who has virtue in abundance behaves as though it were not enough."

These last two sentences occur in the Tao-Tê-Ching, ch. xli, and also in the works of Lieh Tzŭ as part of that author's own text. See The Remains of Lao Tzŭ, p. 29.

Yang Tzŭ Chü changed countenance at this, and replied, "I hear and obey."

translation:
Nine out of ten of my words are put in the mouths of others; seven out of ten carry weight because they are borrowed from the honored; the goblet-words (zhī yán 卮言) pour out fresh each day, harmonized by the whetstone of tiān 天. Nine in ten spoken through others—one borrows an outside voice to make the point. A father does not act as matchmaker for his own son; better that another praise the boy than his father. This is not my fault; it is how people are: what agrees with them they accept, what differs from them they oppose; what matches their view they call right, what departs from it they call wrong.

Seven in ten that carry weight are meant to stop dispute—these are the words of elders. But if a man is ahead only in years and has no grasp of the warp and weft, the root and branch fitting to his age, then he is not really 'ahead.' A person with nothing to place him ahead of others lacks the way of a human being; and a person without the human way is simply called a stale relic.

The goblet-words pour out fresh each day, harmonized by the whetstone of tiān, spreading out endlessly, and so one lives out one's years. When nothing is said, things are level and equal; but that equality plus speech is no longer equal, and speech plus that equality is no longer equal. So it is said: 'Say nothing.' Yet to speak the unspoken—you may speak all your life and never have really spoken; you may say nothing all your life and never have failed to speak.

There is a reason things are acceptable, and a reason they are not; a reason they are so, and a reason they are not so. Why so? Because they are made so. Why not so? Because they are made not so. Why acceptable? Because accepted. Why unacceptable? Because rejected. Every thing has its 'so,' every thing has its 'acceptable.' No thing is not so; no thing is not acceptable. Without goblet-words pouring fresh each day, harmonized by the whetstone of tiān, who could last long? All the ten-thousand things are seeds, handing on their differing forms in turn; beginning and end are like a ring whose sequence no one can trace. This is called the leveling wheel of tiān (tiān jūn 天均), which is the whetstone of tiān.

Zhuangzi said to Huizi: 'Confucius at sixty had changed sixty times. What he first held as right he came in the end to reject—so who knows whether what he now calls right is not the same as what he called wrong at fifty-nine?' Huizi said: 'Confucius worked hard at his purpose and put knowledge to use.' Zhuangzi said: 'Confucius gave that up—he simply never spoke of it. Confucius said: We receive our talents from the great root and recover our spirit to live. Our singing should fit the pitch, our words fit the standard. When profit and duty are laid out before people, and likes and dislikes, right and wrong are used, one only subdues their mouths. To make people submit in their hearts, not daring to stand against you, and so establish the settledness of the world—enough, enough! I could never reach that.'

Zengzi served in office twice and his heart changed twice. He said: 'When I served while my parents lived, three fu of grain made my heart glad; later, serving for three thousand zhong that they never reached, my heart grieved.' A disciple asked Confucius: 'Can someone like Zeng be called free of any attachment that binds him?' He said: 'He was already bound. One truly unattached—could he feel such grief? Such a one would watch three fu and three thousand zhong the way you watch sparrows and mosquitoes passing before your eyes.'

Yancheng Ziyou said to Dongguo Ziqi: 'Since I heard your words: after one year I grew wild and plain, after two I followed along, after three I broke through, after four I became just a thing among things, after five they came to me, after six the spirit entered, after seven tiān was complete in me, after eight I no longer knew death from life, after nine—the great marvel. Life is doing; death is loss. Do you hold that death has a cause, while living-yang has none? Is that really so? Where is the fitting? Where is the unfitting? Tiān has its cycles of number, earth has its human holdings—where should I seek it? No one knows where it ends; how then can there be no fate? No one knows where it begins; how then can there be fate? Since things respond to one another, how can there be no ghosts? Since nothing determines the response, how can there be ghosts?'

When it comes I come with it, when it goes I go with it, when it surges I surge with it. Surging like that—what is there to ask about!'

」顏成子游謂東郭子綦曰：「自吾聞子之言，一年而野，二年而從，三年而通，四年而物，五年而來，六年而鬼入，七年而天成，八年而不知死、不知生，九年而大妙。
生有為，死也虧。
公以其死也，有自也；
而生陽也，無自也。
而果然乎？
惡乎其所適？
惡乎其所不適？
天有歷數，地有人據，吾惡乎求之？
莫知其所終，若之何其無命也？
莫知其所始，若之何其有命也？
有以相應也，若之何其無鬼邪？
無以相應也，若之何其有鬼邪？
」眾罔兩問於景曰：「若向也俯而今也仰，向也括而今也被髮；
向也坐而今也起，向也行而今也止，何也？
」景曰：「搜搜也，奚稍問也！
予有而不知其所以。
予，蜩甲也，蛇蛻也，似之而非也。
火與日，吾屯也；
陰與夜，吾代也。
彼吾所以有待邪？
而況乎以有待者乎！
彼來則我與之來，彼往則我與之往，彼強陽則我與之強陽。
強陽者，又何以有問乎！
」陽子居南之沛，老聃西遊於秦，邀於郊，至於梁而遇老子。
老子中道仰天而嘆曰：「始以汝為可教，今不可也。
」陽子居不答。
至舍，進盥漱巾櫛，脫屨戶外，膝行而前，曰：「向者弟子欲請夫子，夫子行不閒，是以不敢。
今閒矣，請問其故。
」老子曰：「而雎雎盱盱，而誰與居？
大白若辱，盛德若不足。
」陽子居蹴然變容曰：「敬聞命矣！
」其往也，舍者迎將，其家公執席，妻執巾櫛，舍者避席，煬者避灶。
其反也，舍者與之爭席矣！

pratibha_layers.label: Pratibha Translation
pratibha_layers.body: Of language put into other people's mouths, nine tenths will succeed. Of language based upon weighty authority, seven tenths. But language which flows constantly over, as from a full goblet, is in accord with God. When language is put into other people's mouths, outside support is sought. Just as a father does not negotiate his son's marriage; for any praise he could bestow would not have the same value as praise by an outsider. Thus, the fault is not mine, but that of others. To that which agrees with our own opinions we assent; from that which does not we dissent. We regard that which agrees with our own opinion as right. We regard that which differs from our opinion as wrong. Language based on weighty authority is used to bar further argument. The authorities are our superiors, our elders in years. But if they lack the requisite knowledge and experience, being our superiors only in the sense of age, then they are not our superiors. And if men are not the superiors of their fellows, no one troubles about them. And those about whom no one troubles are merely stale. Because it spreads out on all sides, it endures for all time. Without language, contraries are identical. The identity is not identical with its expression: the expression is not identical with its identity. Therefore it has been said, Language not expressed in language is not language. Constantly spoken, it is as though not spoken. Constantly unspoken, it is not as though not spoken. From the subjective point of view, there are possibilities and impossibilities, there are suitabilities and unsuitabilities. This results from the natural affinity of things for what they are and their natural antagonism to what they are not. For all things have their own particular constitutions and potentialities. Nothing can exist without these. But for language that constantly flows over, as from a full goblet, and is in accord with God, how should the permanent be attained? All things spring from germs. Under many diverse forms these things are ever being reproduced. Round and round, like a wheel, no part of which is more the starting-point than any other. This is called the equilibrium of God. And he who holds the scales is God.

pratibha_layers.body: Chapter 27 (Language.) in Giles's 1889 rendering. Pratibha treats the chapter as a philosophical movement: read the anchor appendix for the full Victorian translation, then the Pratibha translation for a modern, source-honest excerpt. Full chapter text remains in the public-domain appendix for philological comparison; the display layers do not reproduce Giles wholesale.

items.definition: 卮言 “goblet words” — speech that tips and rights itself, inexhaustible like a wine vessel -> in this passage (language.), language that does not harden into fixed theses; words that pour with the situation -> trap: relativist chatter; goblet words are a disciplined flexible speaking, not empty irony

道 “path/way” and “to speak/guide” — course that can be walked and barely named -> in this passage (language.), the nameless source-and-course that lets beings move by their own measure -> trap: a deity named Tao, a lifestyle brand, or a fixed doctrine one can possess

齊 “level/make even” + 物 “things/beings” -> in this passage (language.), equalizing things: leveling standpoint claims so this/that lose absolute privilege -> trap: abstract logical identity of opposites; qí wù is perspectival liberation, not flattening reality

自然 “self-so” — thus-of-itself, not “picturesque nature” -> in this passage (language.), spontaneous so-ness: things unfolding without forced contrivance -> trap: Romantic wilderness aesthetics; zìrán is ontological non-forcing, not scenery

pratibha_layers.label: Practice (Abhyasa)
pratibha_layers.body: For 2 minutes, observe inner speech as sound only. Return to the silent awareness that hears it.

items.resonance: Both texts locate efficacy beyond linguistic utterance: Chuang Tzu observes that language placed in others' mouths succeeds nine-tenths of the time (implying a gap between word and reality), while Yoga Spandakarika asks 'what use are words?' when absolute desire pervades everything—both suggesting that true power operates in a register prior to or independent of speech.
items.divergence: Chuang Tzu treats language pragmatically as a tool whose success rate reveals the gap between sign and world, whereas Yoga Spandakarika dismisses words as unnecessary once non-dual consciousness is actualized; the former is epistemological, the latter soteriological.

items.resonance: Both texts locate the origin of manifest appearance in the heart as a generative locus: Chuang Tzu's language succeeds when placed in others' hearts (the seat of reception and resonance), while Siva Sutra traces all appearances to 'the collision of mind in the heart'—both making the heart the threshold where potentiality becomes actualized form.
items.divergence: Chuang Tzu emphasizes the heart as the receptive site where external language takes root and propagates, whereas Siva Sutra posits the heart as the site of ontological generation itself (mind-collision producing dream-like reality); one is communicative, the other cosmological.
