translation:
Confucius was a friend of Liuxia Ji, whose younger brother was named Robber Zhi. Robber Zhi commanded nine thousand followers, ran wild across the land, and preyed upon the feudal lords. He broke into homes and pried open doors, drove off people's oxen and horses, and carried off their wives and daughters. Greedy for gain, he forgot his kin; he cared nothing for father, mother, brothers, and made no offerings to his ancestors. Wherever he passed, large states guarded their walls and small states withdrew into their forts, and the common people suffered because of him.

Confucius said to Liuxia Ji: "A man who is a father should be able to instruct his son; a man who is an elder brother should be able to teach his younger brother. If a father cannot instruct his son and an elder brother cannot teach his younger brother, then there is nothing worth honoring in the bonds of father and son, elder and younger. Now you, sir, are a man of talent in this age, yet your younger brother is Robber Zhi, a plague upon the world, and you cannot correct him — I am privately ashamed on your behalf. Let me go and reason with him for you."

Liuxia Ji said: "You say, sir, that a father should be able to instruct his son and an elder brother should be able to teach his younger brother — but if the son will not heed the father's instruction and the younger brother will not accept the elder's teaching, then even with your eloquence, sir, what can be done? Besides, Zhi's nature is this: his heart is like a gushing spring, his moods like a whirlwind; his strength is enough to fend off any enemy, his cleverness enough to gloss over any wrong. Please him and he is delighted; cross him and he rages, and he easily insults people with words. You must not go."

Confucius did not listen. With Yan Hui driving the carriage and Zigong on the right, he went to see Robber Zhi.

Robber Zhi was just then resting his troops on the south side of the great mountain, dining on minced human liver. Confucius stepped down from his carriage and went forward. Seeing the gatekeeper, he said: "Kong Qiu of Lu, having heard of the general's lofty honor, respectfully bows twice to the gatekeeper." The gatekeeper went in to announce him. When Robber Zhi heard, he flew into a rage: his eyes blazed like bright stars, his hair stood up and lifted his cap. He said: "Isn't this that crafty, false man Kong Qiu from Lu? Tell him for me: 'You concoct phrases and invent sayings, wildly invoking Kings Wen and Wu. You wear a cap branching like a tree, you belt yourself with the ribs of a dead ox, you pile up words and twist meanings. You eat without plowing and clothe yourself without weaving; you flap your lips and wag your tongue, arbitrarily manufacturing right and wrong, so as to delude the rulers of the world and keep the scholars of the world from returning to their root. You fabricate this 'filial piety' and 'brotherly duty' in order to gamble for a fief and wealth and rank. Your crime is enormous and grave — run home fast! Otherwise I'll add your liver to today's dinner menu.'"

Confucius sent word again: "I have the good fortune to know Ji; I only wish to gaze upon your slippers beneath the tent." The gatekeeper announced him again. Robber Zhi said: "Send him forward!"

Confucius hurried in, then backed away from the mat, and bowed twice to Robber Zhi. Robber Zhi flew into a rage, spread both his legs, laid his hand on his sword, glared, and in a voice like a nursing tigress said: "Come forward, Qiu! If what you say pleases my mind, you live; if it crosses my heart, you die."

Confucius said: "I have heard that there are three kinds of virtue in the world. To be born tall and strong, matchlessly handsome, so that young and old, noble and lowly, are delighted at the sight of you — this is the highest virtue. To have knowledge that spans heaven and earth, able to distinguish all things — this is the middle virtue. To be brave and bold and decisive, gathering crowds and leading troops — this is the lowest virtue. Any man who has even one of these virtues is fit to face south, take the throne, and call himself sovereign. Now you, general, combine all three: your body is eight feet two inches tall, your face and eyes shine, your lips are like vivid cinnabar, your teeth like ranked seashells, your voice tuned to the note of the great bell — yet you are called 'Robber Zhi.' I am privately ashamed, general, that you do not take up something better. If you are willing to hear me out, I will go south as envoy to Wu and Yue, north to Qi and Lu, east to Song and Wei, west to Jin and Chu, and have them build you a great city hundreds of li across, establish a settlement of hundreds of thousands of households, and honor you, general, as a feudal lord. You could make a fresh start with the world, disband your armies and rest your troops, gather and provide for your brothers, and jointly offer sacrifices to your ancestors. This is the conduct of sages and men of talent, and what the world desires."

Robber Zhi flew into a great rage and said: "Come forward, Qiu! Those who can be steered by profit and admonished with words are all just stupid, coarse, ordinary folk. That I am tall and strong and handsome, so that people are delighted at the sight of me — this is virtue passed down from my father and mother. Even if you don't praise me, don't I know it myself? Besides, I have heard that those who love to praise a man to his face also love to slander him behind his back. Now you tell me about a great city and a multitude of people — this is wanting to steer me with profit and keep me like some ordinary man. How could that last? Of great cities, none is greater than the whole world. Yao and Shun possessed the world, yet their descendants had not enough land to stick an awl into; Tang and Wu set themselves up as Sons of Heaven, yet their later lines were cut off and destroyed — was this not because their profit was so great? Besides, I have heard that in ancient times the birds and beasts were many and the people few, so people all lived in nests to escape them. By day they gathered acorns and chestnuts, by night they roosted in the trees — hence they were called 'the people of the Nest-Builder.' In ancient times the people did not know clothing; in summer they stored up firewood, in winter they warmed themselves by it — hence they were called 'the people who knew how to live.' In the age of Shen Nong, they lay down calm and content, rose up easy and free. The people knew their mothers but not their fathers; they lived alongside the deer, plowed and ate, wove and clothed themselves, and had no thought of harming one another. This was virtue at its highest flourishing. Yet the Yellow Emperor could not maintain such virtue; he fought Chi You in the field of Zhuolu, and blood flowed for a hundred li. Yao and Shun arose and set up their throngs of ministers; Tang banished his lord, and King Wu killed the tyrant Zhòu. From then on the strong overrode the weak and the many did violence to the few. Tang, ..."

pratibha_layers.body:
孔子與柳下季為友，柳下季之弟，名曰盜跖。
盜跖從卒九千人，橫行天下，侵暴諸侯。
穴室樞戶，驅人牛馬，取人婦女。
貪得忘親，不顧父母兄弟，不祭先祖。
所過之邑，大國守城，小國入保，萬民苦之。
孔子謂柳下季曰：「夫為人父者，必能詔其子；
為人兄者，必能教其弟。
若父不能詔其子，兄不能教其弟，則無貴父子兄弟之親矣。
今先生，世之才士也，弟為盜跖，為天下害，而弗能教也，丘竊為先生羞之。
丘請為先生往說之。
」柳下季曰：「先生言為人父者必能詔其子，為人兄者必能教其弟，若子不聽父之詔，弟不受兄之教，雖今先生之辯，將奈之何哉﹗且跖之為人也，心如涌泉，意如飄風，強足以距敵，辯足以飾非。
順其心則喜，逆其心則怒，易辱人以言。
先生必無往。
」孔子不聽，顏回為馭，子貢為右，往見盜跖。
盜跖乃方休卒徒大山之陽，膾人肝而餔之。
孔子下車而前，見謁者曰：「魯人孔丘，聞將軍高義，敬再拜謁者。
」謁者入通。
盜跖聞之大怒，目如明星，髮上指冠，曰：「此夫魯國之巧偽人孔丘非邪？
為我告之：「爾作言造語，妄稱文、武，冠枝木之冠，帶死牛之脅，多辭繆說，不耕而食，不織而衣，搖唇鼓舌，擅生是非，以迷天下之主，使天下學士不反其本，妄作孝弟，而徼倖於封侯富貴者也。
子之罪大極重，疾走歸！
不然，我將以子肝益晝餔之膳。
」孔子復通曰：「丘得幸於季，愿望履幕下。
」謁者復通。
盜跖曰：使來前！
」孔子趨而進，避席反走，再拜盜跖。
盜跖大怒，兩展其足，案劍瞋目，聲如乳虎，曰：「丘來前！
若所言，順吾意則生，逆吾心則死。
」孔子曰：「丘聞之，凡天下有三德：生而長大，美好無雙，少長貴賤見而皆說之，此上德也；
知維天地，能辯諸物，此中德也；
勇悍果敢，聚眾率兵，此下德也。
凡人有此一德者，足以南面稱孤矣。
今將軍兼此三者，身長八尺二寸，面目有光，唇如激丹，齒如齊貝，音中黃鐘，而名曰盜跖，丘竊為將軍恥不取焉。
將軍有意聽臣，臣請南使吳越，北使章魯，東使宋衛，西使晉楚，使為將軍造大城數百里，立數十萬戶之邑，尊將軍為諸侯，與天下更始，罷兵休卒，收養昆弟，共祭先祖。
此聖人才士之行，而天下之願也。
」盜跖大怒曰：「丘來前！
夫可規以利而可諫以言者，皆愚陋恆民之謂耳。
今長大美好，人見而說之者，此吾父母之遺德也。
丘雖不吾譽，吾獨不自知邪？
且吾聞之，好面譽人者，亦好背而毀之。
今丘告我以大城眾民，是欲規我以利而恆民畜我也，安可久長也！
城之大者，莫大乎天下矣。
堯、舜有天下，子孫無置錐之地；
湯、武立為天子，而後世絕滅；
非以其利大故邪？
且吾聞之，古者禽獸多而人少，於是民皆巢居以避之。
晝拾橡栗，暮栖木上，故命之曰「有巢氏之民」。
古者民不知衣服，夏多積薪，冬則煬之，故命之曰「知生之民」。
神農之世，臥則居居，起則于于。
民知其母，不知其父，與麋鹿共處，耕而食，織而衣，無有相害之心。
此至德之隆也。
然而黃帝不能致德，與蚩尤戰於涿鹿之野，流血百里。

pratibha_layers.body: Confucius was on terms of friendship with Liu Hsia Chi, whose younger brother was known as "Robber Chê." This is an anachronism. Liu Hsia Chi (or Hui) was a virtuous official of the Lu State. He flourished some 80 and more years before the time of Confucius. Robber Chê had a band of followers nine thousand strong. He ravaged the whole empire, plundering the various nobles and breaking into people's houses. He drove off oxen and horses. He stole men's wives and daughters. Family ties put no limit to his greed. He had no respect for parents nor for brothers. He neglected the worship of his ancestors. Wherever he passed, the greater States flew to arms, the smaller ones to places of safety. All the people were sore distressed. "A father," said Confucius to Liu Hsia Chi, "should surely be able to admonish his son; an elder brother to teach his younger brother. If this be not so, there is an end of the value attached to these relationships. "Now you, Sir, are one of the scholars of the age, while your younger brother is the Robber Chê, the scourge of the empire. You are unable to teach him, and I blush for you. Let me go and have a talk with him on your behalf." "As to what you say, Sir, about fathers and elder brothers," answered Liu Hsia Chi, "if the son will not listen to his father, nor the younger brother to his elder brother, what becomes of your arguments then? "Besides, Chê's passions are like a bubbling spring. His thoughts are like a whirlwind. He is strong enough to defy all foes. He can argue until wrong becomes right. If you follow his inclinations, he is pleased. If you oppose them he is angry. He is free with the language of abuse. Do not go near him." pratibha_layers.body: Sit for 3 minutes with natural breathing. At each inhale and exhale, notice awareness before naming experience.

items.resonance: Both texts posit a universal principle (Logos in Heraclitus, the uncarved block or natural way in Chuang Tzu) that operates continuously yet remains imperceptible to ordinary awareness—people fail to recognize what is always already present.
items.divergence: Heraclitus emphasizes the Logos as rational cosmic order that can be intellectually grasped through philosophy; Chuang Tzu suggests the way is accessible only through non-action and forgetting of deliberate knowing.

items.resonance: Both texts warn against exclusive fixation on a single pole (manifest or unmanifest in the Upanishad; the robber's one-sided virtue or the sage's opposite extreme in Chuang Tzu) as a path to error or darkness.
items.divergence: The Isavasya Upanishad frames the problem as metaphysical blindness requiring balanced knowledge of both states; Chuang Tzu frames it as a social-ethical problem where rigid adherence to any single principle corrupts natural awareness.

translation_literal: Of old, Wên Wang of Chao loved sword-play. Swordsmen thronged his halls, to the number of three thousand and more. Day and night they had bouts before the prince. In the course of a year, a hundred or so would be killed or wounded. Yet the prince was never satisfied. Within three years, the State had begun to go to rack and ruin, and other princes to form designs upon it. Thereupon the Heir Apparent, Li, became troubled in mind; and said to the officers of his household, "Whosoever shall persuade the prince to do away with these swordsmen, to him I will give a thousand ounces of silver." To this his officers replied, "Zhuang Zi is the man." Thereupon the Heir Apparent sent messengers to Zhuang Zi with a thousand ounces of silver, which he would not accept, but accompanied the messengers back to their master. "What does your Highness require of me," asked Zhuang Zi, "that you should bestow upon me a thousand ounces?" "I had heard," replied the young prince, "that you were a famous Sage, and I ventured to send this money as a present to your servants. But as you would not receive it, what more can I say?" "I understand," answered Zhuang Zi, "that your Highness would have me cure the prince of his peculiar weakness. Now suppose that I do not succeed with the prince, and consequently with your Highness, the punishment of death is what I have to expect. What good would the thousand ounces be to me then?" "On the other hand, if I succeed with the prince, and consequently with your Highness, the whole State of Chao contains nothing I could not have for the asking." "You must know, however," said the young prince, "that my father will only receive swordsmen." "Well," replied Zhuang Zi, "I am a good swordsman myself." "Besides which," added the Heir Apparent, "the swordsmen he is accustomed to see have all dishevelled hair hanging over their temples. They wear slouching caps with coarse tangled tassels, and short-tailed coats. They glare with their eyes and talk in a fierce tone. This is what my father likes. But if you go to him dressed in your ordinary scholar's dress, the result is sure to be disastrous.

practice: Walk through a space where you normally hurry—a hallway, corridor, or familiar path—and deliberately slow to half-speed, noticing what you usually miss: a crack, a shadow, a sound. As you move, hold the question 'What am I feeding with my attention?' without answering it, letting the passage of Wên Wang's thousand swordsmen move through your body as a warning about what thrives when we fuel it endlessly.

如是三年，國衰，諸侯謀之。

」左右曰：「莊子當能。
」太子乃使人以千金奉莊子。
莊子弗受，與使者俱，往見太子，曰：「太子何以教周，賜周千金？
」太子曰：「聞夫子明聖，謹奉千金以幣從者。
夫子弗受，悝尚何敢言﹗」莊子曰：「聞太子所欲用周者，欲絕王之喜好也。
使臣上說大王而逆王意，下不當太子，則身刑而死，周尚安所事金乎？
使臣上說大王，下當太子，趙國何求而不得也！
」太子曰︰「然。
吾王所見，唯劍士也。
」莊子曰：「諾。
周善為劍。
」太子曰：「然吾王所見劍士，皆蓬頭突鬢，垂冠，曼胡之纓，短後之衣，瞋目而語難，王乃說之。
今夫子必儒服而見王，事必大逆。
」莊子曰：「請治劍服。
」治劍服三日，乃見太子。
太子乃與見王，王脫白刃待之。
莊子入殿門不趨，見王不拜。
王曰：「子欲何以教寡人，使太子先﹖」曰：「臣聞大王喜劍，故以劍見王。
」王曰：「子之劍何能禁制？
」曰：「臣之劍，十步一人，千里不留行。
」王大說，曰：「天下無敵矣﹗」莊子曰：「夫為劍者，示之以虛，開之以利，後之以發，先之以至。
願得試之。
」王曰：「夫子休，就舍待命，令設戲請夫子。
」王乃校劍士七日，死傷者六十餘人，得五六人，使奉劍於殿下，乃召莊子。
王曰：「今日試使士敦劍。
」莊子曰：「望之久矣！
」王曰：「夫子所御杖，長短何如？
」曰：「臣之所奉皆可。
然臣有三劍，唯王所用，請先言而後試。
」王曰：「願聞三劍。
」曰：「有天子劍，有諸侯劍，有庶人劍。
」王曰：「天子之劍何如？
」曰：「天子之劍，以燕谿石城為鋒，齊岱為鍔，晉衛為脊，周宋為鐔，韓魏為夾；
包以四夷，裹以四時；
繞以渤海，帶以常山；
制以五行，論以刑德；
開以陰陽，持以春夏，行以秋冬。
此劍，直之無前，舉之無上，案之無下，運之無旁，上決浮雲，下絕地紀。
此劍一用，匡諸侯，天下服矣。
此天子之劍也。
」文王芒然自失，曰：「諸侯之劍何如？
」曰：「諸侯之劍，以知勇士為鋒，以清廉士為鍔，以賢良士為脊，以忠聖士為鐔，以豪傑士為夾。
此劍，直之亦無前，舉之亦無上，案之亦無下，運之亦無旁；
上法圓天，以順三光，下法方地，以順四時，中和民意，以安四鄉。
此劍一用，如雷霆之震也，四封之內，無不賓服而聽從君命者矣。
此諸侯之劍也。
」王曰：「庶人之劍何如？
」曰：「庶人之劍，蓬頭突鬢，垂冠，曼胡之纓，短後之衣，瞋目而語難，相擊於前，上斬頸領，下決肝肺。
此庶人之劍，無異於鬥雞，一旦命已絕矣，無所用於國事。
今大王有天子之位而好庶人之劍，臣竊為大王薄之。
」王乃牽而上殿。
宰人上食，王三環之。
莊子曰：「大王安坐定氣，劍事已畢奏矣！
」於是文王不出宮三月，劍士皆服斃其處也。

pratibha_layers.body: For 2 minutes, observe inner speech as sound only. Return to the silent awareness that hears it.

items.citation: Tantrasara — Refining Thought – Right Reasoning as Śakti’s Path
items.resonance: Both texts describe a radical cessation of mental elaboration—the sword-play passage implies mastery through the dissolution of deliberate thought, while Śāmbhavopāya names this as 'the flash where everything falls away and only naked awareness remains.' Each treats the disappearance of conceptual mind as the condition for authentic action or realization.
items.divergence: Chuang Tzu frames this through embodied skill and spontaneous response to circumstance, while Tantrasara frames it as a direct non-dual recognition of consciousness itself, making the cessation metaphysically constitutive rather than functionally instrumental.

items.citation: Tilopa Mahamudra — Do Not Contrive, and Wisdom Dawns
items.resonance: Both passages refuse to objectify or grasp their subject through ordinary mental operations—the sword-play master cannot be caught by deliberate thought, and Mahāmudrā 'cannot be pointed to by any symbol' and 'the ordinary mind cannot grasp it as an object.' Each names a reality that eludes the grasping apparatus of conceptual mind.
items.divergence: Chuang Tzu emphasizes the practical paradox of skill (mastery through non-mastery), while Tilopa emphasizes the metaphysical paradox of ultimate reality (it transcends all representation), grounding the elusiveness in different registers.

Of old, Wên Wang of Chao loved sword-play. Swordsmen thronged his halls, to the number of three thousand and more. Day and night they had bouts before the prince. In the course of a year, a hundred or so would be killed or wounded. Yet the prince was never satisfied.

Within three years, the State had begun to go to rack and ruin, and other princes to form designs upon it. Thereupon the Heir Apparent, Li, became troubled in mind; and said to the officers of his household, "Whosoever shall persuade the prince to do away with these swordsmen, to him I will give a thousand ounces of silver."

To this his officers replied, "Chuang Tzŭ is the man."

Thereupon the Heir Apparent sent messengers to Chuang Tzŭ with a thousand ounces of silver, which he would not accept, but accompanied the messengers back to their master.

"What does your Highness require of me," asked Chuang Tzŭ, "that you should bestow upon me a thousand ounces?"

"I had heard," replied the young prince, "that you were a famous Sage, and I ventured to send this money as a present to your servants.

But as you would not receive it, what more can I say?"

"I understand," answered Chuang Tzŭ, "that your Highness would have me cure the prince of his peculiar weakness. Now suppose that I do not succeed with the prince, and consequently with your Highness, the punishment of death is what I have to expect. What good would the thousand ounces be to me then?"

"On the other hand, if I succeed with the prince, and consequently with your Highness, the whole State of Chao contains nothing I could not have for the asking."

"You must know, however," said the young prince, "that my father will only receive swordsmen."

"Well," replied Chuang Tzŭ, "I am a good swordsman myself."

"Besides which," added the Heir Apparent, "the swordsmen he is accustomed to see have all dishevelled hair hanging over their temples. They wear slouching caps with coarse tangled tassels, and short-tailed coats. They glare with their eyes and talk in a fierce tone. This is what my father likes. But if you go to him dressed in your ordinary scholar's dress, the result is sure to be disastrous."

"I will accustom myself to the dress," replied Chuang Tzŭ; and after practising for three days, he went again to see the young prince, who accompanied him into his father's presence.

The latter drew a sharp sword and awaited Chuang Tzŭ's approach. But Chuang Tzŭ, when he entered the door of the audience chamber, did not hurry forward, neither did he prostrate himself before the prince.

"What have you to say to me," cried the prince, "that you have obtained your introduction through the Heir Apparent?"

"I have heard," replied Chuang Tzŭ, "that your Highness loves sword-play. Therefore I have come to exhibit my skill."

"Were I to meet an opponent," said Chuang Tzŭ, "at every ten paces, I could go on for a thousand li without being stopped."

"Bravo!" cried the prince. "There is not your match in the empire."

"When I fight," continued Chuang Tzŭ, "I make a show of being weak but push a vigorous attack. The last to start, I am the first to arrive. I should like your Highness to make trial of me."

"Rest awhile," replied the prince. "Stay here and await orders. I will arrange a day for you."

Thereupon the prince spent seven days in trying his swordsmen. Some sixty of them were either killed or wounded, but at length he selected five or six and bade them attend in the audience-chamber with their swords. He then summoned Chuang Tzŭ and said, "Now I will see what your swordsmanship is worth."

"Does it matter to you," asked the prince, "of what length your weapon may be?"

"Not at all," replied Chuang Tzŭ. "I have three swords, of which I will ask your Highness to choose one. We will then proceed to the trial."

"There is the sword of the Son of Heaven," said Chuang Tzŭ, "the sword of the Princes, and the sword of the People."

"The mountains of Ch'i are its edge. Chin and Wei are its back. Chou and Sung are its hilt. Han and Wei are its sheath. It is enclosed in the four hordes of barbarians, wrapped in the four seasons, surrounded by the great ocean. It is made of the five elements. It is the arbiter of punishment and reward. It operates under the influence of the Yin and the Yang. In spring and summer it is at rest. In autumn and winter it moves abroad. Push it, it does not advance. Raise it, it does not go up. Lower it, it does not go down. Whirl it around, it does not change position. Above, it cleaves the floating clouds; below, it cuts through the density of earth. One flash of this blade, and the princes of the empire submit. Such is the sword of the Son of Heaven."

At this the prince seemed absorbed in his reflections. Then he enquired, saying, "And what is the sword of the Princes?"

"The Wise and brave," replied Chuang Tzŭ, "are its point. The incorruptible are its edge. The virtuous are its back. The loyal are its hilt. The heroic are its sheath. You may push this sword too, it will not advance. Raise it, it will not go up. Lower it, it will not go down. Whirl it around, it will not change position. Above, it models itself upon the round heaven, in order to keep in harmony with the sun, moon, and stars. Below, it models itself upon the square earth, in order to keep in harmony with the four seasons. It adapts itself to the wishes of the people, in order to diffuse peace on all sides. One flash of this blade is like a roaring clap of thunder. Between the boundaries of the State there is not left one but who yields and obeys the command of his prince. Such is the sword of the Princes."

"The sword of the People," replied Chuang Tzŭ, "has dishevelled hair hanging over its temples. It wears a slouching cap with coarse tangled tassel, and a short-tailed coat. It glares with its eyes and talks in a fierce tone. When it engages in conflict, above, it cuts off head and neck; below, it smites liver and lungs. Such is the sword of the People. It is like a game-cock. One day, its life is cut short, and it is of no more use to the State.

"Now you, great prince, wield sovereign power, and yet you devote yourself to this sword of the People. I am truly ashamed of it."

Thereupon the prince drew Chuang Tzŭ up on to the dais, and the attendants served food, the king three times assisting with his own hand.

The prince each time received the dish from the attendants, handed it to Chuang Tzŭ, and then walked round to his own seat again.

"Be seated, great prince," said Chuang Tzŭ, "and compose your mind. I have said all I have to say on swords."

After this the prince did not quit his palace for three months, while the swordsmen, submitting to the new order of things, died in their own homes.

One commentator says "killed themselves in their own dwellings." But if so, Chuang Tzŭ's influence was of small practical value as far as the swordsmen were concerned. They might as well have continued their profession of arms.
abhyasa: Walk through a space where you normally hurry—a hallway, corridor, or familiar path—and deliberately slow to half-speed, noticing what you usually miss: a crack, a shadow, a sound. As you move, hold the question 'What am I feeding with my attention?' without answering it, letting the passage of Wên Wang's thousand swordsmen move through your body as a warning about what thrives when we fuel it endlessly.

translation_literal: Confucius was wandering in the forest of dark curtains and sat down to rest on the Apricot Altar. His disciples were reading their texts while Confucius played the lute and sang. Before the tune was half finished, an old fisherman climbed out of his boat and approached — beard and eyebrows both white, hair loose, sleeves flapping. He walked up the bank and stopped at the edge of the dry ground, left hand resting on his knee, right hand cupping his chin, and listened. When the tune ended, he beckoned to Zigong and Zilu, and both came over. Pointing at Confucius, the stranger asked, 'What sort of man is he?' Zilu answered, 'A gentleman of Lu.' The stranger asked his clan. Zilu said, 'The Kong clan.' The stranger asked, 'And what does this Kong occupy himself with?' Zilu did not reply, so Zigong answered: 'This Kong man is loyal and trustworthy by nature; in his conduct he practices benevolence (rén) and righteousness (yì); he refines ritual and music; he sorts out the proper human relationships. Above he is loyal to the ruler of the age, below he transforms the common people — all to benefit the world. This is what Kong occupies himself with.' The stranger asked further, 'Does he hold land as a lord?' 'No,' said Zigong. 'Is he an advisor to a king or feudal lord?' 'No,' said Zigong. At this the stranger laughed and turned away, saying as he walked: 'Benevolent he may be — but I fear he will not save his own skin. Wearing out his mind and exhausting his body, he endangers what is genuine (zhēn) in him. Alas! Far, far has he drifted from the dào.' Zigong went back and reported to Confucius. Confucius pushed aside his lute and rose. 'Could he be a sage?' he said, and went down to seek him. He reached the edge of the marsh just as the man was about to push off with his pole and pull his boat away. Seeing Confucius, he turned back and stood facing him. Confucius stepped back, bowed twice, and came forward. The stranger said, 'What is it you want?' Confucius said, 'Just now you began to speak and left off. I am unworthy and do not grasp your meaning. I wait humbly downwind, hoping to catch even the sound of your throat-clearing, so as to help me finish my task.' The stranger said, 'Ha! How extreme your love of learning is!' Confucius bowed twice again and rose: 'I have cultivated learning since I was young, up to now — sixty-nine years — and I have never yet heard the ultimate teaching. How could I not empty my mind to it?' The stranger said: 'Like kinds follow one another, like sounds respond to each other — this is simply the pattern of tiān 天. Let me set aside what I hold and go through what you concern yourself with. What you concern yourself with is human affairs. When Son of Heaven, feudal lords, ministers, and common folk — these four — each keep themselves in order, that is the beauty of good governance; when the four leave their places, there is no disorder greater. When officials tend their duties and each person attends to his own task, there is no overstepping. So: fields gone to weeds, roofs leaking, food and clothing insufficient, taxes unpaid, wives and concubines in discord, no order between old and young — these are the worries of a commoner. Abilities unequal to the post, official business unmanaged, conduct not clean, subordinates lax, no fine achievements, rank and salary insecure — these are the worries of a minister. No loyal officials at court, the state fallen into confusion, craftsmen unskilled, tribute goods shoddy, ranking at the seasonal audiences falling behind, disobedience to the Son of Heaven — these are the worries of a feudal lord. Yin and yáng out of harmony, cold and heat coming at wrong times so that all things are harmed, feudal lords violent and rebellious, seizing and attacking one another and ravaging the people, ritual and music unregulated, resources exhausted, human relations undisciplined, the hundred families running wild — these are the worries of the Son of Heaven and his officers. Now you have neither the authority of a ruler, lord, or officer above, nor the office of a great minister below — yet on your own you presume to refine ritual and music and sort out human relations in order to transform the common people. Isn't that meddling in far too much? Moreover, people have eight faults and undertakings have four troubles — these must be examined. To take on affairs that are not yours to take on: this is called overreaching. To push forward when no one has consulted you: this is called sycophancy. To trim your words to a man's wishes: this is called flattery. To speak without weighing right and wrong: this is called toadying. To delight in speaking of others' faults: this is called slander. To break up friendships and estrange kin: this is called wrecking. To praise falsely so as to ruin someone: this is called wickedness. To have no care for good or bad but wear two faces, quietly drawing out what you want: this is called treachery. These eight faults disorder others outside and injure yourself within; the gentleman will not befriend such a man, the enlightened ruler will not make him a minister. As for the four troubles: to love managing great affairs, altering constants, to hang up a reputation — this is called grasping. To monopolize knowledge and act arbitrarily, encroaching on others and relying on yourself — this is called greed. To see your error and not correct it, to grow worse the more you are admonished — this is called stubbornness. To approve only of what agrees with you, and call good things bad when they differ from you — this is called conceit. These are the four troubles. Only when you can drop the eight faults and refrain from the four troubles can you begin to be taught.' Confucius, downcast, sighed, bowed twice, and rose: 'Twice I was driven from Lu; my footprints were wiped out in Wei; a tree was felled over me in Song; I was besieged between Chen and Cai. I do not know what I did wrong — why did these four slanders befall me?' The stranger, his face changing sorrowfully, said: 'How very hard you are to enlighten! There was a man who dreaded his own shadow and hated his own footprints and tried to flee them by running. But the more he lifted his feet the more prints there were, and the faster he ran the more his shadow clung to him. Thinking himself still too slow, he ran faster and faster without stopping, until his strength gave out and he died. He did not know that by resting in the shade he would lose his shadow, and by staying still he would end his footprints. His stupidity was extreme! Now you pore over the space between benevolence and righteousness, examine the boundary of same and different, watch the shifts of motion and stillness, calibrate the measures of giving and taking, order the feelings of liking and disliking, harmonize the pitch of joy and anger — and you are barely escaping ruin. If you carefully cultivated your own person and guarded what is genuine in you, returning things to others, then nothing would burden you. Now instead of cultivating yourself you make demands on others — isn't that looking outward...'
commentary:
This dialogue reverses the usual hierarchy of the Zhuangzi's cast. Confucius, the tireless sage of civilization, is here the pupil, and a nameless old fisherman — hair loose, sleeves flapping, half wild — is the master. The passage dissolves the distinction between the useful busy life and the seemingly idle one. Confucius embodies exhausting usefulness: sixty-nine years of study, ritual reform, moral instruction, wearing out mind and body to 'benefit the world.' The fisherman's verdict is devastating precisely because it is not moral: Confucius is genuinely benevolent, but his frantic doing has drifted him far from the dào and endangers his zhēn 真, his genuine nature. Usefulness pursued anxiously becomes a kind of self-harm.

The fisherman's long catalogue of the eight faults and four troubles looks like a Confucian lecture on virtue, but its point is anti-managerial: nearly every fault is a form of taking on what is not yours — meddling in affairs beyond your station, forcing yourself onto situations that never called for you. Confucius has no official role, yet appoints himself the world's tutor. The teaching is not that ritual is wrong but that self-appointed correction of everyone else is overreach that ruins the corrector.

The parable of the man fleeing his shadow is the crux. The shadow and footprints are consequences that arise from motion itself; you cannot outrun what your own activity generates. The distinction the man cannot see — that the solution lies not in more effort but in the opposite category, shade and stillness — is exactly the distinction Confucius cannot see about his own exiles and misfortunes. His four 'slanders' are footprints of a life spent in relentless intervention. The passage collapses the opposition between problem and solution located in the same register: you do not defeat restlessness with more running, or the burden of managing others by managing harder. The cure is a change of ground — 'rest in the shade,' 'stay still' — cultivate yourself and return things to the people to whom they belong.

Key Terms

**zhēn 真** — The genuine or authentic in a person; one's true, unforced nature, which anxious over-effort damages.
**dào 道** — The Way; here, the natural course one drifts from through frantic intervention in others' affairs.
**rén yì 仁義** — Benevolence and righteousness — the core Confucian virtues, here portrayed as sincere but exhausting and self-endangering when forced onto the world.
practice: Pick one situation today where you are trying to fix or manage someone else — a family member's habit, a coworker's method, a stranger's opinion online. Notice the impulse to intervene, to correct, to improve them. Then deliberately do the fisherman's move: withdraw the effort and turn it inward. Ask only, 'What is actually mine to tend here?' Leave the rest with its owner. Spend the energy you would have spent correcting them on ten quiet minutes of doing nothing — sitting still, like stepping into shade so the shadow disappears. Watch whether the situation you were 'solving' was ever yours to solve at all.

[Spurious.]

Confucius, travelling in the Black Forest, rested awhile at Apricot Altar. His disciples sat down to their books, and he himself played upon the lute and sang.

Half way through the song, an old fisherman stepped out of a boat and advanced towards them. His beard and eyebrows were snowy white. His hair hung loose, and he flapped his long sleeves as he walked over the foreshore. Reaching firm ground, he stood still, and with left hand on his knee and right hand to his ear, listened.

When the song was finished, he beckoned to Tzŭ Kung and Tzŭ Lu, both of whom went to him. Then pointing with his finger, he enquired, saying, "What is that man doing here?"

"He devotes himself," replied Tzŭ Lu, "to loyalty and truth. He practises charity and duty towards his neighbour. He regulates ceremonies and music. He distinguishes the relationships of man. He is loyal to his prince above, a reformer of the masses below. Thus he will be of great service to the whole empire. Such is his occupation."

Then the old man laughed and walked away, saying, "Charity is charity, yet I fear he will not escape the wear of mind and tear of body which imperil the original purity of man. How far, alas, has he wandered from the true path!"

Tzŭ Kung went back and told Confucius, who, laying aside his lute, arose and said, "This man is a Sage!"

Thereupon he followed the old man down the shore, catching him up just as he was drawing in his boat with his staff. Perceiving Confucius, the old man turned round to receive him, at which Confucius stepped back and prostrated himself twice before advancing.

"Just now, venerable Sir," replied Confucius, "you left without finishing your remarks. In my stupidity I cannot make out what you mean. Therefore I have come in the humble hope of hearing any words with which you may deign to help me."

"Well," said the old man, "you are certainly anxious to learn."

At this Confucius prostrated himself twice, and when he got up said, "Yes, I have been a student from my youth upwards until now, the sixty-ninth year of my age. Yet I have never heard the true doctrine, which I am now ready to receive without bias."

This is a law of nature. I will now with your leave apply what I know to what you occupy yourself with,—the affairs of men.

"The Son of Heaven, the princes, the ministers, and the people,—if these four fulfil their proper functions, the result is good government. If they quit their proper places, the result is unutterable confusion. When the officials mind their duties and the people their business, neither is injured by the other.

"Barren land, leaky roofs, want of food and clothing, inability to meet taxation, quarrels of wives and concubines, no precedence between young and old,—such are the sorrows of the people.

"Capacity unequal to one's duties, and inability to carry on routine work, absence of clean-handedness, and carelessness among subordinates, lack of distinction and want of preferment,—such are the sorrows of ministers.

"The Court without loyal ministers and the State in rebellion, the artisan unskilful and the tribute unsatisfactory, the periodical levées unattended and the Son of Heaven displeased,—such are the sorrows of the princes.

"The two great principles of nature working inharmoniously, heat and cold coming at irregular seasons so that men and things suffer, the princes rebellious and fighting among themselves so that the people perish, music and ceremonies ill regulated, wealth dissipated, the relationships of man disregarded, the masses sunk in immorality,—such are the sorrows which fall to the share of the Son of Heaven.

"But now you, Sir, occupying neither the more exalted position of ruler nor performing the subordinate functions of minister, nevertheless take upon yourself to regulate music and ceremonies and to distinguish the relationships of man, in order to reform the masses. Are you not travelling out of your own sphere?

"Further, men have eight blemishes, and there are four things which obstruct business. These should be investigated.

"To give ready assent with a view to worm out the wishes of others, good and bad alike, is to be a hypocrite.

"These eight blemishes cause a man to throw others into confusion and bring injury upon himself. The superior man will not have him for a friend; the enlightened prince will not employ him as his minister.

"To love the conduct of great affairs, and to introduce change into established order with a view to gain reputation,—this is ambition.

"To strive to get all into one's own hands, and to usurp what should be at the disposal of others,—this is greed.

"To know one's faults but not to correct them, to receive admonition but only to plunge deeper,—this is obstinacy.

"To suffer those who are like oneself, but as for those unlike not to credit them with the virtues they really possess,—this is bigotry.

"Such are the four things which obstruct business. And only he who can put aside the above eight and abstain from the above four is fit for instruction."

At this Confucius heaved a sigh of distress. Then having twice prostrated himself, he arose and said, "Twice was I driven from Lu. I was tabooed in Wei. My tree was cut down in Sung. I was surrounded by the Ch'êns and the Ts'ais. I know not what my fault is that I should have suffered these four persecutions."

"There was once a man who was so afraid of his shadow and so disliked his own footsteps that he determined to run away from them. But the oftener he raised his feet the more footsteps he made, and though he ran very hard his shadow never left him. From this he inferred that he went too slowly, and ran as hard as he could without resting, the consequence being that his strength broke down and he died. He was not aware that by going into the shade he would have got rid of his shadow, and that by keeping still he would have put an end to his footsteps. Fool that he was!

"Now you occupy yourself with charity and duty to one's neighbour. You examine into the distinction of like and unlike, the changes of motion and rest, the canons of giving and receiving, the emotions of love and hate, and the restraint of joy and anger. Yet you cannot avoid the calamities you speak of.

"Reverently care for your body. Carefully preserve your natural purity. Leave externals to others. Then you will not be involved. But as it is, instead of improving yourself you are trying to improve other people. Surely this is dealing with the external."

"Then may I enquire," said Confucius in a tone of distress, "what is the original purity?"

"Our original purity," replied the fisherman, "is the perfection of truth unalloyed. Without this, we cannot influence others. Hence, those who weep to order, though they mourn, do not grieve. Those who assume anger, though violent, do not inspire awe. Those who affect friendship, though they smile, are not in unison."

"Real mourning grieves in silence. Real anger awes without expression. Real friendship is unison without the aid of smiles. Our emotions are dependent upon the original purity within; and accordingly we hold the latter in esteem.

"If applied to human affairs, then in serving our parents we are filial, in serving our prince we are loyal, in the banquet hour we are merry, in the hour of mourning we are sad.

"The object of loyalty is successful service; of a banquet, mirth; of mourning, grief; of serving parents, gratifying their wishes. If the service is accomplished, it matters not that no trace remain.

If parents be gratified, it matters not how. If a banquet results in mirth, the accessories are of no importance. If there be real grief in mourning, it matters not what ceremonies may be employed.

"Ceremonial is the invention of man. Our original purity is given to us from God. It is as it is, and cannot be changed. Wherefore the true Sage models himself upon God, and holds his original purity in esteem. He is independent of human exigencies. Fools, however, reverse this. They cannot model themselves upon God, and have to fall back on man. They do not hold original purity in esteem. Consequently they are ever suffering the vicissitudes of mortality, and never reaching the goal. Alas! you, Sir, were early steeped in deceit, and are late in hearing the great doctrine."

Confucius, having again prostrated himself twice, arose and said,

"It has been a godsend to meet you, Sir, to-day. Pray allow me to follow you as your servant, that I may benefit by your teaching. I venture to ask where you live that I may enter upon my duties and learn the great doctrine."

"I have heard," replied the old man, "that if a man is a fit companion, one may travel with him into the uttermost depths of Tao. But that if he is not a fit companion, and does not know Tao, one must avoid his company, that no harm may befall. Excuse me, I must leave you." Thereupon he pushed off his boat, and disappeared among the reeds.

"Yen Yüan then brought up the chariot, and Tzŭ Lu offered the hand-cord to Confucius. But the latter paid no attention. He waited until the ripples on the water had smoothed down and the sound of the punt-pole had died away, before he ventured to get up.

Tzŭ Lu, who was at the side of the chariot, enquired saying, "Master, I have been in your service now for a long time, yet never did I see you treat any man like this. In the presence of a ruler of ten thousand or a thousand chariots, I have never seen you treated other than with great respect, while you yourself would wear a haughty air. Yet before this old fisherman, leaning on his punt-pole, you cringe and bow and prostrate yourself twice before answering. Is not this too much? The disciples do not know what to make of it. Why this behaviour to an old fisherman?"

"Yu!" cried Confucius, resting on the bar of the chariot; "it is difficult to make anything of you. You have long studied ceremonies and duty to your neighbour, yet you have not succeeded in getting rid of the old evil nature. Come here, and I will tell you.

"To meet an elder without respect is want of ceremony. To see a Sage and not to honour him, is not to be in charity with man. Unless you are in charity with man, you cannot humble yourself before a fellow-creature. And unless you can honestly do this, you can never attain to that state of original purity; but the body will constantly suffer. Alas! there is no greater evil than not to be in charity with man. Yet in such a plight, O Yu, are you.

"Further. Tao is the source of all creation. Men have it, and live. They lose it, and die. Affairs in antagonism thereto, fail; in accordance therewith, succeed. Therefore, wherever Tao abides, there is the reverence of the true Sage. And as this old fisherman may be said to possess Tao, could I venture not to respect him?"
abhyasa: Pick one situation today where you are trying to fix or manage someone else — a family member's habit, a coworker's method, a stranger's opinion online. Notice the impulse to intervene, to correct, to improve them. Then deliberately do the fisherman's move: withdraw the effort and turn it inward. Ask only, 'What is actually mine to tend here?' Leave the rest with its owner. Spend the energy you would have spent correcting them on ten quiet minutes of doing nothing — sitting still, like stepping into shade so the shadow disappears. Watch whether the situation you were 'solving' was ever yours to solve at all.

translation: Confucius was wandering in the forest of dark curtains and sat down to rest on the Apricot Altar. His disciples were reading their texts while Confucius played the lute and sang. Before the tune was half finished, an old fisherman climbed out of his boat and approached — beard and eyebrows both white, hair loose, sleeves flapping. He walked up the bank and stopped at the edge of the dry ground, left hand resting on his knee, right hand cupping his chin, and listened. When the tune ended, he beckoned to Zigong and Zilu, and both came over. Pointing at Confucius, the stranger asked, 'What sort of man is he?' Zilu answered, 'A gentleman of Lu.' The stranger asked his clan. Zilu said, 'The Kong clan.' The stranger asked, 'And what does this Kong occupy himself with?' Zilu did not reply, so Zigong answered: 'This Kong man is loyal and trustworthy by nature; in his conduct he practices benevolence (rén) and righteousness (yì); he refines ritual and music; he sorts out the proper human relationships. Above he is loyal to the ruler of the age, below he transforms the common people — all to benefit the world. This is what Kong occupies himself with.' The stranger asked further, 'Does he hold land as a lord?' 'No,' said Zigong. 'Is he an advisor to a king or feudal lord?' 'No,' said Zigong. At this the stranger laughed and turned away, saying as he walked: 'Benevolent he may be — but I fear he will not save his own skin. Wearing out his mind and exhausting his body, he endangers what is genuine (zhēn) in him. Alas! Far, far has he drifted from the dào.' Zigong went back and reported to Confucius. Confucius pushed aside his lute and rose. 'Could he be a sage?' he said, and went down to seek him. He reached the edge of the marsh just as the man was about to push off with his pole and pull his boat away. Seeing Confucius, he turned back and stood facing him. Confucius stepped back, bowed twice, and came forward. The stranger said, 'What is it you want?' Confucius said, 'Just now you began to speak and left off. I am unworthy and do not grasp your meaning. I wait humbly downwind, hoping to catch even the sound of your throat-clearing, so as to help me finish my task.' The stranger said, 'Ha! How extreme your love of learning is!' Confucius bowed twice again and rose: 'I have cultivated learning since I was young, up to now — sixty-nine years — and I have never yet heard the ultimate teaching. How could I not empty my mind to it?' The stranger said: 'Like kinds follow one another, like sounds respond to each other — this is simply the pattern of tiān 天. Let me set aside what I hold and go through what you concern yourself with. What you concern yourself with is human affairs. When Son of Heaven, feudal lords, ministers, and common folk — these four — each keep themselves in order, that is the beauty of good governance; when the four leave their places, there is no disorder greater. When officials tend their duties and each person attends to his own task, there is no overstepping. So: fields gone to weeds, roofs leaking, food and clothing insufficient, taxes unpaid, wives and concubines in discord, no order between old and young — these are the worries of a commoner. Abilities unequal to the post, official business unmanaged, conduct not clean, subordinates lax, no fine achievements, rank and salary insecure — these are the worries of a minister. No loyal officials at court, the state fallen into confusion, craftsmen unskilled, tribute goods shoddy, ranking at the seasonal audiences falling behind, disobedience to the Son of Heaven — these are the worries of a feudal lord. Yin and yáng out of harmony, cold and heat coming at wrong times so that all things are harmed, feudal lords violent and rebellious, seizing and attacking one another and ravaging the people, ritual and music unregulated, resources exhausted, human relations undisciplined, the hundred families running wild — these are the worries of the Son of Heaven and his officers. Now you have neither the authority of a ruler, lord, or officer above, nor the office of a great minister below — yet on your own you presume to refine ritual and music and sort out human relations in order to transform the common people. Isn't that meddling in far too much? Moreover, people have eight faults and undertakings have four troubles — these must be examined. To take on affairs that are not yours to take on: this is called overreaching. To push forward when no one has consulted you: this is called sycophancy. To trim your words to a man's wishes: this is called flattery. To speak without weighing right and wrong: this is called toadying. To delight in speaking of others' faults: this is called slander. To break up friendships and estrange kin: this is called wrecking. To praise falsely so as to ruin someone: this is called wickedness. To have no care for good or bad but wear two faces, quietly drawing out what you want: this is called treachery. These eight faults disorder others outside and injure yourself within; the gentleman will not befriend such a man, the enlightened ruler will not make him a minister. As for the four troubles: to love managing great affairs, altering constants, to hang up a reputation — this is called grasping. To monopolize knowledge and act arbitrarily, encroaching on others and relying on yourself — this is called greed. To see your error and not correct it, to grow worse the more you are admonished — this is called stubbornness. To approve only of what agrees with you, and call good things bad when they differ from you — this is called conceit. These are the four troubles. Only when you can drop the eight faults and refrain from the four troubles can you begin to be taught.' Confucius, downcast, sighed, bowed twice, and rose: 'Twice I was driven from Lu; my footprints were wiped out in Wei; a tree was felled over me in Song; I was besieged between Chen and Cai. I do not know what I did wrong — why did these four slanders befall me?' The stranger, his face changing sorrowfully, said: 'How very hard you are to enlighten! There was a man who dreaded his own shadow and hated his own footprints and tried to flee them by running. But the more he lifted his feet the more prints there were, and the faster he ran the more his shadow clung to him. Thinking himself still too slow, he ran faster and faster without stopping, until his strength gave out and he died. He did not know that by resting in the shade he would lose his shadow, and by staying still he would end his footprints. His stupidity was extreme! Now you pore over the space between benevolence and righteousness, examine the boundary of same and different, watch the shifts of motion and stillness, calibrate the measures of giving and taking, order the feelings of liking and disliking, harmonize the pitch of joy and anger — and you are barely escaping ruin. If you carefully cultivated your own person and guarded what is genuine in you, returning things to others, then nothing would burden you. Now instead of cultivating yourself you make demands on others — isn't that looking outward...'

pratibha_layers.body:
孔子遊乎緇帷之林，休坐乎杏壇之上。
弟子讀書，孔子弦歌鼓琴。
奏曲未半。
有漁父者，下船而來，須眉交白，被髮揄袂，行原以上，距陸而止，左手據膝，右手持頤以聽。
曲終而招子貢、子路，二人俱對。
客指孔子曰：「彼何為者也？
」子路對曰：「魯之君子也。
」客問其族。
子路對曰：「族孔氏。
」客曰：「孔氏者何治也？
」子路未應，子貢對曰：「孔氏者，性服忠信，身行仁義，飾禮樂，選人倫，上以忠於世主，下以化於齊民，將以利天下。
此孔氏之所治也。
」又問曰：「有土之君與？
」子貢曰：「非也。
」「侯王之佐與？
」子貢曰：「非也。
」客乃笑而還，行言曰：「仁則仁矣，恐不免其身；
苦心勞形以危其真。
嗚呼！
遠哉，其分於道也﹗」子貢還，報孔子。
孔子推琴而起，曰：「其聖人與﹗」乃下求之，至於澤畔，方將杖拏而引其船，顧見孔子，還鄉而立。
孔子反走，再拜而進。
客曰：「子將何求？
」孔子曰：「曩者先生有緒言而去，丘不肖，未知所謂，竊待於下風，幸聞咳唾之音，以卒相丘也﹗」客曰：「嘻！
甚矣，子之好學也！
」孔子再拜而起，曰：「丘少而修學，以至於今，六十九歲矣，無所得聞至教，敢不虛心！
」客曰：「同類相從，同聲相應，固天之理也。
吾請釋吾之所有而經子之所以。
子之所以者，人事也。
天子諸侯大夫庶人，此四者自正，治之美也；
四者離位而亂莫大焉。
官治其職，人憂其事，乃無所陵。
故田荒室露，衣食不足，征賦不屬，妻妾不和，長少無序，庶人之憂也；
能不勝任，官事不治，行不清白，群下荒怠，功美不有，爵祿不持，大夫之憂也；
廷無忠臣，國家昏亂，工技不巧，貢職不美，春秋後倫，不順天子，諸侯之憂也；
陰陽不和，寒暑不時，以傷庶物，諸侯暴亂，擅相攘伐，以殘民人，禮樂不節，財用窮匱，人倫不飭，百姓淫亂，天子有司之憂也。
今子既上無君侯有司之勢，而下無大臣職事之官，而擅飾禮樂，選人倫，以化齊民，不泰多事乎？
且人有八疵，事有四患，不可不察也。
非其事而事之，謂之摠；
莫之顧而進之，謂之佞；
希意道言，謂之諂；
不擇是非而言，謂之諛；
好言人之惡，謂之讒；
析交離親，謂之賊；
稱譽詐偽以敗惡人，謂之慝；
不擇善否，兩容頰適，偷拔其所欲，謂之險。
此八疵者，外以亂人，內以傷身，君子不友，明君不臣。
所謂四患者：好經大事，變更易常，以挂功名，謂之叨；
專知擅事，侵人自用，謂之貪；
見過不更，聞諫愈甚，謂之很；
人同於己則可，不同於己，雖善不善，謂之矜。
此四患也。
能去八疵，無行四患，而始可教已。
孔子愀然而嘆，再拜而起，曰：「丘再逐於魯，削跡於衛，伐樹於宋，圍於陳蔡。
丘不知所失，而離此四謗者何也？
」客淒然變容曰：「甚矣，子之難悟也！
人有畏影惡跡而去之走者，舉足愈數而跡愈多，走愈疾而影不離身，自以為尚遲，疾走不休，絕力而死。
不知處陰以休影，處靜以息跡，愚亦甚矣！
子審仁義之間，察同異之際，觀動靜之變，適受與之度，理好惡之情，和喜怒之節，而幾於不免矣。
謹修而身，慎守其真，還以物與人，則無所累矣。
今不修身而求之人，不亦外

pratibha_layers.label: Pratibha Translation
pratibha_layers.body: Confucius, travelling in the Black Forest, rested awhile at Apricot Altar. His disciples sat down to their books, and he himself played upon the lute and sang. Half way through the song, an old fisherman stepped out of a boat and advanced towards them. His beard and eyebrows were snowy white. His hair hung loose, and he flapped his long sleeves as he walked over the foreshore. Reaching firm ground, he stood still, and with left hand on his knee and right hand to his ear, listened. When the song was finished, he beckoned to Zi Kung and Zi Lu, both of whom went to him. Then pointing with his finger, he inquired, saying, "What is that man doing here?" "He devotes himself," replied Zi Lu, "to loyalty and truth. He practises charity and duty towards his neighbour. He regulates ceremonies and music. He distinguishes the relationships of man. He is loyal to his prince above, a reformer of the masses below. Thus he will be of great service to the whole empire. Such is his occupation." Then the old man laughed and walked away, saying, "Charity is charity, yet I fear he will not escape the wear of mind and tear of body which imperil the original purity of man. How far, alas, has he wandered from the true path!" Zi Kung went back and told Confucius, who, laying aside his lute, arose and said, "This man is a Sage!" Thereupon he followed the old man down the shore, catching him up just as he was drawing in his boat with his staff. Perceiving Confucius, the old man turned round to receive him, at which Confucius stepped back and prostrated himself twice before advancing. "Just now, venerable Sir," replied Confucius, "you left without finishing your remarks. In my stupidity I cannot make out what you mean. Therefore I have come in the humble hope of hearing any words with which you may deign to help me." "Well," said the old man, "you are certainly anxious to learn." At this Confucius prostrated himself twice, and when he got up said, "Yes, I have been a student from my youth upwards until now, the sixty-ninth year of my age. Yet I have never heard the true doctrine, which I am now ready to receive without bias." This is a law of nature. I will now with your leave apply what I know to what you occupy yourself with,—the affairs of men.

pratibha_layers.body: Chapter 31 (The Old Fisherman.) in Giles's 1889 rendering. Pratibha treats the chapter as a philosophical movement: read the anchor appendix for the full Victorian translation, then the Pratibha translation for a modern, source-honest excerpt. Full chapter text remains in the public-domain appendix for philological comparison; the display layers do not reproduce Giles wholesale.

items.definition: 自然 “self-so” — thus-of-itself, not “picturesque nature” -> in this passage (the Old Fisherman.), spontaneous so-ness: things unfolding without forced contrivance -> trap: Romantic wilderness aesthetics; zìrán is ontological non-forcing, not scenery

無 “without” + 為 “contrived doing” — action without aggressive interference -> in this passage (the Old Fisherman.), unforced congruence with conditions: skill that does not obstruct the work -> trap: “non-action” as passivity; wúwéi can be highly skilled activity without strain

道 “path/way” and “to speak/guide” — course that can be walked and barely named -> in this passage (the Old Fisherman.), the nameless source-and-course that lets beings move by their own measure -> trap: a deity named Tao, a lifestyle brand, or a fixed doctrine one can possess

心 “heart-mind” — thought, feeling, and responsiveness undivided -> in this passage (the Old Fisherman.), the heart-mind to be emptied, still, or freed from right/wrong warfare -> trap: brain-only “mind” or sentimental “heart”; xīn is the whole affective-cognitive center

pratibha_layers.body: For 2 minutes, observe inner speech as sound only. Return to the silent awareness that hears it.

items.citation: Tao Te Ching — The Paradox of Governance
items.resonance: Both texts model sage-awareness as a receptive attunement that shapes circumstance through non-action: the Fisherman's rest at Apricot Altar embodies the Taoist principle that the ruler's (or sage's) relaxed state directly conditions the simplicity of those around him, not through command but through presence.
items.divergence: Chuang Tzu emphasizes the sage's effortless integration into the Way through wandering and rest; the Tao Te Ching frames this as a political technology of governance, grounding the same principle in ruler-subject dynamics.

items.citation: Mandukya Upanishad and Gaudapada Karika — Verse 12 · The Silence — Turīya as Amātrā
items.resonance: Both passages point toward a state of awareness that transcends ordinary categories and practical engagement: the Fisherman's resting awareness parallels Turīya as the fourth state 'without measure' and 'beyond practical dealings'—a consciousness that is neither active nor passive but foundational.
items.divergence: The Mandukya locates this state within a metaphysical hierarchy of consciousness (waking, dream, deep sleep, Turīya); Chuang Tzu presents it as the natural condition of the sage already present in the world, not a transcendent fourth term.

title: Lieh Tzŭ.
thesis: Chapter 32 (Lieh Tzŭ.) in Giles's 1889 rendering.

His record is not given by the historian Ssŭ-ma Ch'ien, and he may well have been no more than an allegorical personage created by Chuang Tzŭ for purposes of illustration. translation_literal:
Lie Yukou was traveling to Qi but turned back halfway, and ran into Bohun Wuren. Bohun Wuren asked, "Why have you turned back?" Lie Yukou said, "Something alarmed me." "What alarmed you?" "I stopped to eat at ten soup-stalls, and at five of them I was served before anyone else." Bohun Wuren said, "If that's all, why should it alarm you?" Lie Yukou replied, "When the inner sincerity is not dissolved, it leaks out through the body as a kind of radiance, and with this outer glow one dominates other people's hearts, making them slight even the honored and the aged — and this stirs up trouble. Now these soup-sellers only deal in food and broth, with no great surplus of profit. Their gain is thin, their influence slight, and yet they treated me like this. How much more would the ruler of a state of ten thousand chariots! With his body worn out for the country and his mind spent on affairs, he would load duties on me and demand results. That is what alarmed me." Bohun Wuren said, "A fine observation! But even if you settle yourself down, people will still cling to you."

Not long after, Bohun Wuren went to visit, and the space outside the door was full of shoes. He stood facing north, planted his staff, and pressed his chin against it. After standing there a while he left without a word. The doorkeeper reported this to Liezi, who grabbed his shoes and ran out barefoot, catching up at the gate. He said, "Sir, now that you've come, won't you give me some medicine?" Bohun Wuren said, "Enough. I already told you people would flock to you, and sure enough they have. It is not that you can make people gather to you, but that you cannot make them not gather to you. What use is all this stirring, this rushing out to show yourself as different? You are bound to be moved, shaken at your very root — and there's nothing to be said for it. Those who wander with you will not warn you. Their petty words are all poison to a man. None of them wakes, none realizes — so how could they ripen one another? The skillful toil and the clever worry, while the one without ability seeks nothing: he eats his fill and roams free, drifting like an unmoored boat — empty, and wandering."

There was a man of Zheng named Huan who chanted and studied in the region of the Qiu clan. In just three years Huan became a Confucian scholar. Like a river he enriched the land for nine li around, his bounty reaching three branches of kin, and he made his younger brother a Mohist. Confucian and Mohist argued with each other, and the father sided with the younger brother, the Mohist. After ten years Huan killed himself. His father dreamed of him, who said, "It was I who made your son a Mohist. Why have you never looked at my grave? I have already become the fruit of the autumn cypress." When the Maker repays a man, he does not repay the man himself but the tiān 天 (heavenly nature) in him — it was that heavenly source that made the brother what he was. But Huan took himself to be different from others, and so he despised his own kin — like the people of Qi who grab each other by the well they drink from. So it is said: everyone in the present age is a Huan. From this we see that those with dé 德 (inner power) act as if they know nothing — how much more those who have the dào! The ancients called this "the punishment for fleeing from Heaven."

The sage rests in what is restful to him and does not rest in what is not; ordinary people rest in what is not restful and cannot rest in what is. Zhuangzi said, "To know the dào is easy; not to speak of it is hard. To know and not speak — this is the way to Heaven. To know and speak — this is the way to the human. The ancients were heavenly, not human."

Zhu Pingman studied dragon-butchering under Zhili Yi, exhausting his family fortune of a thousand pieces of gold. After three years he mastered the craft, but there was nowhere to use his skill. The sage treats the necessary as unnecessary, and so has no weapons; ordinary people treat the unnecessary as necessary, and so have many weapons. Following the way of weapons, their actions are full of demands. To rely on weapons is to perish.

The knowledge of the small man never gets beyond gifts and letters; he wears out his spirit on shallow, petty things, yet wants to save both the dào and the world at once, to unify the formless in the Great One. Such a man is bewildered by the cosmos, burdened by form, unaware of the Great Beginning. But the perfected person returns his spirit to the beginningless and sleeps sweetly in the village of Nothing-Whatever. His water flows in the formless and pours forth into the Great Clarity. How sad — that you spend your knowledge on the tip of a hair and know nothing of the Great Peace!

A man of Song named Cao Shang was sent as envoy from the king of Song to Qin. On departure he was given several carriages; the king of Qin was pleased with him and gave him a hundred more. Returning to Song, he saw Zhuangzi and said, "Living in some narrow back-alley, weaving sandals in poverty, neck shriveled and face sallow — that is where I'm no good. But winning over the ruler of ten thousand chariots at a stroke and coming home with a hundred carriages — that is what I'm good at." Zhuangzi said, "When the king of Qin is ill and summons his doctors, whoever lances a boil or drains an abscess gets one carriage, and whoever licks his piles gets five — the lower the thing you treat, the more carriages you get. Did you perhaps treat his piles? How else so many carriages? Now be off with you!"

Duke Ai of Lu asked Yan He, "If I make Confucius the mainstay of my state, will it be cured?" Yan He replied, "Danger! Confucius is close to ruin. He would decorate feathers and paint over them, busy himself with flowery words, take the branches for the trunk, force human nature to make a show before the people — not knowing that this cannot inspire trust. It takes hold in the heart, rules over the spirit — how could such a man be fit to govern people? Does he suit you? Would you nourish him? It is a mistake either way. To make people abandon the real and study the false is no way to guide them; thinking of later generations, better to let it drop. It is hard to govern that way."

To do a kindness and not forget it is not the way Heaven bestows. Even merchants disdain such a person; and though in business they may deal with him, in spirit they hold him in contempt. External punishments are inflicted by metal and wood; internal punishments come from agitation and excess. When the petty man suffers external punishment, metal and wood interrogate him; when he suffers internal punishment, the yīn and yáng consume him. Only the True Person can escape both external and internal punishment. Confucius said, "The human heart is more treacherous than mountains and rivers, harder to know than Heaven."
commentary:
This chapter is a chain of anecdotes, and the loose thread running through them is the danger of visibility — of being marked as special, useful, and impressive. Lie Yukou's alarm over the soup-stalls is the hinge. He notices that mere soup-sellers, people with no real stake, jostle to serve him first. Why? Because his inner intensity "leaks out as radiance" and unconsciously commands attention. He has not done anything; his presence itself is doing the work. Bohun Wuren's diagnosis dissolves the ordinary distinction between what we deliberately project and what we cannot help projecting: you cannot make people gather, but neither can you make them not gather. The self we think we control is already broadcasting, and the more we cultivate an impressive inner life, the louder the broadcast. This is why the whole chapter keeps returning to the unmoored boat, the person who seeks nothing — not because seeking nothing is a technique for success, but because only the one who casts no distinctive shadow is genuinely free.

The surrounding stories all torque the same distinction between real worth and its appearances. Huan the scholar produces genuine benefit — his learning "enriches the land for nine li" — yet he claims the credit as his own doing, insists he is different from his brother, and destroys his family. The text's blunt judgment is that the Maker rewards the tiān in a person, the heavenly nature working through them, not the ego that steps forward to take the bow. Dragon-butchering — a perfect skill for a beast that does not exist — is the reductio: mastery detached from any real ground is the most expensive form of vanity. Cao Shang's carriages complete the picture with savage comedy: prestige extracted by degrading yourself before power is, Zhuangzi says flatly, a matter of how filthy the wound you were willing to lick. The lower you stoop, the higher the reward — which inverts the whole scale of value the worldly man is boasting about.

What dissolves, then, is the fixed opposition between success and failure, use and uselessness. The chapter refuses to let "being recognized" count as a good. Recognition is exposure; skill is a liability if it makes you sought after; even virtue, in the true adept, hides itself and acts "as if knowing nothing." The final image of external and internal punishment names the two ways this exposure destroys a person: the visible self gets caught by law and force (metal and wood), while the agitated inner self is eaten from within by its own excess (yīn and yáng). Only the True Person, who has withdrawn from the whole economy of standing out, escapes both. This is not passivity — it is the refusal to convert one's genuine nature into a performance that other people can grip.

Key Terms

**遁天之刑 (dùn tiān zhī xíng)** — "The punishment for fleeing Heaven" — the self-inflicted ruin that follows from claiming as one's own ego what is really the working of one's heavenly nature.
**真人 (zhēn rén)** — The True or authentic person, who escapes both outer and inner punishment by not converting their nature into a display.
**無何有之鄉 (wú hé yǒu zhī xiāng)** — "The village of Nothing-Whatever" — the imageless, ungrasped state where the perfected person rests their spirit.
practice: For one day, run an experiment in un-signaling. Pick a setting where you normally, even slightly, try to make an impression — a meeting, a group chat, a conversation with someone you want to think well of you. Before you speak or post, notice the small impulse to be seen as clever, competent, generous, or right, and simply decline to act on it once. Let the good remark go unsaid, the correction unmade, the credit unclaimed. Watch what happens in your own body: often you'll feel a surprising pressure, the "leaking radiance" Bohun Wuren describes, the felt need to broadcast. That pressure is exactly the thing the passage points at. You are not trying to become invisible or falsely modest — you are learning to feel the difference between doing something and displaying it, so that your worth can rest in the doing and stop recruiting an audience to confirm it.
